arxiv-2601-22878:
Rajini Makam and four co-authors present DIVER, a method for cleaning up underwater photos. Underwater images fade and blur because water absorbs colors unevenly, scatters light, and lights scenes poorly. These problems shift with water type and depth, so one fixed fix rarely works.

DIVER blends hands-on corrections with a physics-guided model, and it learns without labeled examples. The design aims to work across many waters, not just the ones it trained on. Clearer images help divers, biologists, and robots inspect reefs, wrecks, and pipelines. The method is unsupervised, so it needs no hand-cleaned example images, which are almost impossible to gather underwater.
arxiv-2601-22978:
Jonathan Baumann and co-authors build a verified defense against speculative control-flow attacks. These attacks, of the Spectre family, trick a processor into leaking data while it guesses ahead. Their defense, SpecIBT, joins hardware control-flow checks with compiler-added hardening for risky loads.

The key insight is that hardware checks can flag exactly when a guess went wrong, so hardening applies only then. The whole defense is formally verified, meaning its safety is proved, not just tested. Proved defenses matter for chips that guard secrets. Compiler-inserted hardening is applied with precision, guided by exactly where the hardware protection says speculation went wrong.
arxiv-2601-23078:
Timo Feistl, Severin Schraven, and Simone Warzel prove symmetry-protection theorems for quantum lattice systems. The classic Mermin-Wagner result limits which symmetries can break in low dimensions. Their version covers systems with multipole symmetries, symmetries tied to higher moments of charge.

They show that higher-order symmetries protect lower-order ones from breaking. In particular, charge symmetry needs more dimensions to break when multipole symmetries are present. Such theorems set firm rules for what phases of quantum matter can exist. Higher multipole symmetries raise the critical dimension for breaking the charge symmetry, a concrete, checkable consequence.
arxiv-2601-23178:
Chenxi Kong, Michael Gurnis, and Zachary E. Ross run mantle convection both forward and backward with neural operators. Reconstructing the mantle's past thermal state means reversing convection, which is an important but very costly computation. Those reconstructions link seismic images with what we see at the surface.

Neural operators learn the convection mapping itself, making repeated runs far cheaper. Fast forward and inverse runs let geophysicists test many Earth histories against data. That speed could clarify how plates, plumes, and the deep Earth evolved. Seismic tomographic images supply the observations the reconstructions must respect, tying deep structure to present-day measurements.
arxiv-2602-02578:
Baktiar Wasir Farooq and 3 co-authors release a small, open code for three-flavor neutrino oscillation studies, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Neutrinos switch among three flavors as they travel, and the pattern depends on a phase tied to CP violation, the matter-antimatter asymmetry in particle physics. Large toolkits simulate experiments, but their bulk hides the equations.

NeutrinoOsc3Flavor solves the Schrödinger evolution equation directly in the flavor basis. It builds and diagonalizes the effective Hamiltonian in plain view, in both vacuum and constant-density matter, using only NumPy. A separate analytic check computes the matter-modified eigenvalues by the Cardano method and agrees closely with the numerical route. The phase dependence itself serves as a sharp check on numerical stability. The authors aim the tool at checking, teaching, and benchmarking rather than full experiment simulation.
arxiv-2602-02778:
Hao Meng and 2 co-authors weigh the dark matter halos hosting the universe's earliest quasars by measuring how strongly those quasars cluster, in a 2026 paper. The sample combines over twelve hundred spectroscopically confirmed quasars with over eight hundred machine-learning-selected candidates, all near the end of cosmic reionization.

Projected clustering gives large bias values in two redshift slices, translating into characteristic halo masses around ten to the twelfth point six solar masses. Quasar duty cycles come out near one percent in both slices. Only a small fraction of suitable halos host a luminous quasar at any moment. That scarcity suggests much supermassive black hole growth happens during obscured accretion phases, hidden from optical view. The measurements agree with earlier studies and the known duty-cycle relation, tightening constraints on how black holes and large-scale structure grew up together.
arxiv-2602-02878:
Junyi Jessy Li and 4 co-authors describe a new university course in a 2026 paper. The course joins discourse, the study of how language holds together across sentences, with natural language generation. Large language models have changed both fields, yet textbooks rarely connect discourse theory to long-form generation.

The team taught the course first in fall 2025 to advanced undergraduates. It was cross-listed between linguistics and computer science. Lessons mix theory with hands-on exploration, in class and in assignments. The paper details the design and reports survey feedback from an independent survey. It closes with lessons learned and plans for future versions of the course.
arxiv-2602-03078:
Four magnetars are tracked over seven years by Han-Long Peng and 11 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Magnetars are neutron stars with extreme magnetic fields, appearing as anomalous X-ray pulsars or soft gamma-ray repeaters. The team monitored four anomalous pulsars with the NICER telescope from twenty seventeen to twenty twenty-four, watching their rotation timing for sudden changes in spin behavior.

Ten timing events were identified in total. They include glitches, sudden spin-ups, anti-glitches, sudden spin-downs, and one unusual state transition. One source showed both anti-glitches, with hints of regular pulse profile evolution. Another continued to show frequent timing anomalies and underwent the state transition. Pulse profiles of two sources evolved over time, consistent with profile change being a generic magnetar feature.
arxiv-2602-03478:
Routing a question to a small cheap model or a large expensive one is supposed to save money. Guannan Lai and Han-Jia Ye document a failure of that idea in a 2026 paper. As budgets grow, routers default to the priciest model even when a cheaper one would do. They name this failure routing collapse, and it quietly wastes computation.

The authors trace the problem to a mismatch between training and decisions. Routers learn to predict scalar scores, but routing is a discrete comparison, so small scoring errors flip the ranking. Their EquiRouter learns model rankings directly instead. On RouterBench it reaches GPT-4-level quality at roughly 17 percent lower cost than the strongest earlier router.
arxiv-2602-03778:
Safety-critical control cares about the worst tail of outcomes, not the average, and that preference breaks the usual Bellman machinery. Aneri Muni and 4 co-authors repair it for conditional value-at-risk objectives in a 2026 paper. Static CVaR depends on whole trajectories, so naive state augmentation produces sparse rewards and degenerate fixed points.

Their reformulated augmentation yields a Bellman operator with dense per-step rewards. The operator contracts on the full space of bounded value functions, a cleaner foundation than earlier restricted versions. On top of it they build risk-averse value iteration and model-free Q-learning over discretized augmented states, with convergence guarantees and discretization error bounds. Experiments show the algorithms learn genuinely CVaR-sensitive policies.
arxiv-2602-03978:
Transparent reasoning may come free during training, or not. Zidi Xiong and 2 co-authors test when chain-of-thought traces truly reveal a model's internal work. Their 2026 study follows reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards across model families and training domains.

Monitorability improved in some settings but not everywhere. Data diversity and instruction-following data proved key. Clearer traces also did not track stronger performance; openness and skill moved independently. Mechanistic analysis credits sharper response distributions and closer attention to the prompt, not deeper reliance on the trace itself. The warning for safety checkers: do not assume readable traces mean honest ones.
arxiv-2602-04078:
Róisín Luo's 2026 doctoral thesis asks why neural networks resist small attacks and generalize to new data. The central tool is Lipschitz continuity, a bound on how much a network's output can change when its input changes slightly. That worst-case sensitivity governs both robustness and generalization in theory.

Earlier work mostly used Lipschitz ideas through empirical regularization tricks. Luo instead pursues the underlying principles directly, asking what the bound means for how networks should be designed and trained. The thesis aims to turn a widely used constraint into understood science, so robustness can be engineered rather than stumbled upon.
arxiv-2602-04178:
Coordinated gene programs across cell types drive development and immunity. Qi Xu and 2 co-authors estimate those multi-cellular programs with Sparse Group PCA in a 2026 paper. Existing methods are heavy to run and weak in power on huge expression datasets.

Their double-thresholding algorithm alternates between picking gene groups and picking active cell types within them, inside a power iteration. Cost grows only linearly with data size. Theory backs the estimator with guarantees on the components recovered. Group sparsity mirrors biology: whole pathways switch on, but only in the cell types where the program runs.
arxiv-2602-04278:
Training recommenders with reinforcement learning burns data most of which teaches little. Lin Wang and 6 co-authors present MiniRec, a data selection framework tailored to that setting, in a 2026 paper. Generic selection criteria based on loss or coverage misalign with how reinforcement learning actually improves.

MiniRec prunes samples that are too easy or hopelessly hard, judging learnability from reward signals. It keeps samples whose gradients align with the ideal global update direction, and enforces diversity. The goal is a small training set that drives real updates. Data-efficient training matters because language-model recommenders are expensive to tune at full scale.
arxiv-2602-04378:
The Frank-Wolfe algorithm cannot beat a certain speed on strongly convex problems, and Jannis Halbey and 5 co-authors prove it. Their 2026 paper constructs a lower bound matching the known guarantee when both objective and constraint set are smooth and strongly convex.

Extra assumptions about the optimizer's position allow faster linear convergence, but uniform improvement was in doubt. The authors study a strongly convex quadratic over the Euclidean ball with the optimizer on the boundary. A computational approach constructs worst-case trajectories, guiding an analytic proof. The matching bounds close the question: in this regime, Frank-Wolfe's classical rate is exactly right.
arxiv-2602-04678:
Forecasters need not only a best guess but also an honest range of uncertainty. Zhen Zhou and 5 co-authors build a multi-expert forecasting framework in a 2026 paper that predicts full probability distributions for time series instead of single values.

One variant uses several experts with different learned parameters to capture diverse temporal patterns. Another splits a series into interpretable parts: trend, seasonality, sudden changes, and volatility, each handled by specialized sub-experts. A distance measure between distributions drives the learning. On sales data from a major forecasting dataset, the continuous multi-expert version performed best overall. The pattern-aware version added interpretability through component-by-component analysis.
arxiv-2603-01578:
Quantum programs must be mapped onto real chips, where each chip wires its qubits in its own layout. Gabrielius Keibas and Linas Petkevicius present a shared test frame for that mapping job in this 2026 work. Many mapping methods exist, but no common frame compared them fairly across chips and circuits.

Their open-source frame, QuMeld, now holds six mapping methods and sixteen chip layouts. Users can score each method with several metrics and swap parts in or out with ease. New methods, circuits, layouts, and metrics plug into the same frame as the field grows. A single yardstick helps teams pick the right mapper for a given chip instead of guessing from scattered claims.
arxiv-2603-01978:
P. Cataldi, V. Cristiani, F. Rodriguez, and colleagues prepare a way to estimate how galaxies fill dark matter halos for a coming survey. Their 2026 work targets the LSST imaging survey from the Vera Rubin Observatory. The halo occupation distribution links galaxy counts to halo mass and anchors galaxy formation tests.

Their method extends background subtraction to use more photometric information from imaging data. An iterative centroiding tool finds group centers, a step the whole estimate depends on. Each pipeline step faces checks for group size, purity, and completeness of the group catalog. Photometric redshift errors and halo mass uncertainty enter as systematics in the tests. On a mock catalog built from a large simulation suite, the method recovers the target distribution across a wide brightness and mass range.
arxiv-2603-02278:
Phil Attard extends a quantum simulation method in classical terms in this 2026 physics paper. Quantum effects can be folded into classical phase space through a special commutation function. That function encodes the uncertainty principle inside an otherwise classical picture. Attard expands it to third order and simplifies it for use in position space alone.

Momentum is integrated out, leaving a real function over positions only. That form fits standard Monte Carlo sampling, a workhorse of simulation. He reports simulation results for liquid helium-4 in a classic pair-potential model. Runs cover temperatures below ten kelvin, deep in the quantum regime for a light liquid. The paper is the second part of a series on this approach.
arxiv-2603-02378:
Alexander Nemecek, Hengzhi He, Guang Cheng, and Erman Ayday expose a clash between two content checks in this 2026 paper. Provenance records claim to certify who made a file, and watermarks tag AI-made content. The two systems run independently and never consult each other. That gap lets a file pass both checks while telling two opposite stories.

Their Integrity Clash is a file with a valid record claiming human authorship and a watermark marking it as AI-made. Standard editing workflows can wash metadata to create such fakes with no cryptographic break. Only one permitted missing field in the current standard enables the trick. Their joint audit, checking both layers together, classified thousands of test images perfectly. The fix, they argue, is simple and overdue.
arxiv-2603-02978:
Bethany Terris asks what an observer is inside one view of quantum theory. That view treats quantum states as facts for an observer, not as fixed traits of the world. Her 2026 paper presses a basic worry: shared checks need observers who last through time and keep stable records.

Terris argues that the bare rule, any system that interacts counts, cannot support that kind of lasting record. She adds a second layer: the capacity to hold records together across many acts of measuring. With that layer, cases where one observer watches another still yield facts both can confirm. The paper shores up the view's account of shared proof.
arxiv-2603-03078:
Siwei Zhang, Yun Xiong, Xi Chen, and colleagues widen the exploration habits of tool-using language agents during training. Agents trained by reinforcement learning usually learn only from their own rollouts, so they rarely discover reasoning styles outside their current habits. Their 2026 method, RAPO, injects retrieved outside experience into the loop.

Training splits into two phases. During rollouts, the agent reasons continuously over retrieved step-level traces from other policies, extending what it can consider. During updates, a retrieval-aware rule reshapes the gradient with retrieval rewards and importance weighting, keeping training stable. Across fourteen datasets and three agentic tasks, scores rose by about five points on average. Training also ran modestly faster than the baseline.
arxiv-2603-03278:
William Liang, Sam Wang, Hung-Ju Wang, and colleagues let a robot teach itself household skills by playing. Human demonstrations are costly, so autonomous practice is attractive, but play needs a policy that survives unfamiliar states and a routine that keeps producing useful experience. Their 2026 method, Tether, starts from at most ten demonstrations.

An open-loop policy warps those demonstrated actions onto new scenes by anchoring them to semantic keypoints, proving strikingly robust to spatial and meaning shifts. Deployed in a real multi-object household setup, the robot cycles through choosing, attempting, judging, and improving tasks, guided by a vision-language model. Over a full day of play it streamed more than a thousand expert-level trajectories. Policies trained on that self-made data rivaled human-taught ones.
arxiv-2603-03878:
Chetan Choppali Sudarshan and others present CarbonPATH, a framework for designing chiplet-based AI systems with carbon footprint as a first-class concern. AI growth is driving demand for computing while enlarging its footprint on the environment. Makers are shifting to heterogeneous integration, building systems from chiplets, to escape the yield and cost limits of single-die chips. Searching this space means balancing performance, cost, and carbon across apps, architecture, chiplets, and packaging.

CarbonPATH explores the space with simulated annealing, co-designing workload mapping, design settings, and packaging methods. It accounts for compute and memory sizes, chiplet process nodes, wiring protocols, integration styles from flat 2.5D layouts to stacked 3D ones, running and embodied carbon, and link type. By capturing interactions across levels, it finds system-level solutions that narrower methods miss, supporting earlier, carbon-aware decisions in AI hardware design.
arxiv-2604-01178:
Ken M. Nakanishi asks what a good match score should mean in a 2026 paper. His title says it plainly: Screening Is Enough. He calls a score absolute when it sits on a fixed, bounded scale.

An absolute score does not rest on rival keys or on length. It needs no fix-up that changes as the text grows long. All scores for one query can be zero, which must be allowed. His screen uses a set cut line to turn raw scores into match scores. That gives exact refusal, an empty pick, and scores one can read at a glance. The paper offers a simpler path than the standard way of scoring.
arxiv-2605-00378:
William Q. Erickson studies random permutations through the lens of the Robinson-Schensted correspondence, a classic algorithm that assigns each permutation a shape, a partition drawn as a diagram. The shape famously encodes the lengths of the longest increasing and decreasing subsequences, global facts about the permutation. Erickson asks the opposite, local question: fix the shape, and ask how likely position i is to receive value j.

Using the theory of tableaux, the fillings of these diagrams, he derives explicit formulas for those probabilities for hook shapes, two-row shapes, and rectangles. Plotted as matrices, the probabilities form intricate diffraction-like patterns, which he depicts and analyzes. As a surprise application, for hook and two-row shapes the expected share of fixed points tends, as the shape grows, to a classic Wallis integral value. The paper links a global combinatorial machine to fine local statistics.
arxiv-2605-00478:
Masahiro Kaminaga studies the Anderson model, the standard model of a particle moving through a disordered medium, on a Bethe lattice, an infinite tree-like graph. In the strong-disorder regime he examines the root-averaged density of states, an averaged spectral measure at the tree's root. The single-site randomness has bounded range and a smooth density near the energies of interest.

Combining a random-walk expansion with complex analysis of the single-site transforms, Kaminaga proves the scaled resolvent extends holomorphically near the target interval once disorder is large enough. The density of states there is then real analytic, with a finite strong-disorder expansion. Its leading term is the local density of the single-site distribution. All odd corrections vanish, and the rest are finite sums over short closed walks; for the uniform distribution he computes the first nonzero correction explicitly.
arxiv-2605-00578:
Luru Jing and 3 co-authors train cancer-slide models across hospitals without moving patient data. Whole slide images are huge scans of tissue. Hospitals differ in both their model designs and their feature extractors, which breaks methods that assume all sites run the same network. Their system, FedHD, avoids exchanging model settings at all.

Each site distills its knowledge into fake feature summaries, aligned to the real data through local Gaussian-mixture modeling. Every real slide gets its own fake counterpart, keeping the full range of cases instead of squeezing it away. A staged plan folds in other sites' fake features once local gains level off, and an added module rebuilds readable patch images from the fake features so users can inspect them. On three public cancer datasets, FedHD beat leading shared-training and distillation baselines while staying design-agnostic and privacy-preserving.
arxiv-2605-00778:
Jacques Raynal, Pierre Slangen, Elsa Raynal, and Jacques Margerit study gait in a single patient with Parkinson's disease whose bite height was changed as a test constraint. Repeated walking measures were taken under six occlusal probes, meaning six bite settings. The team looked at the case at three levels, from a simple combined score to a map of fifty-five body measures.

The ranking of two close settings changed with how the score was built, and the map showed broad overlap with no separate clusters for each setting. The authors conclude that neither view can uniquely identify a distinct system state. They treat bite height as a constraint, not a proven cause, and stress the findings are exploratory.
arxiv-2605-00978:
Gene C. K. Leung and fourteen co-authors report variability in a quasar seen just 850 million years after the Big Bang, a first for such early cosmic time. In the nearby universe, quasar brightness changes help probe accretion onto supermassive black holes and measure their masses, but detecting variability so early is hard. Infrared changes across five filters trace the accretion disk, while X-ray changes probe the corona.

The variable spectrum shows the disk has a geometrically thin, optically thick structure, even while the quasar accretes at a high rate in an extreme environment. The result shows accretion physics can be characterized through variability in the early universe. Future surveys should find large samples for population studies of early black hole growth.
arxiv-2605-01378:
Muhammad Muneeb and David B Ascher built a tool that gathers genes linked to a trait or disease from many databases in one run. Finding such genes is a common first step in risk scores and drug target work, but the proof sits scattered across sources with unlike formats.

Given a trait term, PhenotypeToGeneDownloaderR pulls gene lists, puts them in a shared form, merges them, and checks each symbol against the NCBI human gene reference. Across 13 traits and 13 sources it drew well over 100,000 raw hits. It kept most symbols after checks. It also recovered nearly all genes in a gold standard set built from three trusted sources. Overlap between sources was low, which shows why pooling helps. The free tool gives later analysis a clean, repeatable starting list.
arxiv-2605-02278:
Fengming Zhang and colleagues present HELIX, a model for filling missing values in time series that gives each feature a lasting identity. Attention methods can use links across features, but they rediscover those links at every layer, with no stable anchor for what each feature means. HELIX assigns a learnable embedding to each feature that persists through the network.

Unlike graph methods, HELIX needs no predefined topology and does not assume uniform spatial links. It learns arbitrary feature dependencies from temporal co-variation, handling data that mix spatial sites with semantic variables. With hybrid temporal-feature attention, it beat sixteen baselines across five public data sets and twenty-one settings. Analysis shows its learned identities align with meaningful feature structure.
arxiv-2605-02378:
Haoyu Wang and colleagues improve multimodal in-context learning, where a vision-language model adapts from a few shown examples. Their analysis finds an inductive gap: models often give correct answers from flawed reasoning and struggle to extract consistent rules across demonstrations. Two visual obstacles widen the gap, a flood of redundant visual tokens that obscure text cues, and attention skewed toward the first image.

Their framework recasts the task as an inductive-deductive process. A similarity-based module compresses visual tokens by filtering redundant patches. A dynamic mechanism rebalances attention across all images more evenly. A chain-of-thought scheme then guides the model to state a rule from the examples before applying it by deduction to the new case.
arxiv-2605-02478:
Feiyi Liu and five co-authors model a failure mode in silicon carbide power switches used in high-voltage systems. A single energetic event can push such a switch into burnout, and near the border between recovery and runaway the outcome is not sharp. Chance variation can tip a device that should recover into failure instead.

The team builds a reduced model that couples heat and charge feedback with random terms, plus a boundary that marks failure. Fluctuations widen the sharp threshold into a band of chance, and rare excursions explain failures below the nominal limit. Timing distributions separate fast, feedback-driven runaway from slow, chance-driven failure. A phase diagram sorts the regimes, giving designers a statistical view of a limit once treated as fixed.
arxiv-2605-02678:
Nicola Apollonio proves a sharp either-or result for graphs whose vertices are colored at random. A graph's degree pattern can be summed up by a normalized quantity built from its degree sequence. When vertices take several colors, with each color keeping a fair share, the question is whether the pieces cut out by the colors match their expected sizes.

Only two regimes occur. If the normalized degree quantity shrinks toward zero, the color-class subgraphs concentrate near their means. If it stays sizable, concentration hinges on color balance: a lasting imbalance keeps the count of same-color edges away from its mean with positive chance, while a fading imbalance restores concentration. The same split holds for a broad class of randomly colored random graphs.
arxiv-2605-02978:
José Luis Delgado presents a framework for measuring whether web connections are ready for post-quantum security. Moving TLS, the protocol that secures web traffic, to quantum-safe methods needs careful evidence. That evidence must separate what a session negotiated from what an endpoint can do. It must also cover what certificates show, and why some records are missing.

The framework splits evidence into four surfaces. One is passive session records. One is active probing. One is certificate chains, and one is registry knowledge. Those map onto planes for session behavior, key setup, endpoint skill, identity checks, lifecycle, and policy. A test artifact enforces schemas on all records and keeps registries versioned. Dozens of controlled scenarios test the design, across protocol versions and key modes.
arxiv-2605-03078:
Christine P. Lee, Min Kyung Lee, and Bilge Mutlu interviewed sixteen workers in health care, finance, and management about AI that does more than assist. As systems gain agency, they can decide, assign work, and shape how staff talk to each other.

Workers described three roles: assistant that supports choices, arbiter that makes key calls staff must explain, and manager that directs work. Needs for explanation, control, and accountability shifted with each role. The authors name an authority-accountability gap, where staff carry blame for outcomes they no longer control, and draw design lessons from it.
arxiv-2605-03278:
Sahil Shikalgar and Md. Noor-E-Alam fix a flaw in doubly robust estimates of treatment effects. The flaw arises when proxy variables are endogenous. Doubly robust methods assume no hidden confounding. Yet proxies like refill rates can track the error term, through hidden behavior or noisy measurement.

Their estimator models that joint pattern with Gaussian copulas. It does so in both the treatment and outcome models. No instruments are needed, and the doubly robust property is kept. Simulations recovered unbiased effects where naive estimates were badly biased. On national survey data, a seeming blood pressure rise from counseling vanished after the fix.
arxiv-2605-03378:
Shihao Weng, Yang Feng, Jinrui Zhang, Xiaofei Xie, Jiongchi Yu, and Jia Liu defend language model agents against prompt injections that hide inside the very evidence an agent must use. Such context-aware attacks differ from generic payloads, and most benchmarks and defenses miss them because their tasks do not depend on runtime context.

Their AgentLure benchmark spans four domains and many attack vectors. Their ARGUS defense audits causal provenance: each proposed action needs a complete benign evidence chain before release. On the benchmark, attack success fell from near three in ten to under four in a hundred, with clean utility largely kept.
arxiv-2605-03978:
Areeda Ayoub, Alfonso Castillo-Gonzalez, and Eric R. Bittner show that steady-state entanglement in open quantum systems is controlled by the phase reference of a phase-sensitive reservoir. Using a covariance-matrix approach for Gaussian-preserving evolution, they show that purely local, phase-sensitive loss can create entanglement. It does so when combined with coherent coupling between modes. That coupling turns local squeezing into nonlocal correlations.

The steady state has a finite entangled region. A best squeezing strength maximizes the size of the entanglement, and how well it survives heat. Coherent coupling does not help in a simple way. It regulates the conversion of squeezing into correlations. Phase-locked rotating-frame and laboratory-frame versions of the reservoir yield clearly distinct steady states. The upshot is a controlled route to steady-state entanglement in continuous-variable systems, through such reservoirs.
arxiv-2605-04178:
Aaron Jarmusch and Sunita Chandrasekaran build analytical performance models for modern graphics processors, aiming to close the gap between theoretical peak performance and what real kernels achieve. Rapidly evolving GPU architectures add complex memory hierarchies, matrix units, and varied precision formats, which naive roofline models handle badly. Their models are grounded in systematic microbenchmark characterization of two flagship architectures.

For NVIDIA's Blackwell B200, the model captures its tensor memory, asynchronous bulk copy engine, and fifth-generation tensor cores; for AMD's CDNA3 MI300A, it captures the Infinity Cache hierarchy, register constraints, and occupancy. Validation errors were near one percent or below on dozens of kernels, while naive roofline baselines erred by over ninety-five percent. Porting the models to Hopper and CDNA2 hardware needed parameter updates but no major restructuring.
arxiv-2605-04278:
Achuth Chandrasekhar and three co-authors present a system that mines materials science papers to build structured databases automatically. Most experimental detail in the literature sits buried in text, tables, and figures, so building databases by hand is slow and hard to scale.

Their multi-agent system takes article files, converts them to readable text and figures in parallel, and assigns sub-agents to extract records paper by paper. Another agent then merges those records into one table. The design aims for production-scale extraction that a single pass or fixed rules would struggle to match.
arxiv-2605-04478:
Yida Gu and nineteen co-authors present a diagnostic system for the slow or hanging communication faults that plague large-scale model training. As clusters grow, the libraries that coordinate thousands of processors hit faults from tangled hardware, software, and environmental causes, and manual diagnosis can take days.

Their system pairs a lightweight rank-level probe with an automated analyser. The probe traces communication traffic across layers in real time. The analyser detects anomalies and locates the faulty processor rank. Deployed for a year on a four thousand processor cluster, it covered nearly all known slow or hang cases. It pinpointed affected ranks within minutes, with high precision.
arxiv-2605-04678:
Yihan Lin and six co-authors systematically compare ways of supervising vision-language-action models, the systems that connect seeing and language to robot control, using latent actions as an intermediate representation. Latent actions promise consistent training across very different data sets, but supervision strategies have been fragmented and never compared head to head.

Under one unified baseline, they test four integration strategies split between image-based latent actions, which regularise the trajectory, and action-based ones, which unify the target space. Image-based supervision helped long-horizon reasoning and scene generalisation, while action-based supervision excelled at complex motor coordination. Directly supervising the model with discrete latent action tokens worked best overall.
arxiv-2605-04778:
Aziz Takhirov and Driss Yakoubi develop a step-by-step method for solving the steady incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. Those equations govern viscous fluid flow at rest in time. Their scheme adapts a viscosity splitting, originally built for unsteady flows, to the steady problem.

At each step, the method solves one elliptic equation for velocity. It also solves one system for pressure. That system's matrix is symmetric and positive definite. It stays the same across all steps, which makes repeated solves cheap. The scheme can also be read as an algebraic splitting. The authors prove boundedness and fast convergence of the steps. Tests show the method's efficiency.
arxiv-2605-04978:
Harry Desmond introduces Exhaustive Symbolic Integration, a method that lists every symbolic function up to a set complexity and tests which ones have closed-form antiderivatives in the same family. That census defines an integrability fraction for each chosen set of building blocks, such as rational functions, powers, exponentials, logarithms, and trigonometric functions.

Desmond finds the fraction falls at high complexity and depends dramatically on the building blocks, with adding the logarithm roughly tripling it. Used as an integrator, the method solved three integrals that resisted six major computer algebra systems and often returned the simplest answer. Enumeration, he argues, can systematically find integrable forms others miss.
arxiv-2605-05278:
Mohammad Reza Deylam Salehi and Ali Khalesi analyse expert routing in mixture-of-experts models through an information-theoretic lens, treating the gate that picks experts as a noisy communication channel. The gate controls computation, communication, and accuracy at once, so the information it carries about the input matters. Finite expert banks make those information quantities measurable rather than purely theoretical.

Using pretrained convolutional experts on a digit task, the authors estimate how much the chosen model reveals about the data with a closed-form estimator. Sweeping a data-dependence parameter, their estimate tracks the generalisation gap closely. They also trace an accuracy-versus-rate curve over the expert bank, offering a practical analysis tool for resource-aware expert systems.
arxiv-2605-05478:
Learning a new task goes faster when an agent can borrow skills from old ones. Mahyar Alinejad, Yue Wang, Amrit Singh Bedi, and George Atia present LANTERN, a transfer framework for reinforcement learning with a symbolic side. Earlier methods needed hand-written task machines, one source task, and fixed rules for mixing knowledge.

LANTERN generates task automata from plain-language descriptions using a language model. It blends several source policies by semantic similarity, and it gates teaching by error and uncertainty signals. Across resource, navigation, and control tasks, sample efficiency rose forty to sixty percent over baselines, and poorly matched sources did little harm.
arxiv-2605-05878:
Moving value across a tangle of blockchains and markets creates risks no single chain explains. Basel Magableh argues the main risk is composite: part route, part sentiment, part liquidity, part the policy a system commits to. He proposes a risk intelligence design of five working engines.

A prediction engine forecasts prices, liquidity, swings, and route health. A verification subnet on Bittensor scores those predictions with money at stake. Sentiment fusion reads text, on-chain flows, and grey sources as one. An agentic engine acts under written, role-bound limits, and a scenario engine turns forecasts into pre-set action programs.
arxiv-2605-06078:
Zixuan Wang and nine co-authors train language agents for long tasks by marking milestones along the way. An agent may need dozens of steps, and plain reinforcement learning blames early good moves for late failures. Scarce successful runs also waste most of the learning signal, the authors find.

Their framework, BEACON, splits each trajectory at milestone boundaries that reflect the task's structure. Reward shaping inside each segment credits partial progress, and advantages are estimated at two scales so distant failures cannot corrupt local judgments. On three agent benchmarks BEACON beat the compared reinforcement learning methods. On long ALFWorld tasks it reached a 92.9 percent success rate, nearly double the 53.5 percent of a leading baseline, and used training samples far more effectively.
arxiv-2605-06178:
Yiming Huang and three co-authors make analog quantum simulators programmable with a hybrid control design. Analog machines evolve continuously under interactions fixed by their hardware, which restricts the Hamiltonians they can realize. That fixed structure limits what many body dynamics researchers can emulate on a given device, however good the hardware is.

Universal Analog Quantum Simulation uses optimized continuous time control fields to engineer target dynamics directly on the native evolution. No decomposition into discrete gate sequences is needed, so the analog character of the device is preserved. Numerical studies on superconducting circuits and Rydberg atom arrays show the method copying non trivial many body dynamics. Those dynamics lie beyond what the bare hardware interactions could express, turning a fixed device into a programmable simulator.
arxiv-2605-06278:
Fabian Akkerman and three co-authors shrink ensemble models by mixing pruning with fresh compression. Ensembles predict very well by pooling many weak learners, but their size blocks deployment, interpretation, and tasks like robustness verification. Pruning discards redundant learners, while compression builds new ones from scratch, and past work kept the two camps separate, the authors note.

Their framework, PACE, first generates new learners with a theoretically grounded procedure that boosts the ensemble's diversity. When no more relevant learners can be found, it prunes the enriched ensemble down. Both phases allow fine control over faithfulness to the original ensemble's behavior. Tests show the method beating prior pruning and compression methods. It also offers clear guarantees on that faithfulness, which black box shrinking methods lack.
arxiv-2605-06378:
Yuanqiu Huang and Licheng Zhang count cliques in highly connected 1-planar graphs and prove sharp bounds. A 1-planar graph can be drawn with at most one crossing per edge, and earlier work fixed the maximum clique counts for such graphs in general. Those extremal examples, though, have low connectivity, leaving the high connectivity end open, which is where this paper works, on graphs that stay connected after removing any six vertices.

Every such graph on n vertices has at most a linear number of edges, triangles, and four vertex cliques, with explicit constants for each bound. Summed together, the total number of cliques stays below a linear cap as well. All of the bounds are sharp for infinitely many sizes. The results complete the clique picture at the opposite end of connectivity from the known examples.
arxiv-2605-06778:
Sean K. Terry and fifteen co-authors present a Hubble Space Telescope imaging survey of just over one square degree toward the Milky Way's galactic bulge. The field overlaps the upcoming Roman telescope's bulge time-domain survey. Imaging it first at Hubble resolution will sharpen Roman's characterization of exoplanet systems and leave a rich legacy archive for the whole community.

Coordinated imaging with both of Hubble's wide-field cameras in two filters ran mostly in Cycle 32, with the remainder in Cycle 33. As the first paper in a series, it lays out the program and observing strategy and shows early results. The dataset will serve studies of stellar populations, dynamics, extinction, and clusters near the galactic center.
arxiv-2605-06878:
Sonu Kumar, Mukul Lokhande, Santosh Kumar Vishvakarma, and Adam Teman present CARMEN, a hardware inference engine that uses CORDIC arithmetic to run neural networks efficiently. CORDIC computes multiply-accumulate operations through shifts and additions, and its iteration depth directly sets accuracy. That lets their engine switch between approximate and precise modes at runtime with no hardware change, supporting both eight- and sixteen-bit precision.

A chip implementation in twenty-eight nanometer technology cuts computation cycles by up to a third and power by about a fifth per stage. A large configuration reaches strong compute density and energy efficiency, and a field-programmable board prototype runs real-time object detection at well under half a watt.
arxiv-2605-07078:
Zekun Wang and three co-authors test whether diffusion models can discover their own concepts at generation time. Making new combinations from familiar parts usually assumes the needed concepts are already supplied. Their method instead works from a single unusual query and the model's own learned scores.

Gradient steps recover local modes in the model's density, which are turned into clean prototypes and selected greedily. The combined teacher model can be sampled directly or used to train a small adapter. On held-out combination tests built from two image datasets, both routes beat query-only and nearest-class baselines, suggesting reusable concepts hide in the model's score patterns.
arxiv-2605-07178:
Kai Zheng and five co-authors extract text descriptions for satellite change detection from the labels already in the data. Change detection supports city monitoring and disaster assessment, but image-only models confuse real changes with look-alike variation. Added text helps, yet existing descriptions are coarse or machine-made and noisy.

Their S2M framework transcribes each labeled change region into structured facts: where it happened, what changed, how, and how many objects were involved. Training aligns images with those precise descriptions at no extra labeling cost. On a new Gaza Strip dataset built for the work, the method beat even systems that use large language models.
arxiv-2605-07578:
Aleksas Mazeliauskas reviews the first light-ion collision program at the Large Hadron Collider, which ran in July 2025. The runs collided protons with oxygen, and oxygen and neon nuclei with each other. Such mid-size systems sit between tiny proton-proton collisions and huge heavy-ion ones, making them a test bed for how collective behavior in hot quantum chromodynamics turns on.

Early results, he reports, give strong evidence that a quark-gluon plasma forms even in these small systems. The review lays out why physicists wanted light-ion runs in the first place, then walks through the initial measurements. It ties the findings to perturbative calculations, hot matter theory, and low-energy nuclear structure, showing where the three fields meet.
arxiv-2605-07978:
Qiwei Wang and three co-authors locate ground photos in three dimensions using satellite and drone imagery together. Classical cross-view localization finds only a position and a heading for a ground image on a satellite tile, because overhead views carry no cues for roll, pitch, or altitude. Those missing angles matter on slopes, ramps, and tilted mounts.

Their insight is to add one drone image as an intermediate viewpoint. It reveals the structure invisible from directly above and needs only to overlap the ground camera's view, with no known relative pose. The Cross3R model takes any combination of the three views and returns a joint point cloud, full six-degree poses for every camera, and on-tile positions. A new tri-view dataset of two hundred seventy-eight thousand images across eighty-five scenes supports training and testing.
arxiv-2605-08478:
Yihe Dong and Boris Shigida ask how to spend a fixed inference budget on competitive programming: think longer in one agent, or sample many independent attempts? They evaluate two hundred sixteen Codeforces problems from divisions one through three, varying both money cost and number of model calls.

Repeated independent sampling won on both trade-offs, across models and difficulty levels, and the gap survived prompt caching inside agent frameworks, which points to weaker per-call value from agentic reasoning. For self-contained algorithmic tasks, breadth beat depth. The authors add a budget analysis proving that a cost-optimal solver minimizes log failure likelihood per dollar.
arxiv-2605-08678:
Bohan Lyu and many coauthors introduce MLS-Bench, a test of whether AI agents can invent better machine learning methods, not merely apply known ones. Each of its one hundred forty tasks across twelve domains asks an agent to improve one targeted part of a learning system, then prove the gain holds across settings and scales. A shared community platform keeps results comparable over time.

Current agents fall well short of reliably beating human designed methods, and routine tuning proves far easier than true invention. Extra search, computing, or context alone does not close the gap, because planning and validating claims need scientific insight. AI research gains a benchmark aimed squarely at discovery itself.
arxiv-2605-08778:
Zhida He and ten coauthors improve credit assignment in multi turn jailbreak research, where harmful intent is spread across seemingly mild conversation turns. Training methods that score only the final outcome reward every turn equally, overpaying filler turns in successes and underpaying useful steps in failures. Their TRACE framework scores turns individually: masking tests measure each turn's contribution in successful attacks, while failed attempts draw penalties tied to harmfulness and relevance.

The same credit signal then serves defense training as well. Across open and closed target models, attack success rises by about a quarter over the strongest reinforcement baseline, and reuse for defense improves the safety and utility balance. Dialogue safety research gains finer supervision.
arxiv-2605-08878:
Yu Chen, Yuanhao Liu, and Qi Cao explain structurally why aligned language models can still be jailbroken. Looking at harmful inputs under smooth perturbation, they identify refusal escape directions: small shifts that move the model from refusing to answering while its grasp of the harmful meaning stays intact. A jailbreak, in this view, is a behavior transition along such a direction, not just a clever discrete prompt.

They prove these directions decompose exactly into contributions from parts of the model's operator structure, with normalization, residual wiring, and output stages analytically constrained. Removing the directions forces shared attention and feedforward modules to kill those contributions while preserving benign skill, creating a conditional safety versus utility trade off.
arxiv-2605-08978:
Xingyuan Hua, Sheng Yue, and Ju Ren teach language model agents to explore only when exploration is worth it. Agents that gather feedback before acting usually explore in a fixed, undifferentiated way, wasting effort when the task is already clear and under exploring when uncertainty runs high. Their exploration aware policy optimization scores exploratory actions by their estimated power to improve later decisions, using a variational inference based reward.

A grouping mechanism separates exploratory moves from task completing moves during training, so each is optimized on its own terms. Across demanding text based and graphical interface agent benchmarks, performance improves consistently. Agent training gains a sense of timing: investigate while confused, execute the moment the picture clears.
arxiv-2605-09078:
Charalambia Varnava and three co-authors report new telescope observations of one of the most luminous quasars known, a galaxy core buried in dust when the universe was young. The James Webb Space Telescope's mid-infrared instrument measured its light in detail, and the team fit models to the full spread of that light.

Their fits say the active black hole supplies most of the galaxy's output, with a mass billions of times the Sun's and stars forming at a furious rate. They also find clear signs of hot dust near the poles of the black hole's dust ring. The authors urge that this polar dust be included when other distant hidden quasars are modeled, since leaving it out skews the results.
arxiv-2605-09178:
Agustín Garrone studies contact Lie algebras, algebraic structures that mix symmetry operations with a contact form from geometry. His 2026 paper focuses on those that are unimodular, a volume-like condition, and asks how a special vector field called the Reeb vector acts inside them. The proof he gives is deliberately basic, avoiding heavy machinery where possible.

Garrone shows that this action must fade under repetition, except for two named algebras, which he identifies in standard notation. He then defines a wider class that includes the K-contact case and shows the same two algebras are its only centerless unimodular members. The result gives a fresh proof of a known fact about Sasakian algebras. Work in dimension five and links to Frobenius algebras and the contact Lefschetz condition round out the study.
arxiv-2605-09578: Implanting nitrogen into gallium oxide — a hopeful wide-bandgap semiconductor — can form small-scale nitrogen trapped inside the crystal. I.N. Demchenko, Y. Syryanyy, A. Shokri, and others study the formation process. The 2026 paper is parts science for next-gen electronics.
arxiv-2605-09878: Ergotropy — the maximum work extractable from a quantum state — meets Clifford operations, the efficiently simulable gates. Somnath Maity and Ryusuke Hamazaki study Clifford ergotropy. The 2026 paper is quantum thermodynamics on exactly what Clifford circuits can squeeze out of quantum states today.
arxiv-2605-10378: Uncertainty appears in both physics and AI — this 2026 paper offers its grouping, quantification, and validation. It surveys the landscape comprehensively. It is uncertainty quantification for two fields. It provides a thorough grouping of uncertainty spanning physics and AI research, in full.
arxiv-2606-00078:
Pavelkin and co-authors teach a generative model to choose what to measure, in this 2026 arXiv proof-of-concept study on compressed sensing. Compressed sensing recovers sparse signals from fewer measurements than classical theory demands, which matters for fast medical imaging and other sensing. Their framework recasts flow matching, a generative modeling technique, so the model learns subsampling masks tuned for the task rather than sampling blindly. One framework serves image classification, image reconstruction, and MRI acceleration.

The learned masks sharply improved reconstruction quality in their tests. On a celebrity face dataset at 5 percent sampling, the method reached a peak signal-to-noise ratio, a fidelity measure, above 25 decibels, the best reported for that setting. For accelerated MRI scans it reached above 29 decibels with minimal computation. The approach's unity is the selling point: conditioning inside the generative model tailors sensing to what the task needs.

arxiv-2606-04178:
Jean Guillaume and Tyriana Williams study the burning number of a graph in 2026. The measure comes from a simple spread game: fires start at chosen points and advance one edge per round. The burning number is the fewest rounds to burn the whole graph.

They pin down the exact number for several families of highly symmetric graphs, the Cayley graphs of certain groups. For others they give tight upper and lower bounds. Along the way they refute a standing guess about complete multipartite graphs, where vertices split into groups with all links between groups. Knowing such numbers helps estimate how fast a process can cover a network. That matters for planning sensor placement and search.
arxiv-2606-04278:
Miro Ronac Giannone and Elizabeth Silber assess in 2026 what decides whether the global infrasound network hears a bolide, a bright meteor exploding in the atmosphere. Infrasound monitoring covers oceans and remote regions where cameras cannot watch, complementing optical surveys.

They matched six hundred twenty-three bolides reported between 2007 and 2025 against recordings from the international monitoring arrays. About half had confirmed detections, a rate near fifty percent and well above earlier estimates, reflecting a maturing network and better automated processing. Detection was selective: steep entries that deposit energy low were heard preferentially, while shallow, high bursts were often missed. Entry angle emerged as the primary control, with energy and atmospheric propagation as secondary factors.
arxiv-2606-04378:
Bingnan Li and a team of co-authors propose DLLG in 2026. It combines several specialized language models by blending their output probabilities token by token. Routing each request to one expert commits too early. Merging weights makes the experts interfere.

A light gating module learns the blending weights from sparse, response-level feedback alone. No token-level labels are needed, and the experts are never retrained. The module links the final answer's correctness back to each fusion step during generation. Across reasoning and code benchmarks and several model scales, the learned fusion beat routing and merging baselines consistently. The authors present it as a robust, scalable pattern for composing expert models.
arxiv-2606-04578:
Pomarède and colleagues map the gravitational basin dominated by the Sloan Great Wall, in a 2026 arXiv astronomy paper. It shows up in galaxy surveys and in distortions of cosmic expansion. The authors use Hamiltonian Monte Carlo reconstruction within the standard cosmology model. They derive probabilistic density and velocity fields. The fields are constrained by the Cosmicflows-4 catalog of galaxy distances and velocities. They then follow streamlines in the velocity field to their sinks. The sinks are the minima of the gravitational potential.

A basin of attraction is the volume whose streamlines end at the same sink. The Sloan basin proves by far the largest in the study region. Its diameter spans about 0.13 times the speed of light in the paper's units. A video and interactive models accompany the paper. They also examine how the Ho'oleilana baryon acoustic oscillation feature relates to this basin.
arxiv-2606-04678:
Kaloga and colleagues make speech recognition accuracy adjustable at test time, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Their recognizer thinks longer by looping its encoder. End-to-end speech systems normally use a fixed-depth acoustic encoder. Extra computation cannot be traded for accuracy without training a bigger model. Reusing one shared transformer block recurrently is natural. But the authors find naive looping fails to exploit the added compute. Their LARM architecture turns recurrent encoder depth into a controllable test-time compute axis.

Together these structure the loop into recognition checkpoints separated by latent refinement phases. They let shared weights specialize across recurrent steps. On LibriSpeech, word error rate improves as the number of inference loops increases. The results extend test-time compute scaling, famous from language model reasoning, to continuous, non-autoregressive speech recognition.
arxiv-2606-05078:
Micaella Bruton, Meriem Beloucif, and Beáta Megyesi test whether an attention-augmented LSTM network can decipher homophonic substitution ciphers in this 2026 arXiv paper. In such ciphers each plaintext letter can be written with several different codes, which on purpose flattens letter-frequency patterns and frustrates automated codebreaking. The setting is historical: all ciphertexts draw on one shared, known pool of codes, while each key uses a different consistent subset of it.

Training used only aligned ciphertext and plaintext pairs, with no external language model, frequency statistics, or key-search tricks. The test ciphers came from historical English and Swedish texts dated 1500 to 1899, generated with ChronoFidelius. The model reached near-perfect character-level decryption accuracy across both languages and all periods, including short and noisy ciphertexts. It failed predictably on ciphers outside the shared pool, marking it as a practical tool when key reuse is suspected.
arxiv-2606-05178:
Tim Dorn, Saara Khan, and Julie Mumford present the Virtual Roundtable in this 2026 arXiv paper, a multi-agent system that simulates brainstorming with AI personas. As AI speeds up building products, the bottleneck shifts to deciding what to build, while brainstorming suffers from groupthink, echo chambers, and limited diversity. The system runs a roundtable in two phases: divergent thinking to generate ideas, then convergent thinking to evaluate and rank them.

Diverse AI personas discuss under an agentic facilitator that steers the discussion. Each persona keeps private thoughts while commenting, ideas emerge through the discussion, and per-persona quotas on submissions and votes keep participation balanced while producing rankings. The system tracks an idea's lineage, showing how concepts originate and mix. In a case study generating ideas for AI smart glasses, the roundtable produced diverse ideas. The exchange of perspectives built a context that deepened the discussion and the ideas.
arxiv-2606-05378:
Yongzhong Xu asks whether mechanistic interpretability recipes identify the circuits in language models, in this 2026 arXiv paper, and finds they do not. The standard recipe finds attention heads selective for a task pattern, then ablates them to test importance. The method was made famous on a model's circuit.

Four tasks, indirect-object identification, greater-than comparison, successor sequences, and variable binding, were run on three one-billion-class models. The models were Pythia 1B, OLMo 1B, and the mixture-of-experts OLMoE 1B-7B. A screen-and-ablate protocol with a matched-random null over seeds produced twelve cells, and no two cells shared the same primary screen at comparable size. Xu introduces a five-category taxonomy of outcomes, from cause down to null, and all five appear in the panel. One hypothesis emerges: the mixture-of-experts model builds its task circuits on a previous-token positional substrate.
arxiv-2606-05678:
Yifan Liao and colleagues move speech attacks off the waveform to dodge modern defenses in a 2026 arXiv paper. Speech recognizers turn audio into text across many languages. Classic attacks add crafted noise straight to the sound file. Such noise transfers poorly to unseen systems, and new defenses are tuned to catch it. The team instead perturbs the richer sound features a self-supervised model extracts.

A vocoder then rebuilds speech from the warped features, so the attack signal sounds like voice, not static. Tuned only on a public Whisper model, the attack fooled black-box recognizers far better than the best baseline. Word error rates rose by about twenty-seven points over that baseline. Against trained defenses the edge grew to about thirty-six points. The results expose a blind spot: guarding the waveform leaves the feature space wide open.
arxiv-2606-05878:
Le Naour, Nabil, and Petralia build one time-series model that fills gaps and forecasts in a 2026 arXiv paper. Real series arrive ragged: sensors drop out and sampling turns patchy. Most foundation models only forecast, assuming tidy histories. TS-ICL recasts every task as regression aligned to timestamps. It learns in context, reading example series in the prompt before answering.

Training data is synthetic, grown from a new causal prior that wires in outside covariates. The model thus learns dependency shapes rather than memorizing one domain. On imputation it set a new state-of-the-art mark. Forecasting stayed competitive with leading specialist foundation models. The edge showed clearest when the look-back window itself was partly missing. That regime, common in energy and sensor work, is where tidy-data models stumble. A single probabilistic model covering both jobs simplifies deployment for messy real feeds.
arxiv-2606-05978:
Lescano's lecture notes open the off-shell double copy to graduate students in a 2026 arXiv paper. The double copy is a surprising bridge: gravity amplitudes built from gauge theory pieces, twice over. Most treatments stay on-shell, among scattering states. The off-shell program rebuilds the bridge in fields and actions. Notes come from an eight-class course at the Universidad de Buenos Aires in spring 2026.

The course is self-contained, asking basic classical field theory of its readers. Early lectures review gauge and gravitational theories, their symmetries, actions, and equations. Higher-derivative models, including the Weyl action, play a significant role. The single copy and double copy frameworks follow in off-shell form. Final lectures reinterpret the two through T-duality-invariant frameworks, where string theory's symmetry organizes the story. Master's and doctoral students are the audience. The notes aim to lower the entry cost to a research frontier.
arxiv-2606-06078:
Peruzzo and colleagues run the first study of shrinking visual autoregressive models by distillation in a 2026 arXiv paper. Image generators that predict token after token are expressive but costly. Language distillation tricks were assumed to transfer. They largely do not: long decoding runs and ambiguous visual tokens make teacher supervision unreliable, most when the student generates the context. Standard distillation still helps a bit, which motivates a vision-specific design.

VarKD distills on the student's own samples, where supervision is needed. Teacher guidance is applied in spots rather than everywhere. Token-level ambiguity, a vision-specific noise source, is cut down. On ImageNet, across several autoregressive backbones, VarKD beat prior distillation baselines throughout. The shrunk students narrowed the gap to their large-scale teachers. Shrinking matters for deploying image generators on products and devices. The warning travels: modality-specific failure modes demand modality-specific distillation, not borrowed recipes.
arxiv-2606-06278:
Akshay Janardan Bankar and co-authors rethink blind image restoration as travel on a curved surface in this 2026 arXiv paper. Blind restoration must recover a clean image when the damage, perhaps blur, haze, rain, or snow, is unknown and possibly mixed. Recent flow based methods morph the damaged image into a clean one along straight line paths. The authors argue that degradation does not live on a flat geometry at all.

They model each damage state as a point on a low dimensional Riemannian manifold, a smooth curved space. Restoration becomes geodesic transport, movement along the surface's own shortest paths, applied jointly to image and manifold position. Mixed degradations then correspond to composing geodesics. Supplementary tests on deblurring sets such as GoPro and RealBlur, plus synthetic dehazing, deraining, and desnowing tasks, kept the method competitive across regimes. Hyperbolic geometry in particular gave structured, stable representations of the damage states.
arxiv-2606-06378:
Zheng Cao and Lie-Wen Chen weigh evidence for a phase change inside neutron stars in this 2026 arXiv paper. Matter squeezed to several times nuclear density might switch abruptly into a new phase, a strong first order transition, rather than changing smoothly. Theory pins down the equation of state near ordinary density and at extreme density, but the middle is guesswork. Neutron star observations are the best probe available.

The authors run Bayesian inference with flexible Gaussian process equations of state, with and without a built in sharp transition. Their data combine the GW170817 merger's tidal signal, NICER mass and radius readings for four pulsars, and both theory constraints. The evidence favors a strong transition, with its onset most likely above the central density of the heaviest stable stars. That placement reconciles the stiffness needed to hold up two solar mass stars with the softening that high density theory prefers.
arxiv-2606-06578:
Jason T Hinkle and co-authors investigate a cosmic no show in this 2026 arXiv paper. A tidal disruption event flares when a black hole shreds a star. In a repeating partial disruption, a bound star survives each pass and gets nibbled again, promising periodic flares. Two sources, TDE 2022dbl and TDE 2020vdq, each flared twice on a pattern that predicted a third flare in early 2026. Surveys watched, and neither flare came.

The limits are strong: any third flare was at least about thirty times fainter than its predecessors. The team weighs explanations, from the star being fully destroyed or knocked off its orbit to the flares never being one star at all. Two independent disruptions in one galaxy within two years, they calculate, has a probability under half a percent at measured rates. The silence thus strains the simplest repeating partial picture and will sharpen how astronomers vet future candidates.
arxiv-2606-06878:
A robot looking at a cluttered corner often cannot see enough of an object to grab it. Kangjian Zhu, Jiang, Qian, and Xie give that robot a second viewpoint in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their framework estimates six degree of freedom grasp poses. That means full position plus full orientation for the gripper. The extra view fills in what the first view hides.

Older fusion methods rebuild the whole scene in three dimensions first. This team fuses after each view is processed, which saves time. A self supervised contrastive strategy teaches matching across views. Points at the same place should agree; points aiming differently should not. A cylinder based module then merges the geometry around each candidate grasp. Attention layers pass information within and across views. The system scored strongly on the GraspNet-1Billion benchmark. It also worked in real world grasping trials.
arxiv-2606-07178:
A magnet that jumps straight from antiferromagnet to a plaquette pattern, skipping everything between, tests theories of quantum phase change. Yin and Liu map that jump in an extended model in this 2026 arXiv paper. The chequerboard J-Q model was built to mimic a famous strontium copper borate material. It pits exchange coupling, which orders spins, against a multi-spin term favoring plaquette singlets.

Monte Carlo simulations scanned the extended parameter space. Everywhere they looked, the transition stayed direct and first order. No intermediate phase appeared between the two states. Along the transition line, an enlarged symmetry emerges, a notable theoretical fingerprint. Locating the boundary precisely is usually painful at first order transitions. The authors found a trick: the Binder ratio of the rival columnar state scales monotonically. That single clean signal pins the transition point sharply. The result constrains debates about deconfined criticality in this material family.
arxiv-2606-07578:
Schmitz scales a transport-based geostatistical simulator to the multivariate, conditional, large-grid regime in this 2026 arXiv paper. Geostatistical simulation generates plausible maps of underground properties that honor measured data and spatial correlation, supporting mining decisions. His MST-Direct method matches target tuples onto a Gaussian backbone using Sinkhorn optimal transport. Because the matching is a shuffle of the tuples, the joint distribution across variables is preserved by design, something approximation-based rivals cannot claim.

Three extensions remove the method's limits. A restricted matcher keeps memory near-linear for grids, and tuple matching extends to many at once. Hard data are honored exactly by pinning measured tuples and conditioning by kriging. Validation used a 6-variable, non-Gaussian reference on grids up to 200 by 200 cells. The method reproduced it with zero count error and exact data honoring, while the competitor remained approximate on both counts.
arxiv-2606-07678:
Yi Nian and colleagues propose DOG-DPO, a way to pick far smaller training sets for teaching language models safer behaviour, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Safety training usually feeds models large sets of preference pairs, examples where one reply is favoured over another, yet much of that data repeats the same lessons. Instead of scoring each pair alone, the method treats each pair as a direction in the model's internal representation space.

The team splits those directions into a shared anchor part, common across datasets, and leftover parts specific to each dataset, then selects pairs that cover the space broadly without repeats. Across six safety benchmarks and two model backbones, training on about eleven percent of the pairs recovered most of the safety gains of full-data training. The selection step needs no teacher model and no training of its own, and it runs much faster than rival selection methods.
arxiv-2606-07778:
Varshney and co-authors argue that good training data hides in the web text that standard filters throw away, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Pipelines that curate pretraining data grade each document with one composite score. Anything the scorer undervalues, however useful, is lost when low-tier data is discarded.

The team instead filters along separate dimensions from a taxonomy of document qualities, adding two new ones: timeliness and cultural specificity. They labelled fourteen million documents with a large model, distilled the labels into smaller ones, and built a tagger running fifty times quicker. A two-pass search then finds strong single dimensions and combines the best into compound filters, avoiding costly full-scale trials. Applied to deprioritised web data, the chosen subsets beat their unfiltered sources. On most benchmarks they even surpassed the corpus's highest-quality tier, and mid-tier data improved clearly over its baseline.
arxiv-2606-07878:
Charles O'Neill and co-authors shrink the memory bottleneck of language models in one pass, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A model's key-value cache, its record of everything read so far, grows with context and dominates deployment costs. Existing compactors either select a subset of the cache, limiting what survives, or synthesise a summary through slow optimisation.

Their system, Still, trains a small Perceiver network once per layer against a frozen base model. At inference it produces compact keys and values in one forward pass, and can be reused along a whole trajectory, even repeatedly. On Qwen and Gemma models it sat on the good side of the speed-quality frontier across compression from eightfold to two hundredfold. On long-context RULER tests it beat the strongest baseline by eight to twenty-two points. The compact cache also supports free-form summarisation, keeping most of the full-context benefit.
arxiv-2606-08078:
Hugo Leguillier and co-authors dissect what extreme compression does to voice identity systems, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Speaker verification checks a claimed identity from voice, and low-bit quantisation, storing network weights in two or three bits instead of thirty-two, makes deployment on small devices feasible. The team applied uniform k-means quantisation-aware training to ResNet-36 and ResNet-200 models and analysed the damage layer by layer and score by score.

They find a clear knee point at two bits: below it, score drift grows and harmful decision flips concentrate near the full-precision threshold, where borderline users live. Weight distortion alone does not explain the damage. Their remedy is a calibrated multi-precision cascade: most trials are resolved by the two-bit model, and only ambiguous cases escalate. The cascade recovers performance close to full precision while keeping most of the efficiency.
arxiv-2606-08678:
Anh-Tuan Dao, Matrouf, Rouvier, and Evans remove the speaker from the evidence a spoofing detector uses, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Generative speech technology undermines voice biometrics. Spoofing detectors excel under in-domain conditions, but their generalization to new settings is often poor. The authors show the issue can be caused by speaker bias: models learn individual voice traits rather than markers of manipulation or generation, so they fail on unfamiliar voices. Their teacher-student framework learns speaker-invariant representations without requiring speaker labels.

A pre-trained speaker recognition model serves as teacher. It guides a student through a gradient reversal layer, which trains the student to hide identity information while keeping spoofing cues. A variational information bottleneck controls the balance between identity cues and detection cues. Evaluations across nine datasets show a relative reduction of roughly a quarter in the equal error rate in the results reported here.
arxiv-2606-08978:
Cho, Kang, and Ko shrink hypergraph neural networks for deployment by teaching a small student only what the teacher gets right, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A hypergraph links many entities through hyperedges, and hypergraph neural networks predict over such structures at high cost. Knowledge distillation trains a student to imitate a teacher. The authors observed that teachers perform worse on heterophilic nodes, nodes whose hyperedge neighbors are diverse, so imitation copies the teacher's weakest knowledge.

Their method, HADES, measures heterophily and uses it to estimate how reliable the teacher is there. Distillation then transfers more knowledge where the teacher is trustworthy and less where it is not. Across real-world hypergraphs, several teachers, and multiple objectives, HADES improved student accuracy. In many cases the students surpassed their teachers while running inference up to 12.3 times faster. The result is a recipe for deploying hypergraph models where compute is scarce.
arxiv-2606-09078:
Aakriti Agrawal and colleagues uncover a bias in the AI tutors that grade reasoning step by step, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Process reward models score each step of a solution to guide learning. Training data is imbalanced, and training amplifies the skew: plausible but wrong steps get overcredited. That difference matters. False negatives slow search, while false positives steer guided decoding and policy training toward flawed reasoning.

PRISM trains on relative comparisons, not absolute labels. It mines contrastive step pairs, using temporal lookahead to generate hard negatives, steps that look right but are not, with no new human labels. A difficulty-aware schedule shapes margins. On PRMBench, PRISM cut false positives by 22 percent and improved macro F1. Plugged into search and training, it raised accuracy by up to 22 percent for guided decoding and 33 percent for Best-of-N selection. The moral: trustworthy oversight means rewarding right reasoning, not confident reasoning.
arxiv-2606-09278:
Cabral and colleagues teach language models to satisfy strict geometric constraints by learning from a solver's residuals, the leftover errors on each constraint, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Given a free-form description, the model must emit exact coordinates honoring dozens of interacting constraints. Plausible-looking output that violates one constraint is a functional failure in diagramming or mechanical design. PyGeoX compiles declarative constraints into a differentiable loss and ships a 300-problem benchmark, PyGeoX-Bench.

Training against one global reward hides a failure they name Outlier Gradient Masking: one badly violated constraint can swamp the norm and nullify the learning signal from the rest. Their Saturating Additive Rewards score each constraint with a bounded term, preserving partial progress and steady gradients. On the benchmark's hard tier, this raised the solving rate 2.3-fold over mean-squared-error rewards. The resulting 8-billion-parameter model proved competitive with much larger frontier systems.
arxiv-2606-09578:
Momina Ahsan and her co-authors test whether the form of a table, not just its facts, changes how well AI models read it in this 2026 arXiv paper. The same table may show up as HTML, Markdown, or LaTeX text, or as a picture of a table. Past tests let facts, form, and layout all vary at once, so no one could tell which part helped or hurt.

Their benchmark, TabVerse, holds the facts fixed across all forms. Each table comes with tags for question type and difficulty. Models face three tasks: answering questions, grasping structure, and rebuilding the table from a form. Both language models and vision-language models were tested. Text forms beat pictures overall, and HTML was the most robust text form. Row-focused structure tasks stayed hard for all. Rebuilding usable LaTeX also proved tough, which warns against treating form as a mere detail.
arxiv-2606-09678:
Aliki Capatos confirms a guessed fix for a quantum memory code and builds the circuit to match in this 2026 arXiv paper. Floquet codes guard quantum data with a timed cycle of two-qubit checks. The catch layer is the circuit that reads those checks. A dynamic circuit, which needs no spare helper qubits, boosted the honeycomb code's threshold but halved its distance.

For the four-eight-eight layout, a dynamic circuit was guessed to keep full distance. Capatos proves the guess right and gives the circuit in full. Four builds then faced circuit-level noise on a torus grid. The dynamic build with resets hit a per-round threshold near zero point four six percent.
