They found health information work is now cross-sector, tech-driven, and tightly linked, with much of it outside hospitals and outside federal job classes. They propose the Health Information Continuum, a framework that sorts work by shared skills and the life cycle of health data. They offer it as a fairer model for training and identity.
pmc-13254978:

In melanoma cells, the combined product reduced melanin production triggered by a stimulating hormone, without obvious cell harm. It also turned down a signaling chain that drives pigment formation. In mice exposed to ultraviolet B light, the treatment visibly lightened back skin and reduced tissue damage linked to the exposure. The authors present the pairing as a gentler, non-invasive option for managing sun-related pigmentation.
pmc-13255078:
Ni Li and colleagues describe a 2026 material designed to stop pleural adhesions, the fibrous bands that can form after chest surgery. Adhesions cause chronic pain, stiff lungs, and risky repeat operations. Existing barrier sheets stick poorly to wet tissue and carry no active drugs.

Their product starts as a powder that turns into an asymmetric glue-like hydrogel within twenty seconds of touching body fluids. The gel seals tissue, stops bleeding, kills bacteria, and mops up harmful oxygen radicals. Embedded fatty bubbles slowly release two agents, a small RNA and simvastatin, that together damp the fibrosis-inflammation cycle. In rats with pleural injury, treated animals developed far fewer adhesions and healed better than untreated ones.
pmc-13255378:
Nicholas P Howard and colleagues trace the wild roots of the cultivated apple in a 2026 genetics study. The domestic apple is thought to descend mainly from three wild species, with possible input from tiny-fruited ones. Using a 20K marker array, the team built a library of species-specific DNA markers from wild trees, then read ancestry in 436 wild accessions and in cultivars.

All cultivars proved to be mixtures of the three main progenitors, and some carried tiny-fruited input too. Older cultivars and those from eastern Europe or western Asia held less M. sylvestris ancestry than modern western ones. The work also flagged taxonomy problems in wild collections.
pmc-13255578:
Keji Guo and a large team present a 2026 camera-trap survey of mammals in Luolong County, Tibet, in an area without formal protection. Notable species included musk deer, Chinese serow, and woolly hares among plant eaters, plus common leopards, snow leopards, red foxes, and stone martens among hunters. Detection patterns for different species were linked through shared environmental factors. The authors argue that this unprotected landscape functions as an intact ecosystem and deserves a place in conservation planning for the region.
pmc-13255678:
Soumya Bhattacharyya, Jose Wojnacki, Nathalie Brouwers, and Vivek Malhotra report a new view of collagen handling in cells in a 2026 paper. Its rigid, long shape poses a puzzle, since standard shipping vesicles are far too small to hold it.

Against the prevailing view, the team reports that procollagen 1 gathers into a liquid condensate inside cells. This droplet-like assembly could explain how cells store and export large amounts of the molecule. The finding reframes a long-standing problem in collagen biology.
pmc-13255978:
Christian Leonardo Molina-Hinojosa and co-authors report a 2026 twenty-year cohort study from a Barcelona hospital on cervical precancer coming back after treatment. Leftover or returning disease struck about a third of women with weak immunity, versus under five percent of the comparison group. pmc-13257078:
Yu Zheng and a large team examine prenatal-onset recessive titin disease in a 2026 cohort study. Faulty copies of the TTN gene, inherited from both parents, can range from fetal loss to slowly progressive muscle weakness. Counseling families is hard because the gene is huge and its splicing is complex.

Reduced fetal movement appeared in most cases, followed by joint contractures and fluid problems. About two-thirds of pregnancies with known outcomes reached birth, while others ended in termination or loss. Variant locations were plotted across gene regions and tested against severe outcomes. Genetic counselors gain pattern data for a rare condition. The authors aim to sharpen predictions made before birth.
pmc-13257178:
Seiichi Shinji and Tomio Arai close a 2026 special issue on colorectal cancer with an editorial synthesis. Colorectal cancer ranks third in diagnoses and second in cancer deaths worldwide. One highlighted stool test combined four markers and ruled out serious disease with high accuracy when all were negative. Other contributions range from crypt cell biology to robotic surgery series and mismatch-repair tumors. Operating room sustainability also appears. Oncologists get a compact map of a wide field. The editors press for methods that move discoveries into clinics faster.
pmc-13257678:

Breeders learn that gene likeness alone cannot call health value.
pmc-13257878:
Giorgio Scivoletto and colleagues hunt predictors of rehabilitation response after spinal cord injury in a 2026 chart review. More than a thousand patients admitted since 1997 were scored for independence and walking gains, stay length, and discharge home. Statistical models searched for factors tied to standout or poor response.

Complications at admission and during rehabilitation consistently cut the odds of top independence and walking gains. Older age and later admission year also lowered top-response chances for independence. Long stays were predicted by age, delay before admission, and complications. Most patients went home, while nursing placement linked to recent years, traumatic cause, and lower discharge independence. pmc-13257978:
Solomon Mohammed Salia and colleagues wrote a 2026 observational study of newborn care quality in Ghana. Observers watched 158 health workers in six facilities and scored their work against World Health Organization standards and Ghana Health Service standards for newborn care. Group talks with the workers afterwards helped explain the scores. Newborn deaths in Ghana remain above the world average, and deaths inside facilities are rising.

Only twenty percent of workers showed good practice on infection prevention and control, while forty-six percent did poorly there. Scores were middling for essential care for every newborn, at fifty-three percent, and for respectful care of mothers and newborns, at fifty-one percent. Workers blamed badly placed handwashing supplies, parent preference for methylated spirit for cord care, and missing rules for checking pain.
pmc-13258078:

pmc-13258278:
Yordanos M. Tiruneh leads a 2026 study of high blood pressure across town and country in Northeast Texas. pmc-13258478:

pmc-13258878:
Zikui Lu and coauthors teach network traffic classifiers to learn new classes from few examples in a 2026 computing paper. Encrypted sensor traffic hides its content, so models must judge from behavior patterns alone. Shared code libraries can blur those patterns and mislead the models.

Their framework pairs labeled distance training with a self taught masking task. Joint training builds features that split true behavior from library noise. Tests across nine datasets beat the strongest prior methods. Few example learning gained several points of precision with firm statistical support. Security teams watching device networks gain a classifier that adapts without huge new labeled sets.
pmc-13259278:
Fazliddin Makhmudov and coauthors detect poplar leaf diseases from photos in a 2026 study. Hand collected images from Uzbekistan and South Korea cover four common diseases, including scab and rust. The image set will be released publicly as the first dedicated poplar disease collection.

Forest managers gain both data and a scalable monitoring method.
pmc-13259478:

pmc-13259578:
Emmanuel Stip wrote a 2026 commentary on preparing Canada's health system for conflict. pmc-13259678:

pmc-13259878:

pmc-13260178:

pmc-13260278:

pmc-13260478:

The authors call eggshell paste a promising sustainable alternative for early decay care.
pmc-13261078:

pmc-13262578:

Treated colitis mice showed calmer tissue and fewer attack-mode macrophages. A partner glowing probe tracked the inflammation and the healing, a first for how this compound works.
pmc-13262678:

pmc-13263278:

Of 2,117 patients, about a third were 50 or older. Yearly relapse rates were slightly lower in the older group, and their risk of a first relapse was lower too in time-based models. pmc-13263478:

pmc-13264178:

The excerpt details group comparisons and modeling plans. Clinicians reading the full paper can judge whether uric acid adds warning value beyond established risk factors.
pmc-13264278:

pmc-13264378:

pmc-13264978:

The authors urge doctors to suspect it when scar pain follows the monthly cycle.
pmc-13265678:

Cell tests measured reactive oxygen and growth pathway proteins. One formulation ratio gave the strongest oxygen signal and pathway suppression. A mouse model of the lesion tested effects in living tissue. Therapy suppressed the same growth pathway in animals. The authors propose the formulation as a strategy to improve light therapy outcomes.
pmc-13266178:

pmc-13266578:

pmc-13266778:

pmc-13266878:

pmc-13267078:

pmc-13267978:
Christopher Seifen and colleagues present a 2026 step-by-step case report on robot surgery for throat cancer. pmc-13269178:

pmc-13269378:
Muhammad Junaid Iqbal and co-authors published a review in 2026 on vitamin D shortage in ataxia-telangiectasia, a rare disorder that affects movement, immunity, and other body systems. pmc-13269678:
Andre M N Renzaho and co-authors published a review in 2026 on food value chain programs and household food security in sub-Saharan Africa. pmc-13270378:
Weihua Zheng and co-authors narrate in 2026 the difficult course of a woman whose giant abdominal fibromatosis resisted drug treatment and then complicated its own surgical removal. A radical operation removed it, but a cascade of abnormal connections, or fistulas, opened afterward between bowel, vagina, and urinary tract.

pmc-13270678:

Both lenses performed much alike, with nearly identical far-focus scores and only tiny gaps at stronger defocus, below what normal vision testing can resolve. pmc-13270878:

Some workers still reported harmful habits, such as tying a tight band above the bite, sucking out venom, or cutting the wound. pmc-13271278:
Byeonggyu Kim is lead author of a 2026 journal article on a gene called AtGATA5 in the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana. Levels of NCED3 and ABI4 rose in the overexpressing plants, and cell tests confirmed AtGATA5 switches both genes on. They propose AtGATA5 as a new regulator of ABA balance.
pmc-13271678:

pmc-13271978:
Mónica Conesa Giménez and coauthors test in 2026 a phone app called Kalmer for young people who injure themselves without suicidal intent. Usability scores were high, and users judged objective quality as good while personal appeal needed work. The authors report gains in self-awareness and willingness to seek help, marking the app as ready for clinical testing.
pmc-13272278:
Nicholas Pischke and Thomas Powell present a 2026 mathematics paper on how fast a noisy step-by-step method settles down. The authors prove rates at which the method becomes steady, called rates of asymptotic regularity. For special cases the rates are linear, matching or beating the best known results. pmc-13272478:
Ting Xu and coauthors pool in 2026 studies of medication literacy among people with cardiovascular disease, the skill of understanding and using medicines safely. pmc-13272578:
Kaitlyn Coppetti and colleagues studied patients with many recorded allergies after gynecologic cancer surgery in a 2026 cohort report. Having four or more allergies listed in the medical record is called polyallergy. The team asked whether these patients use more extra services after surgery.

They also had more visits to emergency, urgent care, primary care, and mental health services in the year after surgery, with a typical count twice that of other patients. The link held after adjusting for other factors. The authors suggest earlier primary care and case support for this group.
pmc-13272878:

They found a three-fold lifespan extension in Heliconius over close relatives, with some species living nearly a year at most. Captive tests showed the longer life came with slower ageing in both survival and body function. The authors present Heliconius as a strong new model for studying how long life evolves and what drives healthy ageing.
pmc-13272978:
Hiroyuki Kodama leads a 2026 case report of a 61-year-old man with esophageal cancer who responded again to an immune therapy he had received before. pmc-13273278: Correction notice for a 2025 paper on upper mantle temperatures, the Iceland hotspot track, and ice-Earth interactions in Greenland. pmc-13273478:

pmc-13273778:

pmc-13273878:

pmc-13274678:

pmc-13275478:

Short sleep loss may briefly raise activity, while repeated disruption or shift work tends to lower it. Disease states often shift the timing or flatten the rhythm rather than erase it. pmc-13275578:

pmc-13276278:

pmc-13276578:

pmc-13276778:

pmc-13277078:

pmc-13277278:

pmc-13278778:

pmc-13278878:

pmc-13279378:

pmc-13279478:

pmc-13280978:

pmc-13281478:

pmc-13281578:

pmc-13281878:

pmc-13282478:

pmc-13282978:

pmc-13283178:

pmc-13283378:

pmc-13284878:

pmc-13285278:

Scan findings shaped the surgical plan. The authors urge early CT when bypass patients show blockage signs, since delays risk bowel damage.
pmc-13285378:

pmc-13285678:

pmc-13286078:

pmc-13286878:

pmc-13287178:

pmc-13288478:

pmc-13288678:

pmc-13288978:

pmc-13289078:

pmc-13289978:

pmc-13290678:

pmc-13290978:
Austrian guidance for opening the chest to restart the heart after severe injury is set out in a 2026 consensus study led by Martin W Dünser. pmc-13291078:

pmc-13292578:

pmc-13292678:

pmc-13293278:

pmc-13293378:

pmc-13293478:

pmc-13293978:

pmc-13294178:

pmc-13295378:

pmc-13295778:

pmc-13297878:

pmc-13298978:

pmc-13303878: Wenqi Chen and colleagues issue a 2026 author correction to a study on epigenetic control of thymus homing and T cell development in embryos. pmc-13305278:

pmc-13305578:

pmc-13306378:

pmc-13307578:

pmc-13308578:

pmc-13308778:

pmc-13309478:

pmc-13310378:

pmc-13310778:

pmc-13310878:

pmc-13310978:

pmc-13311078:

pmc-13311278:

pmc-13311378:

pmc-13311678:

pmc-13312278:

pmc-13312478:

pmc-13313178:

pmc-13313278:

pmc-13315878:

pmc-13316078:

pmc-13316178:

pmc-13316278:

pmc-13316878:

pmc-13317478:

Imaging, they argue, best guides which mechanism to treat in such tangled cases.
pmc-13317778:
Jian Xiao and colleagues review, in a 2026 article, pairing exosomes with engineered materials to treat diabetic skin infections, above all foot ulcers. There, infection, biofilms, low oxygen, and stalled repair gang up against healing. Plain exosome drops wash away too fast to work.

Gels, microneedle patches, membranes, and smart scaffolds can shelter the parcels, hold them in the wound, and release them on cue, while also fighting biofilm and oxygen shortage. Animal evidence shows gains in closure, vessel growth, and infection control. The review is frank about blockers: source choice, dose standards, potency tests, shelf life, and unclear regulatory boxes. Solving manufacturing consistency is the gate to real trials.
pmc-13318878:
Yonglong Yan and co-authors report a 2026 cross-sectional survey of gout patients in Xiamen, China. Questionnaires ran from November 2023 to January 2024 through an online platform. They measured knowledge, attitudes, and daily practices about gout care. Valid answers came from 462 of 622 questionnaires collected.

Median knowledge score was 16 points, with attitudes at 34 and practices at 40 in the reported results. All three domains correlated positively with each other. Knowledge linked most strongly to practice, at r = 0.539 in their analysis. Modelling showed knowledge directly shaped practice, with an effect of 0.644 in the fitted model. The attitude route was not significant. The authors describe knowledge as limited and attitudes moderately negative, yet self-management as fairly proactive.
pmc-13318978:
Konstantin Semash and colleagues describe a 2026 case of closing a large liver shunt in a three-month-old boy through a vein. The rare birth defect let portal blood bypass the liver. He showed lasting jaundice and poor growth. His bilirubin reached 316 µmol/L, and liver enzymes were very high.

Scans found a shunt up to 25 mm wide inside the liver, with an underdeveloped right lobe. A specialist team chose coil closure through the jugular vein. One coil migrated to the lung artery but was retrieved by catheter. Afterwards his liver tests normalised quickly and portal flow returned. Growth caught up during follow-up. The authors present catheter closure as feasible and effective even in very young infants.
pmc-13319078:
Nana Guo and co-authors present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis comparing two anaesthetics for older patients having abdominal surgery. Propofol infusion was weighed against inhaled sevoflurane. The question was which leaves less cognitive dysfunction afterwards. Seven randomised trials with 802 patients met the inclusion rules.

No outcome differed significantly between the two drugs. Operating time, anaesthesia time, and low blood pressure rates were similar. Rates of postoperative cognitive dysfunction matched as well. Severity scores on days one, three, and seven after surgery also showed no gap. The authors conclude neither agent is proven better for elderly patients. Larger trials are needed before any recommendation, they note. The review was registered prospectively on PROSPERO.
pmc-13319178:
Mateja Virovec, Roberto Barumerli, and Paola Cesari present a 2026 brain stimulation study of body perception in girls with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. Participants judged images of spinal curvature to find their detection thresholds. Magnetic pulses over the motor cortex then probed readiness while they viewed distorted spines. Hand muscle responses served as the readout.

Patients detected smaller curvatures than healthy controls. Their sensitivity matched their own trunk appearance ratings, not their measured Cobb angles. Motor excitability in patients peaked right at their low personal threshold. Controls peaked only for curvatures beyond what they could detect. The authors read this as a heightened motor gain tuned to lived body experience. Scoliosis, they argue, reshapes the sensorimotor system, not just the spine.
pmc-13319378:
Yaxin Wang and co-authors report a 2026 study of tiny plastic bits in sewers and how they change sewer microbes. Sewer water is low in oxygen and rich in sulfur gases, a mix that ages plastics and feeds key chemical cycles. Two common plastics were tracked as they broke down and as microbes reacted to them.

Attack by harsh oxygen forms cut key bonds in both plastics, roughened their surfaces, and split their chains. At higher doses the plastics hurt microbe health, cut sulfur gas output, and thinned microbe links. Gas making microbes that release methane grew more common, which hints that plastic loads could shift sewer gases toward more methane over time.
pmc-13319878:
Mohammed Turky and Paul MH Dummer wrote a letter to the editor in 2026 warning about chatty software that agrees too easily in dentistry. Smart tools now help with diagnosis, care plans, and study, and much debate has centered on accuracy, bias, and clear rules. A newer risk is flattery by design, where a tool echoes what the user seems to want rather than weighing the proof.

Such agreeable answers can feel helpful at first, yet in care work they may affirm a wrong call and dull sharp judgment. Unlike bias from skewed training data, this habit grows from tuning tools to please users in live chats. The letter urges makers and clinics to guard against praise that comes without proof.
pmc-13320278:
Yuya Okuzaki and co-authors study a retrovirus like gene in chicken germ cells in a 2026 article on breed saving. Germ cells are the sole seed of eggs and sperm, and growing them in dishes offers a way to bank rare chicken breeds since eggs cannot be frozen like mammal eggs. Some breeds and female lines resist dish growth, for reasons tied here to one gene and its control strip.

Lines that grew well showed higher voice of the gene, while damping its control strip lowered calm keeping genes in the cells. Damped cells stalled their growth cycle, coped poorly with DNA harm, and settled poorly into young embryo ridges after transfer. The gene pair seems to help germ cells adapt to dish life.
pmc-13320378:
Abdirahman Said Deheye and co-authors study sugar control in type 2 diabetes in Borama, Somaliland in a 2026 hospital survey. Data on long term illness care in the region is thin, and daily habits plus money strain may drive poor control more than drug access alone. Adults at one regional hospital were asked about activity, food, and work, and their long term sugar marks were read from records.

Among 152 patients seen from March to September 2023, near two thirds showed poor sugar control in the counts reported. Low activity and poor diet each stood as solo drivers of poor control after full checks, as did jobless or casual work status and low schooling. Age and sex did not hold as solo drivers. Local plans should lift movement, food quality, and work support together.
pmc-13321378:
Selim Mert and colleagues test two feed additives in broiler chickens in a 2026 feeding trial. Humate and Yucca schidigera extract were fed alone and together to 240 Ross 308 birds over 42 days, with a plain feed control group for comparison. Outcomes covered growth, carcass traits, gut shape, nutrient uptake, and antioxidant defences.

Birds on the combined diet reached the highest slaughter weight and the best carcass, breast, and thigh yields. Gut villi grew taller and wider in all supplemented groups, with the combined group strongest, and protein uptake peaked there too at day 21. Antioxidant enzymes rose in yucca fed groups. The pairing looks useful for meat bird production.
pmc-13323678:
Jan Domaradzki leads a four-country survey of nursing students on patient blood management, published in 2026, testing whether global policy reaches the classroom. Replies came from 645 master's students in Poland, Germany, Kazakhstan and Iran between October 2023 and April 2024.

Self-rated awareness sat at moderate levels, while tested knowledge ran consistently low across all countries and topics. Gaps covered alternatives to transfusion, drug-based strategies and risks of blood management itself, with some variation by country. Regression checks linked scores to background and work factors. The authors call the awareness-knowledge gap a curriculum failure and press for structured teaching of blood management in nursing degrees.
pmc-13324578:
Ekaterina Varkentin and colleagues test how sudden stress affects picture story understanding in younger and older adults, in a 2026 study. Modern life leans on images and visual stories, yet the role of stress in reading them was little explored.

Two online experiments covered 203 younger adults and 212 older adults. Timed math and logic tasks with social pressure created stress before a three-panel story task with the middle panel missing. Stress hurt younger adults, who judged the missing event worse and felt less sure of their answers. Older adults scored the same with or without stress. The authors suggest richer life-built story schemas may shield older readers.
pmc-13326778:
Darlene Heinen-Stach and co-authors systematically review randomised trials of nature-based interventions for mental health, from gardening therapy to green exercise and nature walks. Their 2026 review follows standard reporting guidance and requires a non-nature comparison group and at least one mental health outcome.

Of more than ten thousand records, forty-seven trials qualified. Seventeen reported significantly greater improvements with nature interventions than controls, particularly for depression, anxiety, and stress. No trial found nature interventions worse than established treatments such as cognitive behavioural therapy or art therapy. Studies, however, varied widely in design, duration, and outcomes, and many carried moderate to high risk of bias. The authors call the early evidence supportive but ask for longer, higher-quality studies, subgroup analyses to find who benefits most, and tests of combining nature interventions with standard treatments.
pmc-13328378:
Ridha Horchani critically reviews modern active learning for trustworthy AI in a 2026 article. Active learning fights the labeling bottleneck by asking humans to tag only the most useful examples. But the field has splintered across strategies, supervision levels, and test setups, making gains hard to compare. Horchani covers uses from medical imaging to recommender systems.

A four-axis sorting scheme organizes the field by query logic, supervision grain, operating regime, and how realistic the evaluation is. Families from uncertainty sampling to cost-aware and shift-aware methods are weighed for hidden assumptions and failure modes. The core challenge has moved, Horchani argues, from finding informative samples to building labeling pipelines that stay fair and robust in real work.
pmc-13329478:
William Wanzor and Aakriti Bhargava present a 2026 case of fast-spreading skin death in a toddler from West Texas. The boy was 15 months old and had been healthy. Carers found a dusky patch on his buttock that grew within two days, blistered, and turned black in the centre. No bite or injury had been seen.

Doctors cut away dead tissue, placed a temporary skin matrix, and later applied a skin graft. At 60 days a small open area remained and was treated with silver nitrate. The team judged the cause to be presumed brown recluse spider bite damage, based on the look of the wound and the region. Care rests on wound support, with surgery for severe cases.
pmc-13329578:
Henrietta Bánfai-Csonka and colleagues describe a university first aid responder scheme in a 2026 letter. The University of Pécs holds about 25,000 students plus several thousand staff, yet readiness for cardiac arrest varies across workplaces. A campus-wide programme began in 2022 to train staff as first responders.

Since launch, 266 employees finished the first 10-hour course, and yearly refreshers drew 390 attendances in total, as reported in the letter. Training stresses hands-on resuscitation and defibrillator use, taught by paramedics, with yearly 4-hour scenario refreshers. An online group shares updates and case talk between courses. Defibrillator coverage also grew, reaching 15 devices across the university in the account given.
pmc-13330978:
Hui Wang and colleagues scan United States harm reports for dual-target antibodies in blood cancer care in a 2026 study. Reports tied to CD3 by CD20 bispecific drugs were drawn from the FDA system from late 2022 to early 2025. In total, 2,237 reports covered three drugs: epcoritamab, glofitamab, and mosunetuzumab.

Signal counts came to 93 for the first drug, 65 for the second, and 41 for the third in the reported analysis, with methods agreeing closely. Some signals are absent from current labels, including a brain white matter disease and a severe immune overreaction for one drug. Fatal outcome and timing patterns were also charted. The authors urge closer watch and further study of fresh signals.
pmc-13332478:
Myles N. Arrington and co-authors linked brain responses to faces with teenagers' social lives in a 2026 analysis of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study. Social health means having enough good relationships, and early adolescence is when peer bonds take center stage, yet brain studies usually examine single social measures at a time.

They paired brain scans at ages 8 to 11 with social data at ages 10 to 13. The data covered 5,832 adolescents, grouping peer measures such as friend counts, bullying experiences, and peer support into profiles. Three profiles emerged: concerning at 12.96 percent, robust at 33.95 percent, and selective at 53.09 percent. Amygdala reactivity to emotional faces interacted with sex in predicting profile membership, while other regions mattered only for single outcomes. The authors read this as evidence of divergent paths between brain function and social health.
pmc-13332978:
Satoshi Kikuchi and co-authors present early family-tree results for Japan's willows in a 2026 phylogenetics study, with special care for species found nowhere else. Willows are notoriously hard to classify because they hybridize freely and vary widely in form.

The team used multi-locus data from low-copy nuclear genes plus chloroplast sequences for all available native species. They found three major lineages inside the Japanese subgenus Vetrix and showed that subgenus Chamaetia is not a single natural group. Signs of past hybridization turned up in S. miyabeana and S. nakamurana. The authors note tangled gene trees and old cross-breeding mean genome-scale work is still needed.
pmc-13333378:
Stephan Neidhart and colleagues charted the brain-wave fingerprint of epilepsy that follows autoimmune encephalitis in a 2026 study, comparing it with ordinary temporal lobe epilepsy. After the immune attack settles, doctors often struggle to tell whether ongoing seizures stem from that earlier inflammation or from a separate cause.

The team studied 72-hour EEG recordings, scans, and spinal fluid results from 25 patients with post-encephalitis epilepsy and 30 with temporal lobe epilepsy. The autoimmune group showed far more slowing and epileptic discharges arising independently on both sides of the brain, the two patterns often appearing together. It also showed a wider spread in the EEG spectrum across wake and sleep, most over the temporal regions. A combined score built from EEG, imaging, fluid, and clinical features separated the groups sharply. The authors propose the patterns and score as biomarkers to guide immune testing, seizure drug choices, and surgery decisions.
pmc-13336378:
Lingzhi Chen and co-authors built a sensing facemask that screens for tuberculosis from breath droplets or sputum in a 2026 diagnostics study. Conventional TB testing is invasive and slow, which delays control of a disease that spreads through the air.

The mask carries an array of silver-gold nanoflowers. A second sensor uses urchin-shaped gold-silver particles in a covalent organic framework. Together they detect the TB antigen pair ESAT-6/CFP-10 by surface-enhanced Raman scattering. On clinical samples the assay sorted 12 negative and 17 positive patients with 100 percent specificity and 76.5 percent sensitivity in the study, and sputum testing caught two cases droplets missed. It also flagged two of six close contacts with suspiciously high antigen, hinting at hidden infection.
pmc-13336878:
Yan Zu and colleagues identify a protein-tagging enzyme that drives harmful heart enlargement in a 2026 study. RNF115 was high in failing human hearts, in mouse hearts squeezed by a narrowed aorta, and in heart cells dosed with angiotensin II. Quieting it eased cell enlargement in the lab, and removing it only in heart cells protected mice from pressure-induced damage.

pmc-13337078:
Shijie Qian and colleagues unmask a non-enzyme trick behind kidney cancer drug resistance in a 2026 study. Sunitinib blocks tumor blood supply and growth, yet resistance always emerges. pmc-13337878:
Can Cui and co-authors study allergy to hair products in scalp seborrheic dermatitis in a 2026 clinic study. The scaly, inflamed scalp condition weakens the skin barrier and makes topical products hard to tolerate. Links between product allergy and scalp microbes were unclear.

Sixty-three people had patch tests with 62 allergens and were grouped by scalp involvement. Severity, water loss, and moisture were measured, and 36 patients with scalp disease gave samples for bacterial and fungal sequencing. Cobalt, nickel, and several product ingredients were common triggers. Certain allergens tracked with water loss and with microbes such as Malassezia and Candida in the reported links.
pmc-13338678:
Sarah Vollam and a large team review wearable monitoring of hospital patients with COVID-19 in a 2026 data study. Wrist or patch systems track heart rate, breathing rate, and oxygen nonstop. Evidence on real ward use and on how often nurses still take manual readings was thin.

Three isolation wards in a large United Kingdom hospital displayed live readings on a central dashboard. Records were reviewed to describe vital sign patterns outside intensive care. A later exploratory check asked whether showing the data changed manual measurement frequency. Findings help wards judge what continuous monitoring adds beyond standard spot checks.
pmc-13340678:
Breast inflammation in pregnancy caused by an unusual germ is reported by Hassan Alyami's team in a 2026 case report. The 42-year-old woman, early in pregnancy, got pain, swelling, and redness in her left breast that kept returning despite several rounds of antibiotics and repeated drainage work.

Tissue showed non-caseating granulomatous inflammation, and culture in the third trimester grew Mycobacterium avium complex, never before seen in an immunocompetent pregnant patient. Steroids and anti-mycobacterial drugs were held back until after delivery. Eighteen months of rifampin, ethambutol, and azithromycin after delivery then cleared the disease fully, on examination and imaging alike.
pmc-13341078:
Predicting where microRNAs bind their targets is the job of miRNAProtPred, a 2026 software paper by Somenath Dutta and colleagues. The Python package merges seed matching with thermodynamic stability checks from ViennaRNA into one workflow needing little manual setup.

It draws on 2,656 curated human miRNAs and accepts DNA, RNA, or protein inputs, scoring candidates by seed fit, free energy, flanking AU content, and match type. A strict mode demands exact seed pairing, while a relaxed mode allows G:U wobble. pmc-13341178:

pmc-13342978:
Xiaoman Wang and colleagues present a 2026 genomic dataset for Aristida triseta, a protected wild grass in China. The team sequenced its full chloroplast genome from dried leaf material and then built richer DNA barcode sets for the whole Aristida genus by merging new reads with public sequences.

Matching and tree analyses showed each barcode tied the species to its genus while carrying differing signals. The sets support species identification, breeding work, and diversity studies for this protected plant.
pmc-13347078:

One site sits in Memphis, in the United States. The other sits at a health sciences university in Saudi Arabia. Each site will recruit 20 to 30 adults. Clinic partners will help with recruiting. Sampling will vary on purpose.

Each person will join a one-hour guided interview. Daily self-care is one topic. Barriers and supports are others. Views on digital health tools will be asked too. Themes will be drawn out with mixed coding. Enrolment was set to begin in August 2026. The value lies in the comparison plan, not in findings.
pmc-13347778:
Dineo Monaheng and colleagues check lasting hepatitis B protection in South African health students, in a study from 2026. Antibody levels marked whether protection still held.

At entry only 43 percent held antibody levels counted as protective, a gap that matters for ward work where exposure risk is real. pmc-13348378:

Spores came from spotted leaves in Florida. A trial field supplied the leaves in 2016. Treated agar cleaned the spores. Long-read sequencing then read their DNA. pmc-13349778:

Treatments that can suit both diseases are set against those that help one organ and harm the other, guiding patient grouping by signs, markers, and past therapy.
pmc-13349978:
Hua Zhong and co-authors used an image-generating AI in 2026 to map lung blood vessels from scans taken without dye. Planning partial lung removal needs a clear three-dimensional picture of arteries and veins near a nodule, but some patients cannot receive contrast dye.

Their generative model learned from paired spectral scans in 130 patients to fake contrast-style images from plain ones, using attention and a mixed slice approach to handle breathing shifts. It was then tested on 82 patients scanned on machines from two makers. Vessel rebuilding within a zone around each nodule was checked. Success could widen safe surgical planning to dye-free patients.
pmc-13350178:
Cassandra A. Omane and Sarah Forberger reviewed in 2026 how young adults judge online nutrition information. Young people search the internet daily for diet advice, while traditional health gatekeepers matter less and misinformation spreads fast.

Screening five databases and grey literature through late 2024 yielded 48 papers and 82 separate factors shaping trust. Clear writing was named most often, followed by the reader's own prior knowledge and education. Far fewer studies covered the channel, setting, or design of the information. Knowing what earns trust helps health communicators present sound diet advice in forms young adults will actually believe and use.
pmc-13351378:
Yuxin Jiang and colleagues proposed a framework in 2026 for reading kidney harm from antibody-drug conjugates, cancer drugs that carry a toxic payload to tumour cells. Their review links each drug's construction and inner cell processing to how much free payload reaches the kidney, then matches those patterns against the well-known kidney effects of ordinary chemotherapy. Evidence is layered by source quality rather than pooled. A mechanism-first map could help oncologists anticipate which patients will develop which kidney problem.
pmc-13351578:
Lydia Viviana Falsitta leads a 2026 scoping review of brain scan changes around seizures in children. Twenty-seven studies met the criteria, most on long febrile seizures and status epilepticus. Early scans often showed swelling and bright signals in the hippocampus, while later scans showed shrinkage and scarring in some children. Blood-flow scans showed early high flow at the seizure site. The authors stress uneven evidence and call for larger studies split by seizure type.
pmc-13351978:
Fawen Dai and co-authors test finely ground bamboo powder in layer hen feed in 2026. Bamboo powder is rich in insoluble fibre, but its value and best dose in hen diets were unclear. A total of 480 Hy-Line Brown hens aged 42 weeks were split into four groups for 28 days after a 7-day settling period.

Groups ate a plain diet or diets with 2, 3, or 4 percent bamboo powder added. The 4 percent group laid fewer eggs and had lower egg mass in the second half and overall. Blood fat, protein, and sugar levels did not differ clearly. Nutrient uptake fell in the highest dose group. Gut structure and gut microbes in droppings were also checked to guide a sensible dose.
pmc-13356778:
Paula Diaz and co-authors studied in 2026 why sensory nerves fail to regrow in skin affected by recessive dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa, a severe blistering disease from a faulty collagen gene. Patients live with chronic wounds, pain, and itch, and often lose small nerve fibers. The team compared wounded skin and skin cells from patients with healthy responses.

Fluid from patient blisters made sensory nerve tips collapse and blocked new growth in lab tests. The authors say this hostile mix both blocks regrowth and fuels nerve pain.
pmc-13359878:
Leilei Zhang and co-authors forecast good fishing spots for chub mackerel in a 2026 study. This Northwest Pacific fish shifts its grounds with the seasons and ocean state, so fishers waste fuel hunting for it. The team built a prediction model from ocean data and asked which time spans of data matter most: the moment, the recent week, or the long background.

Blending time scales helped in different ways: a week of recent ocean data sharpened overall sorting, while mixing short and long views caught more of the truly rich grounds. An explanation method showed which ocean factors drove each call. Better forecasts can raise catches while easing pressure on the stock.
pmc-13359978:
Atsushi Ogura and co-authors test tailor-made treatment for advanced rectal cancer in a 2026 study. Standard care gives radiation before surgery to nearly everyone, yet radiation can cause lasting harm and some patients may not need it. The team instead shaped each plan to the tumor's traits and to how it answered an opening round of chemotherapy.

Nearly a third of patients safely skipped radiation altogether, with no loss in complete cancer removal at surgery. A subset responded strongly enough to skip surgery altogether. The early outcomes suggest that customizing care can prevent overtreatment, preserve organs, and protect quality of life while keeping cure rates strong.
pmc-13361678:
Kaltrina Veseli and co-authors surveyed tooth care habits and bite alignment in young children in a 2026 study. Good habits in childhood prevent oral disease and may shape how the jaws and teeth develop. The team studied 90 children aged six to nine in the Pristina region of Kosovo. They used the World Health Organization's standard oral health questionnaire for children.

The survey covered brushing habits, fluoride awareness, dental visits, diet, mouth symptoms, and quality of life. Each child's bite was also classed by the Angle system, which sorts how the upper and lower teeth meet. The team then looked for links between habits and bite class. Such links can guide school and family programs that build good habits before crooked bites set in.
pmc-13362478:
Ryang Soon Lim and colleagues report a 2026 before-and-after study of a smart drug cabinet in a Korean hospital emergency department. The cabinet links to the hospital record system and controls how drugs are stored and handed out. The team compared drug use, errors, and costs in the months before and after the cabinet arrived, then checked again three years later.

Drug errors fell from 41 in the first window to 14 in the next, with the biggest drop in delivery mistakes. Stored drug items in the department shrank by more than nine tenths, and upkeep costs fell sharply too. Nurses rated drug safety high, and the gains held at three years, which supports wider use of linked cabinets.
pmc-13364378:
Yakubu Zakaria and co-workers build a 2026 low cost soil wetness node that runs on sun power for farms in Ghana. Cheap probes drift by soil type, so the team first tuned three probes in loam sand in the lab. They then set the node in a drip fed onion field.

Lab tuned reads matched the hand weigh method well, with small error. The node sent field data by long range radio to a small local server and a cloud store. With wider field proof, such nodes could time watering by real soil need and save scarce water.
pmc-13366178:
Theyazn Aldhyani builds in 2026 a deep learn frame to spot Parkinson ill from hand draws and hand write bits. Folks with the ill gain most from early care. Hand tasks show its marks in a cheap, safe way. The frame pairs a known image net with a sight form net.

Its test set holds spiral, wave, and round draws, plus two words in Arabic script, from ill and well folks. The form net scores full marks on the draw sets and on one word set. With more data, such hand checks could back fast, low cost calls in clinic.
pmc-13367078:
Carolina Schinke and co-workers give in 2026 a plain words sum of how a bone marrow cancer drug, talquetamab, shapes how patients feel and act day to day. The sum rests on a trial of folks whose ill came back or shrugs off past care. Folks fill three forms on health and acts at set rounds.

First rounds feel worse, the sum says. Past round three, body, mood, and mate acts hold or rise, with less tire, pain, and breath short. Gains hold to round twenty one. The plain sum helps patients weigh care by life feel, not just lab marks.
pmc-13371878:
Andrea Navalón Calzada and co-authors report a rare gut tear in a 2026 case report. A man aged 74, who had a kidney swap and took drugs to calm his immune system, came in with belly pain, fever, and loose stool. Small pouches in his small gut had grown sore.

Scans showed a pouch with air in the gut wall and a small leak held in by nearby tissue. At surgery the team found the tear and cut out the bad gut part, then joined the ends. He did well after the work. The case shows why fast scans and surgery count in patients with weak immune defenses.
pmc-13372378:
Arman Athwal and co-authors tested how scan settings shape eye response reads in a 2026 study. The method watches the light cells at the back of the eye shrink and stretch when light hits them. It uses a common type of eye scanner, set up as clinics might use it.

Seven healthy eyes were scanned while beam width, scan speed, and image blends changed. The two-step response showed each time. A wider beam showed cells more clearly but did not lift the response much. More blends of shots cut noise a lot. The work gives plain rules for clinics that want to add this test on standard gear.
pmc-13372678:
Nancy Morrow-Howell and co-authors asked older adults about age bias in a 2026 study. They ran nine group talks with 58 people aged 60 and up. Most were women, and the most common age band was 75 to 79.

Some had not heard the term for age bias, and some said they had not felt it. Once the idea was clear, most named slights at work, in clinics, in shops, and in the home. Bias turned inward was less known but came up in talk. The team says anti-bias work should speak to older adults first, not just to the young or to staff.
pmc-13374378:
Jon Azpeitia and co-authors watched a small molecule land on a prized sheet stuff in a 2026 study. The sheet is a two-part crystal used in chips and sensors. Dressing its face with molecules can tune its traits, but the type of bond has long been in doubt.

The molecule was laid down in a vacuum on sheets with few and with many face gaps. Fine scope views showed it lay flat and kept its sulfur tip whole. It roamed the face with ease and gripped gaps hard. The clear bond tale helps chip staff dress the sheet with more trust and less waste.
pmc-13378178:
Jessica C Costa-Pinto and co-authors set out a 2026 trial protocol called ARROW, on preventing repeat hospital stays for preschool wheeze. Wheezing illness is one of the most common reasons young children are admitted to hospital. Many are readmitted, and few preventive options exist.

Children in the trial receive either OM-85, a product made from killed bacteria that is taken by mouth, or a dummy treatment, with neither families nor staff knowing which. The main question is whether OM-85 cuts admissions for wheeze over twelve months of treatment. The trial also counts wheeze episodes and their length, and weighs the cost of treatment against any savings from fewer admissions.
pmc-13378378:
Xinyu Wang and colleagues present a 2026 review of a family of enzymes in heart failure, where the heart cannot pump well enough. These enzymes, called ADAM and ADAMTS proteases, cut other proteins and thereby shape inflammation, scarring, and heart muscle growth. Earlier accounts often treated them one by one.

The review joins the picture in two directions: members of the family meet within each disease process, and single enzymes such as ADAM17 act across several processes at once. Some actions harm the heart while others protect it. That fuller view may guide drugs that block only the harmful members, and it supports using some members as blood markers for diagnosis.
pmc-13383978:
Gioele Pecin and co-authors uncover a new cell-killing compound from a little-studied fungus in 2026 work. The fungus, gathered from a rare Spanish plant, was grown under 78 conditions to wake up its chemistry. Screening and molecular networking mapped a wide set of toxins and active compounds it can make.

Among them sat spectabilide A, a ring-shaped molecule built from three amino acids and a fatty side chain. It killed breast cancer cells strongly in lab tests, the team reports. Gene and chemistry evidence also moved the fungus into a new genus placement, which the authors formalize with a new name combination.
pmc-13384778:
Watanabe and Inaba reviewed in 2026 how zinc ions steer two quality-control proteins that cycle between the endoplasmic reticulum and the Golgi, the cell's folding and shipping stations. Zinc is the second most common trace metal in cells and serves as enzyme helper, structural brace, and signal. Two transporter families keep its levels tight, feeding it into or out of the cell's compartments.

Recent structural work shows zinc binding reshapes the chaperone ERp44, which retrieves stray proteins. The cargo receptor ERGIC-53, which ferries select proteins onward, switching their grip and release in step with zinc and acidity changes along the route. These findings cast zinc as an active regulator of the early secretory pathway, not just a nutrient. The authors say the mechanism helps explain how metal balance supports proteostasis, the upkeep of a healthy protein set, and may inform disease linked to these proteins.
pmc-13385078:
Wei Zhao and co-authors organize cancer drug design around the pyridine ring in a 2026 medicinal chemistry review. Pyridine appears in many approved cancer drugs, yet its value depends heavily on context, the authors stress. Sections sort compounds by what the ring actually does, from target binding to property tuning.

Examples span classic drugs, antibody-drug conjugate payloads, targeted degraders, and metal complexes with several pyridine units. Each case is weighed for structure-activity patterns and for body handling and safety liabilities. The closing message treats pyridine as a design module to validate case by case, not a magic scaffold.
pmc-13386678:
Ellen Gabrielsen Hjelle and a large team test a coordinator-led support program for Parkinson's patients and family carers in 2026 work. OPTIM-PARK ran across Denmark, Norway, Spain, and the United Kingdom in community settings. A named coordinator assessed personal needs, gave support, and linked health, social, and voluntary services over three months.

The program enrolled 130 people, 72 with Parkinson's and 58 family carers, typically across three consultations. Active listening and tailored information anchored the coordinator's work, the team reports from logs and interviews. The mixed-methods study weighs feasibility and acceptability to guide wider rollout of multisector care.
pmc-13388478:
Tuck Wah Siew and co-authors describe a new filler technique for hollows under the eyes in a 2026 report covering three patients. The area is hard to treat because the skin is thin and fat is sparse, and standard filler placed deep in the muscle can still cause swelling or a bluish tint.

Called BB8, the method dilutes a cohesive hyaluronic acid gel with saline and places it just under the skin through a cannula. Photos were taken before care and again afterwards. Follow-up ran for six to nine months, with hollow severity scored on a standard scale. Clinicians interested in facial aesthetics get a detailed early account of the approach, its steps, and its safety record in this small group.
pmc-13390378:
Jonghoon Kang writes, in 2026, a letter offering a fresh thermodynamic reading of how a heat-loving bacterium gathers plant sugars. The letter responds to work by Tjo and colleagues on an uptake system in Anaerocellum bescii, a microbe that breaks down tough plant material at very high temperatures.

Because the original work reported full heat, disorder, and energy values for sugar binding to two carrier proteins, Kang argues that an extra layer of analysis is possible. The letter contrasts the distinct strategies the two proteins use to bind chains of sugar units. Biochemists gain a compact reinterpretation showing how complete thermodynamic reporting lets other scientists extract new meaning without new experiments.
pmc-13393278:
Keunho Soh and seven colleagues put two kinds of memristor into a single probabilistic computing chip. A memristor is an electrical part whose resistance remembers current history. Hard pairing problems can be cast as energy landscapes stored in a grid of such devices, while flickering probabilistic bits explore the landscape. Their design uses volatile memristors, whose filaments form and break at random, as the flickering bits, and stable memristors in a selector-free grid to hold the problem itself.

Because the stable devices form reliable nanocluster paths, the grid works without extra selector parts that usually clutter arrays. The combined system ran reversible AND and NAND logic in both forward and inverse directions, a hallmark trick of probabilistic machines. Tests of a small binary multiplier suggest the approach scales, and the authors present it as a practical route to fully hardware-based probabilistic computing.
pmc-13394278:
Annisa Zahra Ahdaliza and eight colleagues improved air-made perovskite solar cells by stirring caesium iodide directly into the lead iodide layer before the crystal forms. That sidesteps solubility limits that normally keep caesium unevenly spread. Making these cells in open air suits mass production, but moisture spoils crystallisation. The pre-mixed approach distributes caesium uniformly and steers crystal growth toward larger grains with fewer defects.

At the best dose, grains grew by well over half, dislocation density and deep trap states fell, and strain in the lattice relaxed, cutting wasted charge recombination. Champion cells converted sunlight at over twenty-three percent efficiency with little hysteresis, and a glovebox version did slightly better still. Unsealed devices kept nearly all their output under continuous light and most of it after a month in ambient storage. The authors offer the recipe as a scalable path to stable cells.
pmc-13394878:
Yuvraj Pathak, David Muhlestein, and Matthew Balcarras show, in 2026, that one doctor can charge many prices for the same office service. New United States rules force insurers to post the rates they strike with providers. The team pulled files from the biggest national payers for late 2025. They studied the twenty most used office services.

For a single provider, the gap between the lowest and highest rate averaged a large share of the public Medicare rate. The same visit or test can thus cost plans very different sums. The authors say employers and rule makers can use the data to pick leaner networks. Sunlight on rates, they argue, is a first step to lower spending.
pmc-13395478:
Mitchell Manware and co-authors measure, in 2026, how far public views of deadly weather stray from science in the United States. Death rates from wildfire smoke, heat, cold, floods, and drought have now been mapped by county. Yale survey maps give what adults in each county think about climate harm. The team set views beside the death maps to size the gap.

Perception gaps followed the same map pattern as real death rates. Counties where more people accept that warming is happening showed smaller gaps for every weather type. Fewer than half of adults think warming will harm them in person. The authors say lifting basic climate grasp is key to cutting health risk.
pmc-13395978:
Marcus Vinicius Almeida Marques and co-authors hunted for new chemistry in a fungus living inside a plant, and report a new compound in 2026. The fungus, Talaromyces pinophilus strain J6, came from the plant Euphorbia umbellata and was part of a wider search for useful natural products.

Rather than test every extract blindly, the group first scanned the fungus with high-resolution mass spectrometry and matched signals against a home-built library of known Talaromyces compounds. Seven known products were named that way, which pointed them toward one unknown. Purifying the extract yielded a new polyketide, named (-)-R-talaropinophiloic acid, plus a known relative, and lab methods fixed both structures.
pmc-13396178:
Guo and co-authors optimize, in 2026, a bacterial gene-insertion system for use in human cells, for therapies that need whole genes delivered to exact addresses. The IS621 recombinase uses a bridge RNA with two programmable loops, one gripping the target site and one the donor DNA. The team engineered the protein and its RNA partner, producing a system they call enIS621-tebRNA, and tested it across five cell types including kidney, colon, retinal, immune, and liver lines.

The engineered system inserted kilobase-scale DNA cargos at rates up to 27.75 percent of treated cells, without leaving scar sequences. As a demonstration, they installed the gene for a CD19 chimeric antigen receptor, the targeting unit of CAR T-cell cancer therapy, at chosen loci. They also integrated the gene encoding Factor IX, the clotting protein missing in hemophilia B. The authors present the platform as a versatile route to gene insertion.
pmc-13396378:
Zhang and colleagues identify, in 2026, a biomechanical driver of radioresistance in glioblastoma, the brain tumor that accounts for 50.1 percent of primary intrinsic malignant brain tumors and still carries a median survival under two years. Stiffening of the tumor's surrounding matrix helped cancer stem cells survive radiation. Gene analysis showed stiff matrices switch on the protein IQGAP3 through the YAP1 and TEAD transcription factors in these stem cells.

IQGAP3 binds and stabilizes SOX2, a core stem-cell transcription factor, sustaining self-renewal and survival after irradiation. Blocking IQGAP3 lowered SOX2 levels in cells and animals, resensitizing tumors to radiation and slowing growth in their models. Screening approved drugs for ones that disrupt the IQGAP3-SOX2 grip identified trimetrexate, an existing drug that reaches the brain, as a pharmacologic disruptor. The authors propose pairing such a drug with radiotherapy to attack the stem-cell niche that stiffness creates.
pmc-13396578:
Hannah Demleitner and co-authors evaluated what it was like to build a patient guide with patients, rather than for them, in palliative care. Their 2026 qualitative study follows the making of a German patient guide linked to a best-practice recommendation on intentional sedation at the end of life.

Between April and September 2024, participants answered open-ended questionnaires and then sat for interviews about the joint work. The authors sorted what helped the partnership, such as clear roles and time to build trust, from what hindered it. Patient involvement is praised worldwide in guideline work, but reports on how it plays out for patient-facing material in palliative care remain rare.
pmc-13396778:
Itsuma Nagao writes a 2026 perspective on gut-on-a-chip systems that grow human intestinal microbes alongside gut tissue, and what they could do for drug testing. Many swallowed drugs are changed by the gut before reaching the blood. This first-pass effect varies by person, which helps explain why the same dose acts differently across patients.

Chips that pair a living gut lining with a cultured microbial community let researchers measure host, microbe, and drug acting on each other directly. Nagao argues such platforms could feed predictive models of a person's gut ecosystem, guiding dose choices and flagging drug-microbe clashes that current rules-based testing barely covers.
pmc-13397578:
N A Vernice and co-authors review what to do when a silicone breast implant breaks silently in an older patient. Their 2026 scoping review searches medical databases through January 2025. Regulators advise scans starting five to six years after placement, yet no guidance covers symptom-free ruptures in elderly patients, whose surgical risk and life horizon differ.

More than 3.5 million people in the United States carry implants, and break risk grows as devices age, though modern gel implants last better. The review weighs watchful scanning against removal or exchange, balancing operation risk, comfort and quality of life. From the gathered evidence the authors draft practical advice meant for shared decisions with older patients.
pmc-13399078:
The Journal of Diabetes Investigation issued this Expression of Concern in 2026 about a 2017 article by M. Xue and colleagues. That article studied fatty change in donor livers as a risk factor for new diabetes arising soon after liver transplantation. The journal, its editor-in-chief, and the publisher Wiley agreed to alert readers.

A third-party organization raised doubts about where the transplanted organs came from. The study covered transplants done between 2001 and 2014, when most cases in China predated the voluntary donation program. Reporting suggests organs were widely taken from executed prisoners before 2015. The authors did not answer the publisher's questions, so consent records and ethics approvals could not be checked. Readers are warned that the organ sourcing may not have met the ethics standards of its time.
pmc-13399478:
Jie Gao and colleagues propose a combined scheduling and routing system for fleets of automated guided vehicles in warehouses with movable containers, in a 2026 engineering study. The team's design attacks all three problems at once and tests the result in a simulated multi-zone warehouse.

First, each job is split into two sub-tasks: a long-distance haul and a precision in-racking placement, each handed to the vehicle type built for it. Second, a pre-allocation algorithm lines up a vehicle's next assignment before it finishes the current one, cutting the empty running that plagues conventional dispatch. Simulation comparisons showed a lower system no-load rate, less path congestion, and better overall throughput than the baseline methods. The authors present the package as a step toward warehouses that replan themselves continuously.
pmc-13400478:
Zirui Luo leads a randomized trial, published in 2026, of combined magnetic stimulation for swallowing problems after stroke. The method pairs stimulation over the brain with stimulation of peripheral nerves. How it changes brain networks was unclear, so brain activity was measured alongside swallowing tests.

Forty-four patients were split into four groups mixing real and sham versions of each stimulation type. The fully active group gained most on eating ability and on a scale grading how safely food passes the airway. Video X-ray measures of throat movement also improved most there. Light-based brain scans showed stronger links within the front and movement-sensing network on the stroke side, tied to better throat closure.
pmc-13400578:
Francisco José Navarro-Triviño and colleagues review, in 2026, a signaling pair called OX40 and OX40L that helps T cells persist in inflamed skin and airways. The pathway was long tied to type 2 inflammation, the kind behind allergy. New work widens its role across both tissues.

Acting late in T cell activation, OX40 keeps effector cells alive, builds tissue-resident memory and tunes regulatory cells. Alarm signals from surface tissue switch on its partner on presenting cells, reinforcing allergic-type responses. The axis feeds chronic disease in eczema, asthma, rhinitis and nasal polyps, and also appears in other immune patterns and disorders. Antibody drugs targeting the pathway are discussed as a shared treatment angle.
pmc-13400678:
Iulian D Toader argues, in 2026, that the nineteenth-century mathematician Hermann Hankel held to his guiding principle for extending number systems for a subtle reason. The principle says formal laws should stay permanent when mathematics grows. Hankel used it both to extend numbers and to justify formal theories detached from intuition about size.

Yet he admitted limits: some extensions clashed with the principle, and a formal account of irrational numbers looked inconsistent to him. Toader reads his loyalty as a conservative strategy that still allows revising basic arithmetic laws when reasons to revise outweigh reasons to keep them. Later critics, by contrast, hardened the principle into an anti-revision stance that cost them parts of modern mathematics.
pmc-13400878:
Alicia-Sophie Schebesta and colleagues test, in 2026, whether the chemistry and length of separation columns still matter for proteome depth on the fastest mass spectrometers. Protein detection once depended heavily on good separation. Modern instruments sample so quickly that the balance may have shifted.

The team ran five column chemistries across eight lengths on a high-speed instrument. Despite differing materials and sizes, results converged. The standard chemistries all found over 150,000 precursors and roughly nine thousand protein groups. Retention patterns still differed by chemistry. Yet those differences did not turn into real coverage gains. Column choice, within modern ranges, appears far less critical than before.
pmc-13401278:
Amirali Alizadeh wrote a 2026 letter to the editor about a study by Kalantari and colleagues that counted workflow interruptions during 251 operations in five academic teaching hospitals. That study logged over fifty thousand minutes of operating room activity and attributed 45 of 319 identified causes, about 14 percent, to teaching and trainees.

Alizadeh argues the harder question is what those trainee-related pauses actually do. The 14.1 percent figure is a share of identified causes, not of the 281 interruption events, since one event could have several causes. A pause might mean poor preparation, slower supervised learning, or a senior surgeon stopping a trainee to prevent harm. Lumping them together, the letter warns, hides whether teaching moments protect patients or simply disrupt work.
pmc-13401378:
Corneille Kabagale Ansima and a large team of co-authors describe a 2026 study of past records on drug-resistant bacteria. The records come from Bukavu Provincial General Referral Hospital in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. Data on resistance in the region are scarce, even though resistant germs hit low- and middle-income countries hardest.

The team analysed 1,801 distinct bacterial strains from routine samples collected during 2024. Standard lab methods named the germs, and drug response was read against EUCAST 2024 rules. Enterobacterales dominated the set, at just over 80 percent of strains, followed by Gram-positive cocci at about 11 percent and non-fermenting Gram-negative bacilli at about 8 percent. Results are broken down by bacterial group, antibiotic class, and major resistance patterns, giving a local picture of how much multidrug resistance the hospital faces.
pmc-13401678:
Addae Boateng Adu-Gyamfi analysed anaemia among women of reproductive age in Lesotho using the country's 2023 to 2024 Demographic and Health Survey, in a 2026 study. Globally, more than 600 million women aged 15 to 49 live with anaemia, with the heaviest burdens in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa.

The analysis covered 3,105 women with complete haemoglobin measurements, surveyed between late November 2023 and the end of February 2024. Overall prevalence came out at just under 54 percent of women, a level classed as a severe public health problem. Descriptive statistics set the scale, and a binary logistic regression model identified associated factors, reported as crude and adjusted odds ratios with confidence intervals. The findings give Lesotho's health planners a current national estimate and a set of risk markers to target.
pmc-13401778:
Inès Lakbar and Daniele Poole wrote a 2026 essay on why meta-analyses of the same question can disagree, using melatonin drugs for preventing delirium in critically ill patients as their worked example. Meta-analysis is widely treated as the top of the evidence ladder, but the authors argue the pooled number is built, not simply found.

Investigators must decide which studies are similar enough to combine and how much to trust each one, and those judgement calls construct the estimate. Chaves and colleagues included both melatonin and ramelteon and found support for prevention. The authors' own group restricted the pool to melatonin alone and concluded the evidence was too weak to recommend routine use. Quantitative pooling, they warn, can hide the contribution of the most credible studies rather than clarify it.
pmc-13402878:
Motahare Baghestani and co-authors set out reference values for healthy bone density around tooth roots, measured from digital dental images. Bone density reflects the balance of bone building and breakdown, shifts with age, hormones, and diseases from osteoporosis to thyroid trouble, and guides dental decisions from implants to treatment planning. The bone holding teeth differs between jaws, with upper jaw bone typically thinner and more porous.

Their descriptive analysis reads normal periapical density, the tissue at root tips, on digital radiographs to define what healthy looks like before disease enters the picture. Such baselines matter because dentists judge loss against an expected norm, and alveolar bone thins naturally with age even without illness. The authors frame the values as groundwork for spotting abnormal change and for planning care around teeth and implants.
pmc-13403278:
Tanemura and co-authors report, in 2026, a severe complication of leadless pacemaker implantation. During retrieval of the device in an 86-year-old man treated for heart block and syncope, the heart's papillary muscle was caught between the delivery sheath and the pacemaker. It tore away, causing massive leakage through the tricuspid valve. Leadless devices avoid many lead-related problems, but effects on the tricuspid valve were known; this rupture route was new.

Resistance during removal was the warning sign of the entrapment, a lesson the authors stress for operators. The patient then developed worsening heart failure needing non-invasive ventilation and intravenous furosemide at 20 milligrams twice daily, and imaging showed sharply reduced left ventricular function with an ejection fraction of 26.7 percent in follow-up studies. He received a transvenous pacemaker, recovered on medication without valve surgery, and transferred to rehabilitation, a benign ending the authors document.
pmc-13403478:
Madeleine Nicolas led a 2026 map study of child leukemia deaths across Mexico over two decades. Death records for ages 0 to 19 covered every local district from 2003 to 2023. The team hunted for clusters and then matched them against land, water, and industry data.

Ten strong clusters appeared, five with high death rates and five with low rates. High-rate areas hugged the Gulf coast and the southeast. All five high clusters overlapped oil and gas sites, on wet land where rain can soak pollutants into ground water. Low clusters sat mostly in the dry west. The pattern points to preventable local causes worth urgent checks.
pmc-13403678:
Monika Stompor-Gorący and colleagues gave a first review in 2026 of pedalitin, a plant compound in the flavonoid family. Plants make such compounds as pigments and as part of their chemical defenses. Lab reports credit pedalitin with fighting cancer cells, easing swelling, and guarding inner organs.

It may also sharpen insulin response and shield nerve cells, based on early studies. The review gathers how the compound is obtained and how its actions have been tested. Small chemical changes to its shape could yield new drug leads. The authors frame it as a hopeful base for work on diseases tied to modern lifestyles.
pmc-13403778:
Ji-Seok Yoon and co-authors tested in 2026 a long-acting form of human C-peptide as a shield for the mouse retina. Excess glutamate signaling kills the nerve cells that carry sight, a process tied to glaucoma. Their version links the peptide to a carrier polymer for slow release in the eye.

A toxin that mimics glutamate harm raised cell stress, swelling signals, and nerve cell death in untreated eyes. The treated eyes kept more nerve cells, a thicker retina, and working signal flow along the optic nerve. Protection lasted at least three weeks from delivery. Calmer cell stress, not calcium change, seemed to drive the gain.
pmc-13404178:
Phung Van Nguyen laid out in 2026 a simple rule for picking how to rebuild a missing eyebrow with hair-bearing tissue from the temple. Eyebrows frame the face and shield the eye, so rebuilds must restore cover plus hair grain and density. The choice turns mainly on whether the temple on the same side can spare tissue.

Two cases show the rule at work. When the same-side temple was intact, a flap swung over on its own stalk did the job. When past surgery had spoiled that side, a free flap crossed from the other temple. Both flaps lived fully, and both patients liked the lasting match.
pmc-13404378:
Arianna L Williams-Katek and a ten-author team showed in 2026 that two probe sets can fish for gene messages on one tissue slide at once. Tissue gene mapping tools force a trade: small probe sets read each gene keenly, while large sets cover far more genes. Their test used 17 human lung samples on one shared slide platform.

The hybrid run paired a keen set of up to 480 genes with a broad set covering 5,000 genes. Early prep steps for the two chemistries already matched, which made the pairing workable. Readout steps differ sharply, so the blend needed care. Success gives labs both depth and breadth in a single pass.
pmc-13405178:
Sajid and colleagues chart an American trend: deaths where heart failure and psychoactive substance abuse appear together, using a quarter century of death records before and after COVID-19. Either condition strains the heart and health system; together they mark a growing overlap. Their 2026 study mines the CDC WONDER database for 1999 to 2023, computing age adjusted death rates and trend breaks by sex, age, race, and region.

Deaths reached 771,739. The rate climbed from under two per hundred thousand people in 1999 to over twenty by 2023. The steepest surge came in the first six years, with steady growth after. Men died at more than double the women's rate, and the burden sat heaviest on adults over sixty five, non-Hispanic White Americans, and rural counties. Most deaths occurred in facilities or at home. The authors argue the overlap needs integrated cardiac and addiction care, not two doors.
pmc-13407678:
Oluwatoba T. Balogun and co-authors audit, in 2026, misleading reporting, known as spin, in the summaries of systematic reviews published by leading upper-extremity surgery journals. Such reviews steer practice guidelines, so spin in an abstract can distort what surgeons take away, and the team scored ten years of abstracts against nine recognised spin types.

Spin appeared in 28 of 54 reviews, just over half, and 21 reviews carried more than one type. The commonest trick, found in exactly half, was claiming benefit while glossing over a high risk of bias in the underlying studies. Other spin types included selective framing of results. The authors call for stronger reporting frameworks so that evidence summaries in hand and arm surgery can be read at face value.
pmc-13408478:
Salif Komi, August Winther, and colleagues propose in 2026 that the geography of the spinal cord, more than any single cell type, explains how walking rhythms arise. Central pattern generator circuits in the cord produce locomotion, yet linking their many neuron types to the rhythm has resisted decades of work. The team built a model mouse spinal cord wired by rules drawn from gene-expression maps.

Connections were sampled from measured projection patterns of each cell type, producing a network with nearby excitation, longer-range inhibition, and a lengthwise skew. Rhythmic, controllable locomotion emerged without heavy parameter tuning, and the model predicts waves of activity travelling along the cord during movement. The authors argue these spatial principles may be universal, offering neuroscientists testable predictions about how descending commands find the right spinal targets.
pmc-13411278:
Worapong Kosaruk, Patcharapa Towiboon, and Sarisa Klinhom review in 2026 whether dung samples can reveal immune health in zoo and wild mammals. Catching and bleeding wild animals disturbs them and skews results, so non-invasive markers are prized. An antibody called IgA, active at gut surfaces, washes out in feces and can be measured there.

Twenty-one studies across many species showed fecal IgA is measurable and shifts with real biology. In wild animals it tracked parasites, breeding effort, season, and gut microbe patterns. In captivity it moved with management and individual differences, and matched stress hormones only loosely. Differing lab methods block tidy cross-study comparison, so IgA reads best as a context-sensitive signal.
pmc-13411578:
Xiudong Guan and colleagues develop in 2026 a spinal fluid test for lung cancer that has spread to the membranes around the brain and cord. Scans and cell hunts in spinal fluid often miss this dangerous spread. Tumor DNA in spinal fluid is scarce, which defeats deep sequencing, yet rich in chromosome-scale changes.

Their shallow genome method reads copy-number changes from trace amounts of fluid DNA. Samples from 57 patients showed stronger tumor signals in spinal fluid than in matched blood. A genome amplification score separated membrane spread from brain-only spread with high sensitivity and no false alarms in this group. Repeat sampling also tracked treatment-driven shifts, which supports use in monitoring.
pmc-13414178:
Gulseren Dinc and colleagues test in 2026 whether oridonin, a plant compound, can shield rat ovaries from the chemo drug cisplatin. The drug saves lives yet burns through egg stores, a threat to young patients who want children. Thirty female rats formed three groups. One group stayed clean. One got cisplatin alone. One got cisplatin plus a daily dose of oridonin. After four weeks, ovaries and blood were checked for eggs, a reserve hormone, and harm signals.

Cisplatin cut egg counts at each growth stage and raised scarring in the ovary. Oridonin lifted egg counts back up and cut the scarring by a clear margin. The reserve hormone, pushed down by cisplatin, moved back toward normal. Harm and swelling signals fell too. The team credits a calmer TGF-beta and Smad3 path.
pmc-13415178:
Gadah Ali Alshahrany and co-authors combine a ginger compound with a licensed drug in a mouse model of multiple sclerosis, in 2026. Mice drank cuprizone, a toxin that strips myelin from brain nerves, for five weeks. Four weeks of recovery followed, with no treatment, 6-shogaol from ginger, ibudilast, or both.

Combined treatment improved movement, muscle strength, and memory more than either agent alone during recovery. Brain tissue showed lower activity in genes that drive inflammation and higher activity in calming pathways. Multiple sclerosis damages myelin and axons with no cure at present. A two-pronged pairing like this may support repair once the toxin stops, the authors suggest.
pmc-13415678:
Si-Zu Lin leads a very large team presenting the genome of Chinese fir, an important timber conifer, in 2026. The assembled genome spans about 11.24 billion letters, bloated by ancient repetitive DNA that the species clears slowly. Chinese fir belongs to the cypress family, whose place in gymnosperm family trees has been disputed.

Family analysis refined how cycads and ginkgo relate to gnetophytes and the pine family. No extra whole genome doubling appeared in the Chinese fir line beyond one shared by all seed plants.
