Population history clues point to glacial refuges and spread centers. A revised model of cone organ development may apply across gymnosperms.
pmc-13415978:
Ferdinand Medard Shilikale and colleagues describe team based care for a baby girl with Currarino syndrome, in a 2026 case report with a literature review. Currarino syndrome is a rare birth fault with three marks: a gut end made wrong, a bent sacrum bone, and a lump in front of the sacrum. Long term stool blocks plus sacrum faults should raise doubt in infants.

Scans confirmed the pattern in this child, and child surgeons, scan experts, and gene experts planned staged care as one team. The gene MNX1 drives many cases passed down in families, though how it shows varies widely. Early spotting guards against bowel blocks, infection, and nerve harm, the authors stress.
pmc-13416078:
Florian Sommer and colleagues track natural killer cells in colorectal cancer patients whose tumors carry the SARIFA pattern, in 2026. SARIFA marks tumors touching fat directly at the invasion front and predicts worse outcomes. Blood was sampled before surgery, a week or so after, and six months later in forty patients plus twenty-seven healthy controls.

Before surgery, SARIFA positive patients already had fewer natural killer cells. After surgery, counts dipped in SARIFA negative patients, then recovered by six months. Low counts persisted in SARIFA positive patients at six months. Inflammatory mediators rose after surgery equally in both groups. A built in immune trait may help these aggressive tumors arise.
pmc-13417478:
Junhee Lee and colleagues feed a blend of amaranth protein hydrolysate and Korean mint extract to mice with cancer related wasting, in a 2026 study. Wasting, called cachexia, drains muscle and fat and weakens patients. Tumour bearing mice received the blend by mouth for 14 days at two dose levels.

Weight loss eased, muscle and fat stores were partly preserved, and grip strength improved. Blood inflammation signals fell, muscle breakdown genes quieted, and a growth pathway switched back on. Fat tissue also shifted away from wasteful browning toward storage. The blend is proposed as a nutrition strategy, pending human study.
pmc-13418478:
Song Hu and co-authors trace a drug resistant Klebsiella strain carrying a rare resistance gene in a newborn intensive care unit, in a 2026 study. Three critically ill infants yielded isolates resistant to carbapenems, last line antibiotics. Genome sequencing, drug testing, and clinical timelines were combined to judge relatedness and spread.

All three isolates shared sequence type 35 and carried the gene on the same plasmid type. Analysis suggested the third case caught the strain from the second inside the unit, while the first was unrelated. The bacteria grew strongly, formed biofilms, and killed all infected mice at the test dose. Vigilance in neonatal units is urged.
pmc-13418778:
Jinyi Hou and colleagues argue that chronic kidney disease should be read as a failure of a gut-liver-kidney axis rather than of the kidney alone. Kidney disease often arrives with gut imbalance and fatty liver disease, and that liver state raises kidney risk by 38 percent on its own. Their 2026 review pulls the three organs into one systems view.

The authors map signals running both ways across microbe, metabolic, immune, and blood-flow channels. Tools from network analysis and dynamic modeling help chart those links, with diabetic kidney disease as the lead example. Reading the axis as one system points to combined microbe and metabolite tests for earlier diagnosis. It also suggests trials that act upstream, before kidney damage is locked in, instead of treating each organ apart.
pmc-13418878:
Writing to the editor, Yanyu Qiu and colleagues present a 66-year-old woman found to have two separate cancers at once, one in the gallbladder and one in the stomach. Gallbladder cancer is rare, fast-moving, and often found late, which narrows treatment options from the start. The woman came in with upper belly pain and gallstones, plus a family history of stomach cancer.

Scans showed a mass reaching from the gallbladder into the liver, with wall changes that raised concern. A scope exam found deep ulcers in the upper stomach, and biopsy proof showed a poorly differentiated stomach cancer. Holding two cancers at once forces a joint plan that treats both without stacking side effects. The letter gives cancer teams a worked example of that balancing act.
pmc-13419678:
Helen Killaspy and colleagues compare inpatient mental health rehabilitation run by the National Health Service with the same care run by independent providers in England. More than 350 such services care for adults with complex psychosis, split roughly half and half between the two sectors. Whether sector changes the care patients get had not been tested at this scale.

The team recruited 411 patients from 48 NHS services. Another 172 patients came from 20 independent services. Patients, clinicians, and managers gave interviews, and records were reviewed for service traits. Cost modeling cited by guidelines had already suggested large savings if all such care sat in the public sector. Fresh patient-level data let commissioners judge whether the sectors differ in who they serve and how.
pmc-13420278:
Samuel Alomatu and colleagues report liver injury caused by tuberculosis drugs at Tamale Teaching Hospital, then weigh the hurdles of handling it where resources run thin. The standard TB drug set carries a real risk of idiosyncratic liver damage, with pooled rates near 11.5 percent in the figures cited. Their patient showed jaundice, pale tone, leg swelling, and fluid in the belly on exam.

The referral center lacked liver biopsy and routine baseline liver tests, and patients paid out of pocket for repeat labs. Those gaps delay both spotting the injury and proving recovery. Risk runs higher with hepatitis coinfection, HIV, older age, and poor nutrition, traits common in the same clinics. The case argues for baseline liver checks as a funded part of TB care, not a luxury.
pmc-13420378:
Wan-Zeng Wang and colleagues name a new stonecrop species, Sedum guniuensis, from the Guniujiang Mountains of southern Anhui, China. The genus is large and long neglected in field surveys, so unnamed kinds still surface in mountain country. Wild plants and specimens were gathered for close comparison with their nearest relatives.

Shape measures from more than 10 living plants of a close relative set the bar for judging difference. Gene-based family trees joined the shape work to place the new plant among its kin. Both lines of evidence held the plant apart as its own species. Formal naming is the step that lets conservation lists, floras, and seed banks begin tracking a plant that was always there.
pmc-13421378:
Benevolenskaya and colleagues write an obituary and memoir of Vladimir A. Gvozdev, the Russian Drosophila geneticist who lived from 1 May 1935 to 13 June 2025, published in 2026. Gvozdev worked at Moscow State University through the Soviet and post-Soviet eras, upholding, the authors stress, the highest standards of scientific integrity in turbulent times. Born in Moscow to a family of nobility, he was educated at home in European languages by his mother.

The memoir places his career in the history of Russian genetics, beginning with Hermann Muller's 1922 visit bringing fruit fly strains to Nikolai Koltsov's institute in Moscow. Gvozdev built his research direction on that Drosophila tradition, studying how genes are organized and silenced in the fly genome across decades when Soviet genetics faced ideological pressure. Colleagues remember his exacting standards and mentorship. Benevolenskaya presents his life as a thread of continuity for genetics from Koltsov's school to the present.
pmc-13421478:
Zhaojie Yu leads a fifteen-author team explaining, in a 2026 study, banded rainfall anomalies across Asia-Pacific on orbital timescales. The Indo-Pacific Warm Pool drives global moisture, yet sedimentary records show a coherent precipitation pattern that local dynamics alone cannot explain.

Combining sediment proxies with transient climate simulations, the team shows that deep convection over the warm pool launches planetary Rossby waves. Over thousands of years, paced by Earth's precession, those waves reorganise moisture transport toward mid and high latitudes. Precession also shapes the background circulation that steers the waves. The authors offer the mechanism as a physical link between tropical forcing and rainfall variability across Pan-Asia in past climates.
pmc-13422878:
Sam Daftari, Mojgan Salavati and Manoochehr Mortazavi Chamchali test, in a 2026 study, whether modified Iranian clay can pull copper and zinc out of contaminated water cheaply. Bentonite is abundant and naturally absorbent. They made two upgraded versions: one baked after nitric-acid activation, and one treated with hydrochloric acid and layered with chitosan, a shellfish-derived polymer.

Bench tests varied acidity, contact time, dose, starting concentration and temperature. Uptake followed the pattern expected for chemical binding to a surface, fastest for the acid-and-heat version, and peaked near neutral acidity. Capacity reached about ninety-nine milligrams per gram under the best conditions. Microscopy and spectroscopy showed the changes took hold. The authors present the clays as a green, sustainable treatment option.
pmc-13423478: Advanced Science published this 2026 correction to a paper by Xia and co-authors on how the protein POU2F1 drives chemotherapy resistance in colorectal cancer cells. During revision, supplementary Figure S6 was wrongly uploaded in place of the main Figure 6. So the published figure duplicated the extra file. It did not match its legend or the results text. The notice presents the correct Figure 6, showing experiments on PPP1R11 lactylation and MDR2 ubiquitination, and explains the mix-up.
pmc-13425078:
Niamh Kearney and coauthors published a 2026 post hoc analysis of guselkumab treatment in psoriasis across three phase III trials. Earlier results from VOYAGE 1, VOYAGE 2, and ECLIPSE showed lower inflammatory markers through weeks 12 to 16. The new analysis asks whether those reductions held through week 48 and tracks measures such as the neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio.

Sustained biomarker lowering matters because systemic inflammation in psoriasis may raise the risk of major cardiac events. Readers see longer-term laboratory follow-up from randomized trial populations rather than short treatment snapshots alone. The work keeps the focus on care that lasts well past the first weeks of skin care.
pmc-13425578:
Besnier Marc, Christophe Bonnet, and Anne Lore Coudert compared artificial intelligence with general practitioners at history taking in a 2026 cross-sectional study in France. Clinician skepticism about gaps and bias has slowed AI use in general practice despite rapid gains in performance. In an online study, 204 French general practitioners produced 942 patient histories for comparison with AI-collected histories.

Each record was sorted into chronic disease, medical, surgical, obstetric, occupational, allergy, and family cancer categories to judge completeness. The reported results favor AI on several categories, giving practices concrete evidence about where automated intake might help daily work. The trial also shows why trust in new tools grows when staff can see plain gains in the day to day work of the clinic.
pmc-13425878:
Liu Xuexin, Jiang Lihua, and Kong Xiaoxu analyzed China's low-carbon policy system quantitatively in a 2026 study of policy texts. They coded 1,008 policy documents issued from 2007 to 2024 and judged each by instruments used, objectives pursued, and effectiveness signals. Carbon disclosure rules and green transformation goals tied to the national dual-carbon strategy dominate the objective side.

Environment-type instruments outweigh supply-side and demand-side tools, which remain comparatively scarce in the mix. Attention to goals beyond the national strategy also looks limited, giving policymakers a map of where the system is crowded and where it is thin.
pmc-13426078:
Gendrot and Le Faou surveyed high school students in the Paris region in 2026 about e-cigarette use, gathering answers from 1,187 students with a median age of seventeen. The anonymous online survey ran across six schools in early 2021 and asked about tobacco habits, reasons for vaping, and how students view its effects.

Nearly forty-seven percent had tried e-cigarettes, about nineteen percent currently used them, and about nine percent vaped daily, starting at about fifteen years old on average. Curiosity was the top reason, named by over ninety percent of triers, followed by flavor variety and being able to vape at home without tobacco smell. Having friends who vape more than tripled the odds of trying. Most users worried about lung health and addiction, yet nearly a quarter of all students did not know if their liquid contained nicotine.
pmc-13426478:
Leticia Tornyevah and colleagues studied how depressive symptoms after birth relate to the emotional bond between mothers and babies in Ghana. They mixed surveys with interviews at three health facilities during the first year after delivery.

Of 399 mothers surveyed, 29 percent screened positive for depressive symptoms on a standard nine-question checklist. Mothers with symptoms scored about 3 percent lower on bonding than mothers without them, a small but real gap. Interviews with 31 mothers showed bonds held up through instinct, daily caregiving, family support, and faith in both groups. Tornyevah advises care that eases mothers' distress while strengthening the family and cultural supports that protect bonding.
pmc-13426878:
Selman and colleagues published a 2026 guide to examining the shoulder blade during shoulder checks. The shoulder blade anchors the arm and guides smooth shoulder motion. When its muscles fall out of balance, motion goes off track and pain follows. Standard shoulder exams often skip the blade, missing quiet but telling changes.

The note lays out a standard order for a full blade exam. It covers key hand tests, surface landmarks, and motion patterns to watch. Weak muscles such as the trapezius and overactive ones both get attention. The authors link off-track blade motion to cuff tears and pinching pain. Their routine aims to make blade checks a habit in shoulder clinics. Spotting the pattern early can steer therapy before damage sets in.
pmc-13427578:
Chenlin Hao and colleagues report, in 2026, quick farm-side test strips for a pig coronavirus that causes severe diarrhea in newborn piglets. Porcine deltacoronavirus spreads fast in herds and costs the swine industry heavily. Lab testing confirms cases but takes time and equipment most farms lack. The team built strip tests much like home pregnancy kits, using either gold particles or black carbon particles.

Both strips picked up the virus in diluted samples and ignored three related pig viruses. On 137 stool samples from farms, the gold strip agreed with standard lab tests in about 93 cases out of 100. The carbon strip topped 88 percent agreement and marks a first use of carbon in this kind of viral test. Faster answers can help farmers isolate sick animals sooner.
pmc-13427678:
Tiantian Liang and colleagues present, in a 2026 study, a neural network that finds pores inside concrete from CT scans. Pore patterns govern how long concrete lasts, yet pores can be tiny, faint, and oddly shaped, which defeats simple image tools. Their network, ECS-Net, pairs a multiscale encoder with a decoder that adapts to fuzzy edges and low contrast. Three purpose-built modules help it catch both large structure and fine detail.

Tests on the team's own concrete scans, a public crack dataset, and aggregate images beat mainstream rival models. Rebuilding the pore space in three dimensions from a few specimens gave stable porosity estimates. Inspectors could use such a tool to check bridges and buildings for hidden damage without cutting into them. Generalization beyond the lab datasets remains the test ahead.
pmc-13427778:
Hübner and colleagues ran a pilot study in 2026 at two trauma centers in different countries. They tested whether both sites could measure immune cell markers the same way, right in the trauma bay. Neutrophils, the first-response white blood cells, change their surface markers in patterns that reflect how the body reacts to trauma. A bedside flow cytometry setup, which sorts cells by the tags they carry, promises fast readings without a central lab.

Twenty-eight badly injured patients were tested at both centers with one shared automated protocol. Readings for key markers of cell maturity and activation matched closely between sites, in healthy controls and patients alike. The team concludes that the setup transfers cleanly between centers, opening the door to joint immune monitoring studies after trauma.
pmc-13427878:
Gačević and colleagues ask whether premature babies with swollen brain ventricles after a brain bleed can avoid a shunt by draining fluid for longer through a port. Dutch guidance set twenty eight days of taps through a ventricular access device before moving to a shunt, a tube that drains brain fluid to the belly. Their 2026 study reviews a Rotterdam children's hospital for babies treated from 2010 to 2020.

Of 55 babies, 23 whose ventricles shrank but stayed enlarged were tapped at low frequency past the twenty eight day mark. Only 14 of those 23 ended up needing the shunt. The final shunt rate for the whole group fell by a reported fifteen percent with the longer course. Patience, in babies whose course is improving, spared operations with lifelong hardware and its infection and blockage risks. The authors call for research on how long the tapping window should run.
pmc-13428078:
Castillo and colleagues chart early onset gastric cancer, stomach cancer diagnosed by age 45, in the United States National Cancer Database. The team studies patients with stage two or three disease who had curative stomach surgery between 2006 and 2022. It compares the young group with older patients on traits, treatment, and survival. Young cases made up a small slice of the cohort.

Early onset cases clustered among Hispanic, Black, and Asian patients. Their tumors more often showed diffuse or signet ring cell patterns, poor differentiation, meaning cells looked abnormal, and heavier lymph node spread. Young patients received drug treatment around surgery more often than older patients, yet full tumor disappearance under those drugs stayed rare. Survival did not beat the older groups despite the stronger therapy. The authors call the young disease a high risk entity that needs targeted treatments and earlier detection in the groups hit most.
pmc-13430478:
Vangipuram Harshil Sai published a 2026 essay on the words doctors borrow when they speak with very sick patients. The writer recalls hearing a senior doctor tell a man whose cancer had spread that the team would keep fighting. The room calmed at once, even though the outlook had not changed at all.

Over months on wards and in clinics, the writer heard the same plural phrasing again and again. Doctors spoke of what the team would try or endure together. Patients, in reply, spoke in the singular, saying they felt tired or wished to go home. The essay traces how such phrases pass from one group of doctors to the next. They travel on rounds, never taught in class. The essay asks what the shared pronoun truly shares.
pmc-13433178:
Yize Qi and co-authors reported seven cases in 2026 of stent care for heart artery mouths narrowed by late syphilis, guided by a sound probe run inside the vessel. The germ's late stage swells the main artery wall and chokes the mouths where heart arteries branch off. Bypass surgery has long led care, while stents offer a less harsh route.

All seven patients, seen from 2019 to 2026, won proof of the germ by blood tests. Probe reads showed ring-like fiber growth and inward wall shrink, with none of the usual fatty plaque marks. Fresh drug-coated stents went in for all. Six patients, whose stents jutted a touch into the main artery, stayed free of major heart events across a mid watch of four years. The authors call the route workable.
pmc-13433978:
Sarah M H Einerhand and co-authors trialed immune pairs in 2026 with or without a taxane drug for bladder-lining cancer that had spread and shrugged off two care classes. Fresh plans stay scarce for this group. Three arms split forty-four patients: drug plus high-dose brake lift, drug plus low lift plus a twin brake drug, or high lift alone.

Tumor shrink rates led in the drug-plus-high-lift arm, at near a quarter, with the twin arm mid and lift alone last. Grave side harm struck most in the twin arm and least in lift alone. Mouse work showed the pair beat each part alone at curbing growth. On-care tumor snips lit swelling marks. Immune fire can still wake after brake failure, the authors say.
pmc-13434378:
Min wrote a 2026 review on plastic dust reaching the nose and upper airway. Microplastics are plastic bits smaller than five millimeters, now found worldwide. Breathing is a main route into the body, yet research favored the lungs. The nose is the first filter in that path, so Min surveys it closely.

Studies have found plastic bits in nose washings from healthy and sick people. Samples came from allergy and sinus patients, and even the brain's smell center. Sources range from city air and masks to rinse bottles and sleep apnea machines. Proof of harm stays early, with no firm links to nose disease yet. Min calls for better sampling methods and longer health tracking studies.
pmc-13434578:
Thays Nascimento Souza and colleagues build a score for how well Brazilians follow national diet advice in 2026. The score covers ten food groups, with points for foods to eat, foods to limit, and foods to avoid. Data came from a national survey of 46,164 people aged ten and up.

Scores run from zero to 100, and higher means closer to the advice. Older adults and rural residents scored higher than other groups. Diets built by diet experts scored near the top, which supports the scale. Links with total energy intake were weak, as hoped. Health teams gain a shared ruler for surveys and programs.
pmc-13435678:
Bjørg Bolstad and coauthors give a new antibiotic helper its first test in healthy adults in 2026. The helper, APC148, blocks metal enzymes that destroy meropenem, a last line drug. Forty six volunteers took single vein doses from 50 to 760 milligrams across six groups.

All doses were well tolerated, with only mild side effects and no serious events. Drug levels rose in step with dose, and half the drug cleared in about 2.6 hours. Lab work pairs the helper with meropenem and avibactam for wide cover. Patient trials for hard infections come next. The clean first pass clears a key hurdle.
pmc-13436078:
Zhang and colleagues publish a 2026 protocol for a systematic review of non-drug treatments for lactational mastitis, the painful breast inflammation that often pushes mothers to stop breastfeeding early. Antibiotics are standard, but resistance worries and effects on the baby's gut microbes drive interest in other options. These include probiotics, therapeutic ultrasound, acupuncture, and manual therapy, whose relative value is unclear.

The team will search eight English and Chinese databases plus trial registries through March 2026. Only randomised trials in adult breastfeeding women with mastitis will count. Success means fever gone and local pain, redness, and swelling resolved. Two reviewers will screen, extract data, and grade bias independently. Planned analyses pool results with random-effects models and check pain scores, abscess rates, side effects, and how many mothers keep breastfeeding. No results exist yet; the value will come when the review reports.
pmc-13436378:
Tingxiu Peng and coauthors compare airway germ mixes in sixty four bronchiectasis patients by Pseudomonas carriage in 2026. Lung wash fluid from twenty nine carriers and thirty five non carriers was profiled. Disease scores and lung function were set beside the germ data.

Carriers scored worse on severity scales and blew lower lung volumes. White cell and neutrophil shares also ran higher, which signals more swelling. Their airway mix lost variety and tipped toward Pseudomonas dominance. Non carriers kept a richer mix of mouth linked germs. Carriage marks a distinct, harsher disease state that may need its own care path.
pmc-13436678:
Ilma Nascimento and Caio Julio Cesar dos Santos Fernandes argue in 2026 that patient knowledge in AI aided lung hypertension care needs a defined trigger for action. Diaries, free text notes, and symptom scores can flag fading stamina before lab marks move. Two disease specific scales capture daily limits that routine tests miss.

Recognition alone does not guarantee a response, the authors warn. Pathways must name who reviews patient input, how fast, by what rules, and with what power to escalate. Scores can wobble from mood, other illness, or noise, so blind escalation is risky. Stability in lab marks should not silence a clear patient decline either. Action rules complete the loop.
pmc-13437078:
Armita Hamedi Mobarra, Thomas Liang, and Alp Sener tested whether teaching material made by students could lift what Canadian undergraduates know about organ donation. Their 2026 survey at Western University gave students content from a student-led advocacy group, then measured knowledge and attitudes before and after. Ninety replies were usable, and sixty-two surveys were finished in full.

Knowledge scores rose after students used the material, the team reports. Students in health-related fields started ahead of peers in other fields, who more often worried that donated organs might be misused. That worry eased after the session among non-health students. Willingness to sign up as a donor held steady among health students and dipped slightly among the others. The authors say student-led teaching shows promise, while urging wider reach across varied groups and follow-up over time to see whether gains last.
pmc-13437278:
Shitao Lei and co-authors argue that judging liver cancer surgery by tumor size alone misses the deeper question of whether the cancer has truly been tamed. Conversion therapy uses drugs and local treatments to shrink tumors once thought beyond surgery. Their 2026 piece proposes a shift from anatomical resectability, whether the tumor can be cut out, to biological resectability, whether its behavior makes surgery worthwhile.

Strong treatment pressure can backfire, the authors warn. It may drive hidden tumor clones to adapt and resist, through growth signals or shifts in how cells fuel themselves. Early signs suggest good downsizing also warms the tumor's immune surroundings, drawing in killer T cells. They propose measurable tests for the new standard, such as cleared tumor DNA in blood and mature immune clusters in tissue. The framework is provisional, built to help doctors time surgery and catch resistance early.
pmc-13437578:
Liberata Sportiello and a large team mined Italian drug safety reports for mouth and throat harms tied to medicines and vaccines. Such events are easy to overlook, yet they can be an early window on wider health. Their 2026 study pulled three years of reports, 2022 to 2024, from three Italian regions. Of 47,664 reports, 1,740 held at least one mouth or throat event.

Most patients were women, with a median age of fifty-five. Two-thirds of the events were classed as not serious, and most ended well. Drugs accounted for nine in ten reports, while the vaccine share shrank sharply. One grave pattern stood out: 129 cases of jaw bone death linked to medication, most serious with poor endings. Reporting differed by job, with doctors less likely than patients to file such events. The authors urge doctors, dentists above all, to treat mouth events as worth reporting.
pmc-13437678:
Zhenhua Guo and co-authors pooled trials of visual art therapy as an add-on treatment for depression in adults. Drug-free options matter for people who cannot take or do not want standard medicines. Their 2026 review searched eight databases through March 2026 and kept twelve randomized trials with 741 adults.

Art therapy eased both. Depression scores fell by a large margin against controls, and anxiety by a solid one too. Program shape mattered: for depression, gains ran larger in plans under twelve weeks, with fewer than twelve meetings, and with sessions of an hour or less. Anxiety answered best to a different recipe, more frequent meetings packed into six weeks or fewer, again in short sessions. The authors present art therapy as a promising companion to standard care, not a stand-alone cure. They also note the small trial count, which leaves the best dose unsettled and invites larger studies.
pmc-13439278:
Lee and Lee reviewed in 2026 ways to judge biopsy quality on the spot during pancreas sampling. Doctors take pancreas tissue with a needle guided by endoscopic ultrasound, an internal scan. The review compares rapid on-site evaluation by a cell specialist, gross visual checks, and a newer microscope method.

The newer method, called SOSE, uses a stereomicroscope to spot white core tissue in the sample. In one study it matched specialist checks and took a median of only 47 seconds per sample. In another, about 73 in 100 lesions met the white-core cutoff after the first needle pass, so most patients needed just one puncture. The authors caution that seeing enough tissue is not the same as proving a diagnosis.
pmc-13439978:
Van Esch and colleagues published a 2026 study on new staffing models in intensive care. Dutch intensive care units face staff shortages, so care assistants now join nursing teams. The team asked nurses and assistants how the shared model felt early on. Focus groups gathered 33 nurses and nine care assistants at two units.

Three themes stood out across the four focus group meetings. Clear, ongoing communication helped staff settle into their new roles at work. Team spirit grew, yet questions on who owns each task stayed tense. Assistants added real value in daily basic care for patients. Task cards and guidelines were suggested as practical support tools. The authors stress giving teams time to adjust before judging the model.
pmc-13440578:
Alvi and co-authors run a pilot evaluation in this 2026 study of deep learning image reconstruction for newborn brain MRI, a scan notoriously degraded by head motion. The algorithm cleans up noisy magnetic resonance images after acquisition, and the team asked whether stronger cleaning settings truly help radiologists see early myelin, the insulating coating forming on infant brain wiring.

Fifteen neonates scanned on a 3-tesla machine had their images reconstructed at low, medium, and high denoising levels. Three radiologists scored eight early-myelinating structures for noise, artifacts, and clarity, while software measured objective signal and contrast ratios in white and gray matter. Every measure improved as denoising increased, with nearly all pairwise comparisons reaching significance in the quantitative analysis. The authors caution that fifteen babies and no diagnostic accuracy testing make this a promising pilot, not proof of clinical benefit.
pmc-13441378:
Alexa House and colleagues test whether family climate changes how strongly discomfort with uncertainty feeds suicidal thoughts in teenagers, reporting in 2026. Intolerance of uncertainty is a trait-like habit of reacting badly to not knowing, and it tracks with suicidal ideation. The study drew 184 young people aged sixteen to nineteen, all at elevated risk for escalating alcohol use. Questionnaires measured the trait, current severity of suicidal thoughts, and two family composites built from risk and protective factors.

Each of the three factors mattered on its own. The trait-to-ideation link, though, depended on family ground. Under high family risk, stronger intolerance tracked with stronger ideation, while low risk muted the link. Low family resilience showed the same amplifying pattern, and high resilience muted it. The authors suggest that strengthening family-level protection could blunt a known personal vulnerability, a route worth testing in prevention work.
pmc-13441778:
Yirong Wang and colleagues report a hormone-secreting adrenal tumour in a nineteen-month-old girl whose body began masculinising, publishing a 2026 case. Over six months she developed a deepening voice, pubic hair, and an enlarged clitoris, without breast changes or bleeding. Blood tests showed suppressed puberty hormones, a non-pubertal stimulation response, advanced bone age, and a raised adrenal androgen marker. Imaging found a right adrenal mass of about five centimetres.

Open surgery removed the tumour. Tissue study scored it as a paediatric adrenocortical tumour of uncertain malignant potential under child-specific criteria, with brisk division figures and capsule invasion. Marker stains supported a steroid-making origin, and the division index ran high in hotspots. Androgen levels fell sharply after surgery, and remission held at four and eight months. The authors stress adrenal-first thinking when virilisation races ahead in very young girls.
pmc-13442678:
Sophie Cleanthous and colleagues ask patients and doctors what counts as real change on a Parkinson rating scale in a 2026 study. Drug makers who chase early disease need scale items that track daily life, not just clinic scores. Talks covered 40 patients and 20 movement experts, with views sorted through a shared frame.

Patients rated all 18 movement items at least somewhat tied to daily life. Twelve items earned a high-meaning tag from patient views. More than 90 percent of experts backed four items as core for early disease checks. Experts backed six items as strong tools for tracking decline over time. Six named items, from stiffness to toe taps, won joint praise. The authors urge trial teams to weight those items first when they judge new drugs.
pmc-13445378:
Dainis Krievins and colleagues ask whether heart artery plaque load, measured before leg artery surgery, predicts death over five years in patients with no known heart disease, in a 2026 study. Blocked leg arteries often travel with silent heart disease, a main driver of poor survival. Scans gave both plaque volume and a flow measure for each heart lesion.

The group held 124 patients cleared for planned leg surgery, most of them men near age sixty-seven. More than half had silent flow-limiting heart disease, and plaque load ran high overall. Over five years, thirty-two patients died. Those who died carried near twice the plaque volume of survivors, and high plaque load marked a far worse outlook, which supports heart checks before leg surgery.
pmc-13446078:
Veit-Lorenz Heuthe and colleagues turn a swarm of tiny active beads into a computer that learns from motion itself, in a 2026 physics study. In reservoir computing, a lively physical system transforms inputs, and only a simple readout layer needs training, which saves energy. Most such systems cannot tune how their parts interact.

Hundreds of swimming beads, coupled through the fluid around them, form the reservoir here, and their coupling and memory can be tuned in place. The swarm forecast chaotic series with skill, working in parallel without time-slicing tricks. It also caught hidden anomalies in real time, flaws so subtle that the signal's plain statistics never changed. The work casts interacting beads as a flexible base for smart sensing.
pmc-13447178:
Alexander Yahanda and colleagues describe a 2026 operation to remove a rare bone tumour from the upper neck in one piece. Chordomas grow slowly yet invade nearby tissue, so leaving no tumour at the edges gives the best chance of control. Growths near the skull base and top spine vertebrae are among the hardest to remove safely.

A sixty-six-year-old man had a tumour starting at the second neck vertebra and reaching neighbours above and below. Surgeons worked in three stages from back, front and back again under one anaesthetic, lasting about twenty-nine hours. Breathing support took time to withdraw afterwards, yet he stayed free of recurrence with full strength beyond two years. The report also applies a new scoring frame to grade how complex such surgery is.
pmc-13447378:
Matthew Baugh leads a team building three-dimensional anomaly spotting for medical scans in 2026 work. A common strategy trains a model only on healthy scans, then flags anything the model cannot rebuild in a healthy-looking way. Older versions worked slice by slice, losing depth context, and ran slowly in full image space, while rebuild errors also produced false alarms.

The new method restores images inside a compressed three-dimensional space learned by a separate encoder, using a flow-based generator guided by the input scan. Comparing the restoration with the encoder's own rebuild, rather than the raw scan, cuts false alarms from compression. Models trained on fake faults in both image and compressed space performed best as a team across brain scan benchmarks. Speed rose roughly tenfold, though the newest benchmark remains far from solved.
pmc-13447578:
Tianyu Wang and co-authors frame eye melanoma as a stress-dependent cancer in a 2026 review. Uveal melanoma is the most common primary eye cancer in adults, and it spreads to the liver in most fatal cases, where survival drops below a year. Drugs that work on skin melanoma largely fail here, pointing to distinct survival machinery worth mapping.

Tumour cells must survive two harsh homes, the sheltered eye and the demanding liver, by rewiring oxygen sensing, metabolism and internal clean-up under stress. Oxidative stress is cast as both shield and weakness, since pushing it past a threshold can trigger iron-driven or immune-visible cell death. Clean-up pathways sustain spread and drug resistance in the account. Named stress nodes, from redox balance to clean-up control, are proposed as drug targets to break adaptation.
pmc-13447978:
Takashi Miida writes in 2026 about standardising measurement of lipoprotein(a), the cholesterol-carrying particle tied to heart disease, in molar units. Levels of the particle vary by assay because its attached protein comes in many sizes, confusing doctors for decades. A mass spectrometry reference method endorsed in 2023 and a certification programme launched in 2026 now anchor global values.

A multicentre Japanese study covered here converted results from different assays for over six thousand patients onto the standard scale. High standardised levels tracked with more coronary disease, kidney disease and inherited high cholesterol. Two decision cut-offs were proposed to sort patients into low, middle and high risk bands, a first for globally standardised values. New drugs that slash the particle by up to ninety percent sharpen the need for trustworthy numbers.
pmc-13448078:
Tan and colleagues test whether an inflammation protein called pentraxin 3 drives harmful heart thickening under hormone stress. Angiotensin II, a hormone that raises blood pressure, was infused into mice for four weeks to force the heart wall to thicken. Their 2026 study compares normal mice with mice bred to lack pentraxin 3, and pairs the animal work with heart cells from newborn rats stressed the same way in dishes.

The hormone raised pentraxin 3 levels in both mouse hearts and rat cells. Mice without the protein developed far less thickening and scarring, and their heart stress markers, including two natriuretic peptides, stayed lower. Inflammatory signals such as tumor necrosis factor alpha also rose less, and chemical stress damage in heart tissue eased. Blocking this protein, the authors propose, could become a route to treat thickened heart muscle driven by inflammation.
pmc-13448478:
Kim and colleagues review in 2026 how brain imaging can reveal what non-invasive brain stimulation does after stroke, and why patients respond so unevenly. Stimulation aims to boost the brain's rewiring, but clinics lack objective markers of the changes it causes. The review unifies evidence from EEG, which records brain waves, and functional MRI, which maps activity through blood flow.

EEG measures such as wave patterns, stimulation-evoked responses, and balance between the two brain halves track excitability changes from treatment. MRI studies show altered activation and connectivity, especially in motor networks. Combining both scans, and adding computer models of the electric field, sharpened the picture and improved prediction of recovery. The authors propose biomarker-guided, adaptive stimulation tailored to each patient's brain state.
pmc-13448678:
Dongwoo Ki and colleagues describe in 2026 a structural feature that slows enzymes able to break down PET plastic. In one such enzyme from Cryptosporangium aurantiacum, a loop sticking out from the surface limits how well the plastic can reach the working site. The loop sits far from the active center, about 25 angstroms away.

Swapping that protruding loop for a flatter version sped up PET breakdown in the team's tests. Kinetic and adsorption studies showed the change eased productive access without altering how tightly the enzyme binds plastic. Similar swaps in other PET-cutting enzymes support a design strategy based on access, not only on the catalytic site itself.
pmc-13448878:
Ryan Perkins and co-authors test in 2026 whether twelve weeks of supervised aerobic exercise changes two blood markers tied to inflammation in type 2 diabetes. Thirty-three sedentary adults were randomized, twenty to training and thirteen to standard care. The training group exercised sixty minutes a day, five days a week, at about 70 percent of peak oxygen capacity.

Blood levels of sRAGE, a soluble decoy receptor thought to soak up harmful sugar-damaged molecules, rose across the training period, while a related marker, sTLR4, stayed unchanged. Trained participants also gained fitness, lost body fat, and improved insulin sensitivity on a standard index. Muscle samples showed shifts in ratios of tissue-remodeling enzymes, though not in the receptor protein itself. The authors say the pathways behind the sRAGE rise remain unclear and need more study.
pmc-13449078:
Mohammed Barghash and a large team pool in 2026 the results on endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty, a stomach-shrinking procedure done through the mouth without external cuts. Their systematic review gathered 33 studies with 8,880 patients, searching the literature to September 2025. Weight outcomes were split into short follow-up, up to six months, and long follow-up of a year or more.

Total body weight loss rose from 8.66 percent at one month to 16.13 percent at six months and 17.88 percent at one year. Longer horizons showed gentle fading, to 15.67 percent at three years, and only 6 percent of patients regained weight. Remission reached 62 percent for type 2 diabetes and 43 percent each for high blood pressure and abnormal blood lipids. Higher starting body mass predicted greater percentage weight loss, supporting the procedure's place in multidisciplinary obesity care.
pmc-13449178:
Lv and colleagues ask whether lymphoma that has spread into the bone marrow at diagnosis later blocks stem cell collection for transplant. Collection requires coaxing blood stem cells out of the marrow, and success means gathering at least a set minimum dose. Their 2026 study reviews 669 patients at four Chinese centers who had a first collection attempt between 2017 and 2023, and uses matching to balance the groups on other traits.

Of the patients, 138 had marrow involvement at diagnosis. Success rates barely differed: about 79 percent with marrow involvement against about 81 percent without, and the gap stayed small after matching. The amount of stem cells gathered per kilo of body weight was also like in both groups. Marrow involvement at diagnosis, the authors conclude, does not in itself spoil collection, so it should not by itself deter a transplant plan.
pmc-13449378:
Fatima Sharif and colleagues catalog in 2026 the gene mutations behind drug resistance in Pakistani patients with chronic myeloid leukemia. The study ran from January to June 2025 at the Armed Forces Institute of Pathology and enrolled 133 adults whose leukemia no longer responded to tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Targeted genetic tests hunted four known mutations in the BCR::ABL1 kinase domain, the engine of the disease.

Mutations turned up in 57 patients, 42.9 percent of the group. E255K dominated at 33.8 percent of all patients, followed by E255V at 8.3 percent, while the notorious T315I and Y253H appeared once each. Carrying any mutation came with significantly higher white cell counts. E255K specifically was tied to blast crisis, the dangerous advanced phase, at a significance level of 0.048. The authors press for routine molecular testing so resistant patients can be switched to fitting drugs sooner.
pmc-13449478:
Rafael Sala and colleagues propose in 2026 that ordinary blood tests, watched over time, can flag colorectal cancers headed for early spread long before the diagnosis lands. Stage decides survival in this cancer, falling from 93 percent at stage one to roughly ten percent at stage four, and most treatment advances still react to disease found late. Their concept, haematological pre-staging, reads complete blood count trajectories in the twenty-four months before diagnosis.

The study's highlights report that these pre-diagnostic blood paths separate metastatic from non-metastatic cases. Progressive anemia and rising inflammation, in particular, appear ahead of cancers that present already spread to distant sites. Dynamic trajectories carried more signal than any single measurement. The authors suggest such patterns could one day steer who gets imaging sooner and who enters closer surveillance, shifting part of cancer detection from reacting to established tumors toward anticipating them.
pmc-13449778:
Hosein Rostamian and colleagues publish in 2026 a faster protocol for editing the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae genome with CRISPR. The usual bottleneck is not the cutting enzyme but building the plasmid that carries each new guide RNA. That job is traditionally done with restriction enzymes and ligation steps that fail in fiddly ways. Their workflow swaps that cloning for whole-plasmid PCR: primers write the new guide straight into the plasmid, and seamless assembly closes the circle again.

The protocol covers guide and repair-donor design. It details insertion into a drug-selectable Cas9 plasmid with a redesigned guide site and extended scaffold, verification in bacteria, and delivery into yeast by a standard chemical method. The run typically takes ten days. Because the backbone works in strain backgrounds common in research, the authors pitch it for laboratories that iterate through many guides, from deletions to point mutations and protein tagging.
pmc-13449878:
Buytenhuijs, Schröder, and Textor apply an old immunology idea, shape space, to T cell recognition in this 2026 theoretical paper. Shape space pictures antibodies and antigens as shapes that fit or fail to fit, and it underlies maps used to track virus evolution. The authors ask what the equivalent landscape looks like for T cell receptors facing peptide-MHC complexes, the displayed protein fragments that T cells inspect.

Binding depends on several structural constraints, they propose. Those constraints can conflict. So the fragments one receptor recognizes form several separate, non-convex islands, rather than one tidy region. That model predicts small structural changes can sharply alter whether a fragment provokes immunity, and that two recognized fragments can look very different. Published mutation experiments offer some support, and the authors discuss consequences for predicting immune responses in cancer therapy.
pmc-13450578:
Sara Buchmuller and co-authors follow in 2026 how Swiss adults who had cancer as children rate their first long-term check-up visits. Late health harms are common in this group, so ongoing care matters. The study took in 145 survivors at two Swiss clinics and asked them to rate visits before and three months after.

Ratings were very high for care that felt centered on the person and for how well facts were shared. Worry levels sat near the middle of the scale. Covering more of the topics a survivor wished to raise lifted the care rating, while weaker mental health tracked with more worry. The authors suggest added mind care for survivors who arrive with low mood.
pmc-13451278:
Wu and colleagues built a staged robot framework for inserting metal valve parts into holes with precision. It is a classic assembly task. Shiny surfaces, lost depth cues, and occlusion blind the cameras exactly when accuracy matters most. Their design treats insertion as a handover. Vision shrinks the error to a small neighborhood, then touch takes command.

Three phases follow in sequence: camera-guided coarse alignment, force-guided correction of the remaining offset, and compliant insertion with stiffness tuned live to the contact state. During correction the gripper traces a tiny spiral. The system watches lateral forces and torques settle toward a convergence criterion for centering. Experiments on clearance-fit and interference-fit tasks beat baseline methods on success rate, insertion time, and peak contact force in the reported comparisons. The authors argue explicitly coordinating vision-dominant and force-dominant stages is the key advantage.
pmc-13451878:
Jiangquan Zeng and co-authors build in 2026 a vision model that counts rubber trees from drone photos across all seasons. Exact counts guide yield guesses and farm care, yet crowns overlap and wild growth muddies the view. Their model, CSAF, stacks three parts: one that sharpens crown edges, one that enforces crown-like shapes, and one that adapts across seasons.

The team also released a data set of over 5,000 sharp drone images that span the full leaf cycle, from bud to leaf fall. On that set the model beat rival methods on crown spotting scores. Tests on three public sets checked that the gains travel beyond rubber farms.
pmc-13452178:
Ebba Elofsson, Magdalena Johansson, and Marcus Lind ask in 2026 whether how people rate their own health foretells a later heart rhythm disorder. Their cohort held over 100,000 middle-aged adults in north Sweden, free of the disorder at entry between 1988 and 2014. Health ratings came from a visit form, and new cases of atrial fibrillation were tracked for years.

Near 4,800 people later got the disorder. Each step down the self-rating scale, from very good toward poor, came with a higher risk, even with classic heart risks counted. The link also split by sex. The authors offer a one-line self-rating as a cheap early flag for rhythm risk in clinic visits.
pmc-13452278:
Alireza Sazmand and co-authors report in 2026 a tick-borne blood germ found for the first time in a striped hyena in west Iran. The germ, Cytauxzoon banethi, was known only from two European wildcats in Romania. The team read two genes from the hyena's blood and set them against known kinds.

One gene matched a kin species too closely to settle the name. The second gene sat near identical to the reference for this species and grouped with its line on the family tree. The find is the first in the hyena family, the first outside Europe, and the first in Asia. The authors urge wider wildlife checks with more than one gene.
pmc-13452778:
Maxime Remy and seven co-authors test whether gene sequencing of pancreas growths changes what doctors decide to do. The growths, called branch duct IPMNs, are fluid filled sacs that may turn to cancer, and rule books often leave doctors unsure. Their 2026 study gave 132 doctors in France four hard cases, each judged once before and once after gene results were shown.

Gene results swung choices hard in every case. When no risky mutation showed, plans for surgery flipped to watchful waiting in 43 to 61 percent of cases. When a risky mutation showed, waiting flipped to surgery in 72 to 90 percent of cases. Doctors also felt surer of their calls, and agreement between doctors jumped from near none to a solid level. The authors present sequencing as a strong aid for these borderline calls.
pmc-13453778:
Burcu Senkalfa and six co-authors chart the long course of pseudohypoparathyroidism, a rare disorder where the body resists its own hormones. Their 2026 study follows 19 children from 17 families at one center, with diagnoses from 1992 to 2025. Cases split into forms called PHP1A, PHP1B, and a milder relative, sorted by gene and clinical signs tied to the GNAS gene.

Nearly all children in the two main forms resisted parathyroid hormone, with resistance arriving near age 6 in PHP1A and age 11.2 in PHP1B. Thyroid underactivity showed in every PHP1A case and most PHP1B cases. Three children showed a rarer pattern that points to resistance in the brain's own thyroid control path. Half the PHP1A children had intellectual disability, and the same gene change gave varied pictures in different children.
pmc-13454278:
Xiaoli Huang, Tao Xu, and Min Du published a 2026 commentary on a case of liver cancer that had spread to the duodenum and caused severe bleeding. The case, reported by Zhang and colleagues, involved a patient whose tumor had also grown into the portal vein. Treatment combined a procedure to block the bleeding vessel with immune-based drug therapy, and the cancer shrank for a lasting period.

The commentary asks why spread to the gut is so often missed, noting that fewer than one in a hundred cases of liver cancer reach the digestive tract. The authors point to warning signs such as tumor growth in the vein and tumors near the duodenum. They also ask whether long-term survivors with high-risk features need closer checks for rare spread sites, while noting that one case cannot settle how care should change.
pmc-13454478:
Amos J. Nissley and five colleagues identify, in a 2026 study, a family of proteins that park and protect ribosomes in dormant archaeal cells. When food runs short, microbes shut down their protein factories for safety, yet the archaeal version of this hibernation was poorly mapped. The team worked with a methane-making archaeon and named the four proteins SriA through SriD.

All four genes sit together in one cluster, and each protein blocked protein making in test tubes. Cells missing the genes recovered poorly after long rest and lost part of their small ribosome stock. Frozen microscope images showed the proteins binding the ribosome in pairs, sharing neat contact surfaces. The family turns up across many archaeal branches. The authors say these guardians explain how archaea keep ribosomes intact through dormancy.
pmc-13455278:
Modanloo and an Iranian team co-built a program for anxiety in women facing gynecological surgery under spinal anesthesia. They used joint action research at a referral center from 2020 to 2023. Sixteen expert and planning sessions shaped steps aimed at providers, the ward, and patients across three action cycles.

Patient anxiety scored 6.1 on the visual scale before any step in the program's first evaluation round. After the provider-focused cycle it fell to 4.66, after ward changes to 2.86, and after patient-focused work to 2.64, each step statistically significant in paired testing. Early interviews and observations had generated 20 subcategories and six main categories of anxiety sources that the program design targeted. The authors conclude that involving patients and staff in designing the fixes, not just receiving them, drove the stepwise reductions achieved.
pmc-13455778:
Linnea B. Linde-Krieger leads a twelve-author study, from 2026, of the people who staff opioid treatment programs and the toll the work takes. These programs are the only United States settings allowed to dispense methadone, and their counselors absorb clients' trauma stories daily. The team surveyed 44 administrators across 21 states and 83 staff members, with 30 counselors reporting on supervision.

Training about trauma and burnout was widely on offer, and most leaders and staff wanted reflective supervision tailored to their setting. A surprise split appeared in the numbers. Staff with clinical supervision reported lower vicarious trauma and burnout. Staff at sites merely offering training reported more of both. The authors read this as a warning that information alone does not protect workers, while a steady, relational supervisor does. They urge programs to expand supervision first.
pmc-13459278:
Xumao Deng and co-authors built a new heart risk index for middle aged and older Chinese adults by combining a fatty cholesterol measure with blood sugar and belly fat. Standard indices capture how much fat circulates but miss small dense LDL cholesterol, an artery damaging particle type. Their 2026 study followed 3,969 adults aged forty five or older from a national aging cohort, none with cardiovascular disease at the start. It compared candidate indices on how well they forecast new heart disease and stroke.

During follow up, 1,029 participants developed cardiovascular disease. The new sdLG index beat the standard triglyceride glucose index at long term discrimination. Pairing it with a Chinese visceral fat measure, forming sdLG-cVAI, discriminated and reclassified risk best of all. People in the highest quarter of that combined index faced a hazard ratio of 1.77 for new disease versus the lowest quarter. Persistently high readings raised risk further.
pmc-13459678:
Iqbal and colleagues wrote a letter to the editor in 2026 about bias in artificial intelligence tools for Alzheimer's disease. These tools read brain scans and mix them with gene data, blood markers, and behaviour scores. The authors warn that training data lean heavily toward people of European ancestry. 

In one cohort of 1,730 people, the models missed more true cases among Hispanic patients than among non-Hispanic patients. Gaps also appeared for Black and Asian patients when set against White patients. Tools that scored very well inside the main data set scored lower on outside hospital data. The authors call for training sets that include more regions and ethnic groups. They also want routine fairness checks before such tools guide real diagnosis in clinics.
pmc-13461478:
Xu Yang and colleagues traced how a tiny RNA, miR-140-3p, restrains osteosarcoma, the commonest primary bone cancer of the young. The RNA runs low in osteosarcoma cells, and patients with low levels survive more poorly, the team found.

Single-cell data and database survival analyses guided the experiments. Boosting the RNA in dish and mouse tests slowed tumour growth and spread, stalled the cell cycle, and pushed cancer cells to die. Cutting it had the opposite effect, speeding growth and lung spread in mice. The RNA works by silencing a gene called UBE2C, which feeds a growth pathway named PI3K-Akt. Yang proposes this three-part axis as a treatment target for osteosarcoma.
pmc-13462278:
Bouketta and colleagues tested in 2026 whether common farm chemicals can be sprayed together with pest-killing fungi, a pairing that could cut costs in biological control. Two fungal strains that attack the olive fruit fly were challenged with five fungicides and four herbicides. The standard check mixes chemicals into the fungi's growth medium. Field spraying coats the fungal spores directly, so the team compared the standard method with a direct spore-mixture method and with live fly tests.

The methods disagreed. For one fungus, the standard check passed only one of four herbicides, while the direct method passed all four, and fungicide verdicts shifted from toxic to moderately toxic. The direct method's calls matched the live fly results more closely for both fungi, though the second fungus was weaker and less tolerant overall. The authors recommend the direct test as the more realistic gate for mixing fungi into spray programs.
pmc-13462678:
Fabio Pelle and colleagues report, in a 2026 case report with a literature review, a single-stage operation for a 40-year-old woman found to have two cancers at once. She had a thymoma in the chest and HER2-positive breast cancer. Two cancers together usually mean staged operations in separate sessions, which can delay cancer care. A multi-team evaluation planned one combined operation.

Robotic chest surgery removed the thymus tumor first, from the left side, with the specimen taken out below the breastbone to keep breast cuts untouched. Breast removal preserving the nipples, armpit node removal, and reconstruction followed through scar-sparing cuts. The breast cancer showed a complete response in the removed tissue, the chest tumor came out with clean margins, and the cosmetic result pleased the team. The authors frame combined cases as planning challenges, solvable when chest, breast, and reconstruction teams coordinate early.
pmc-13463578:
Xingyu Wang and five co-authors ask whether two amino acids, leucine and valine, can make pork more tender. Amino acids are the building blocks of protein. The group first compared pork of high and low tenderness, then fed the two acids to pigs and checked the meat.

Tender pork held more leucine and valine than tough pork did. Pigs fed both acids gave meat that cut more softly, held a larger share of unsaturated fats, and resisted spoilage by oxidation for longer. Gene reads tied the gains to shifts in fiber type, fat handling, and defense against cell damage. Meat producers gain a feed-based route to softer, sound pork.
pmc-13464278:
Lai, Lee, and Yang comment on a case reported by Gitte and colleagues, where imaging steered rescue of a blocked mechanical heart valve. The patient, a young adult on a weak blood thinner dose, had a stuck artificial mitral valve. The question was what blocked it: a clot, which drugs can dissolve, or pannus, scar tissue drugs cannot remove. Their 2026 piece uses the case to argue that imaging should answer the treatment question, not just confirm the block.

Four dimensional ultrasound from inside the food pipe showed a moving mass and a fixed layer, letting the team judge the clot as the blocker. They chose clot dissolving drugs, and later scans showed the valve leaflets moving freely again while the harmless pannus layer stayed. Lai and coauthors lay out a stepwise plan that pairs standard ultrasound, X-ray motion checks, and the four dimensional view to guide such calls.
pmc-13464378:
Giffin and colleagues studied in 2026 how early amyloid deposits, the protein clumps linked to Alzheimer's disease, change the brain's response to sepsis, a severe body-wide infection. They induced sepsis in young adult mice bred to develop amyloid early, then tested behavior and brain tissue after recovery.

Mice with amyloid showed a generalized fear response and worse performance on a puzzle box problem-solving task after sepsis. Brain gene activity showed inflammation pathways still switched on long after the infection cleared, more strongly in the amyloid mice. Immune cells in the brain called microglia also ate more synapses, the connections between nerve cells, three weeks after infection. The authors argue amyloid acts as a hidden risk factor that amplifies post-sepsis brain harm.
pmc-13465178:
Sinan Mutlu and three co-authors test neck ultrasound measures for spotting hard airways in 713 adults expected to be easy cases. A surprise hard airway, where mask breathing or tube placement fights back, carries the worst harm in anesthesia. Three quick front-neck measures were taken before surgery by a scanner blinded to clinic scores.

Trouble arose in about twenty-eight percent of patients, counting mask, scope, and tube difficulty together. Tongue thickness and skin-to-hyoid distance each linked to trouble on their own strength and sorted cases modestly well. A third measure, membrane length, sorted near chance and added nothing. The useful pair mainly lower the odds of trouble rather than prove it, so the authors frame ultrasound as a helper beside bedside checks.
pmc-13465478:
Zhou and co-authors examined a 2026 food safety study of piperonylpiperazine, a compound from black pepper, against Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a leading meat spoilage bacterium. Heavy preservative use has bred resistant strains, so helpers that weaken the bacterium are wanted. At doses below those needed to stop growth, the compound was tested for anti-virulence action.

The compound strongly suppressed virulence factor production and made the bacteria far more sensitive to EDTA, a common preservative, Zhou found. Binding tests and gene knockouts showed it latches onto RhlI, the enzyme that makes the bacteria's quorum sensing signal molecules. Blocking that chatter cut virulence and weakened the worms used as infection hosts less severely. The disrupted signalling also raised oxidative stress that damaged membranes, explaining the EDTA boost.
pmc-13465678:
Qianyun Nie and colleagues use mice to test whether losing a protective protein called Nrf2 makes methamphetamine brain damage worse, in a 2026 study. The drug harms thinking and kills neurons, yet the exact chain of injury stays unclear and treatments are few. The team exposed lab-grown mouse neurons to the drug and also dosed mice bred without the Nrf2 gene.

Drug exposure raised oxidative stress, disturbed the balance of mitochondrial splitting and fusion proteins, and pushed more neurons toward cell death. Animals and cells lacking Nrf2 showed stronger memory problems and heavier damage than normal ones facing the same dose. Brain tissue from the front cortex and hippocampus carried the same pattern of injury markers.
pmc-13466278:
Sophia Lutz and colleagues check whether blood sugar markers after a diabetes-complicated pregnancy line up with depressive symptoms in new mothers, in a 2026 study. German guidance already advises mood screening after gestational diabetes, yet links to later metabolic readings were unclear. Records came from postpartum checks held six to twelve weeks after birth at one clinic.

Mothers completed the Edinburgh scale, a ten-question screen where scores of ten or more flag possible depression. Readings compared included long-term sugar levels, a glucose drink test, insulin, and a resistance index built from them. Among just over a hundred women screened, the team used rank-based tests and curve analysis to hunt for thresholds that separate higher from lower mood scores.
pmc-13466778:
Aleksandra Stańska, Wojciech Karolak, Jacek Wojarski, and Sławomir Żegleń examine whether substance worries in lung transplant candidates travel with wider psychosocial strain, in a 2026 Polish study. The group covered 491 adults admitted for first transplant evaluation in Gdańsk between late 2021 and late 2025. Every candidate completed the standard psychosocial assessment used in transplant work.

To keep the math honest, the team scored each person's burden using only the sections that do not mention substances. That score was then set against alcohol, nicotine, and drug concerns recorded separately. Transplant teams often treat substance history as a lone flag; the study tests whether it instead marks a broader pattern of vulnerability.
pmc-13466978:
Małgorzata Stachowicz and colleagues study breathing in competitive swimmers, a group with strong lungs yet frequent sinus trouble, in a 2026 analysis. Twenty-nine swimmers, average age about twenty-one, had nose examinations, breathing tests, and nasal airflow measures at rest and right after a hard thirty-second tethered sprint. Twenty also had cone-beam scans scored for sinus mucus load.

Sinus burden and the exercise change in nasal flow did not track each other in a clear statistical way. A component analysis grouped the measures into two bundles explaining about two thirds of the variation, but the bundles did not split neatly into a mucus dimension and a lung reserve dimension. Cluster work probed whether mixed profiles define swimmer subgroups.
pmc-13467078:
Małgorzata Maciejewska and Barbara Gawdzik synthesize porous plastic microspheres from two methacrylate monomers, then chemically modify them, in a 2026 study. One monomer carries a naphthalene unit; the other, a three-armed crosslinker, stiffens the network. Toluene in the mix acted as a pore former during the suspension polymerization.

Surface areas ran high, in the several hundreds of square meters per gram. More crosslinker meant earlier separation during formation, finer pores, and greater area. A Friedel-Crafts style treatment with carbon tetrachloride and a catalyst then altered the structure modestly while keeping the mid-size pore character. The most heavily crosslinked beads survived modification most stably, and heat testing rounded out the profile.
pmc-13467478:
Zeynep Nur Demirok and colleagues examine in 2026 how violence by a partner relates to mental well-being in married women who attend psychiatric clinics. Much earlier work measured distress, while this study also measured positive well-being as its own dimension. The team asked how childhood trauma and self-compassion, meaning kindness toward oneself in hard times, shape that link. In total, 340 women aged 18 to 65 completed questionnaires on all five themes.

Self-compassion accounted for the largest share of differences in well-being, more than violence exposure or childhood trauma alone. Childhood trauma also changed the strength of some pathways between violence and well-being in the team's models. The results suggest that building self-compassion in therapy may protect well-being even when past violence cannot be undone, a practical lead for clinicians treating this group.
pmc-13467578:
Toleu and co-authors report long-term outcomes of advanced stroke procedures in Kazakhstan. Their 2026 retrospective cohort covers 328 adults who received endovascular or stent-based treatment for ischemic stroke in Almaty between 2014 and 2024, spanning thrombectomy, intracranial stenting, and embolisation procedures. Survival, recorded disability, and neurorehabilitation exposure were analysed, a rare dataset from a middle-income health system.

Thirty-nine percent of patients received neurorehabilitation, and their raw survival looked much better: about 94 percent alive at one year against about 77 percent without it. But the advantage vanished after adjustment, suggesting healthier patients were likelier to be referred. The stable mortality predictors were older age and total days spent in hospital beds. Male sex was the only consistent correlate of recorded disability, more than doubling its odds. The authors call for rehabilitation access and evaluation to be built into stroke system planning.
pmc-13468078:
Luo, An, and Luo present in 2026 the second round of a journal set on food based fixes for long term ills. Fat gain, sugar ills, heart ills, and gut ills all trace in part to a fuel system out of tune. The set holds seven fresh studies and one full review. Mouse and human work sits side by side, from gut germs to plant goods.

Three studies chase lost muscle in age: a fuel acid, broccoli born chains, and whey chains for worn out mice. One feeds a gut germ that lifts food uptake in old mice. One swaps in toddler gut germs to calm a raw colon. Plant brews trim sugar spikes in pre sugar ill adults, and a zinc fed germ calms acne. A last review maps diet and nose ill.
pmc-13469178:
Shao and a team in China fed in 2026 urolithin A, a gut made compound from nuts and berries, to rats with a blocked brain vessel. The compound is known to shield cell power plants. Stroke harm runs through rust stress and brain swelling, and few drugs guard the brain past the first hours. The team tied off a mid brain vessel, dosed the compound, and ran gait and maze tests, with brain cuts and gene reads.

Dosed rats moved, felt, and thought far better than plain kin. Their brain dead zones shrank. The compound woke a shield path, Nrf2 and its aide HO-1, which raised the cell's own rust guards and cut a rust scar mark. Swell marks fell in step: three heat signals dropped, and a calm signal rose. Gene reads tied the shield to a curbed alarm switch.
pmc-13469278:
Yu-Ligh Liou, Jin-Wei Miao, and Wichai Termrungruanglert wrote this editorial, published in 2026. It introduces a research collection on new biomarkers. The biomarkers target gynaecological tumours. These are cancers of the cervix, uterus, and ovaries. Such cancers remain major causes of illness and death in women. Ovarian cancer is usually found late. Better early markers are a pressing need.

The editors report strong interest in the collection. It drew 49 submissions from around the world. Nineteen papers were accepted after review. The contributions fall under three themes. Early detection and non-invasive screening form one theme. Cervical cancer screening and triage form another. Further work on diagnosis and therapy forms the third. Liquid biopsy tests are highlighted. These tests read tumour DNA circulating in blood.
pmc-13469378:
Ádám Nagy and co-authors present in 2026 a way to label training images for monitoring breathing in premature babies without hand annotation. Cameras can track breathing in intensive care units, yet software first needs to find the chest or belly region in each frame. Teaching that step usually takes thousands of images labeled by people, which is slow and costly.

Their method looks for body areas that move in a steady rhythm, matching the breathing cycle. Independent experts checked the automatic masks, and agreement on the torso was high, with overlap scores the authors call solid for this task. The labels then trained standard segmentation networks directly. The group argues that automatic labeling can supply the large, clean datasets this field needs.
pmc-13469678:
Jixiao Jiang, Anastasia Feofilova, Ivan Topilin, and Nikita Beskopylny present in 2026 a cleaning and forecasting pipeline for road sensor data used in traffic prediction. Road sensors in budget limited traffic systems produce noisy readings with outliers, which drags down forecast quality. Their pipeline first splits the signal by frequency to strip out unstable noise better than older decomposition tools.

A cleaned signal then feeds a bidirectional recurrent network whose settings are tuned by an improved whale inspired search algorithm. Automatic tuning removes the guesswork of setting parameters by hand. The authors report stronger denoising and better forecasts than rival setups built on common decomposition methods. They frame the full chain, from raw sensor output to prediction, as a workable option for traffic centers with limited computing resources.
pmc-13469878:
Nahar and fellow spine trainees in India set out in 2026 what they learned from their first eight cases of two hole scope surgery for low back ills. The method, short named UBE, works through two small cuts: one for a camera, one for tools. It treats slipped discs and tight spine canals with less harm than open work. Their cases came from a month of fellowship drills at a busy spine hub.

Each one level case took near forty minutes on mid count. No snags hit in or after the work. Back pain scores fell by half by the first day, and leg pain fell near as much. By day seven, both sat at low marks. All eight went home in three days and were back to daily life in a week. The authors call the method safe, cheap in gear, and quick to learn.
pmc-13471278:
Michael Weinbren and Susanne Surman-Lee argue in 2026 that the fight against drug resistant infections is aimed at the wrong target. A decade after a landmark report warned of antimicrobial resistance, resistant infections keep accelerating. Stewardship programs, which police prescribing, have not reversed the trend, and the authors say that is because resistance is treated as a behavior problem when it is mainly an environmental one.

Most of an antibiotic dose can leave the body unchanged and wash into hospital drains. Those drains, loaded with microbes, drug residues, and disinfectants, become highways that breed and spread resistant organisms into city systems. Pollution from drug manufacturing adds a smaller share. Standard precautions, the authors contend, barely guard against threats arriving through wastewater, and policy must follow the drugs into the environment.
pmc-13471378:
Chen and co-authors studied clitocine, a natural compound, as a possible weapon against triple-negative breast cancer, an aggressive subtype that lacks the hormone targets most drugs aim at. Their 2026 laboratory and mouse study traced how the compound attacks tumor cells and reshapes the immune surroundings of the cancer. Such tumors make up about 15% to 20% of all breast cancers.

Clitocine slowed tumor cell growth and spread in two human cell lines and triggered cell death through the mitochondria, the cell's energy centers. It switched on CCRL2, a receptor gene that acts as a tumor suppressor, and patients with low CCRL2 levels tend to survive less long. In mice carrying 4T1 tumors, the compound shrank tumor growth without obvious whole-body toxicity, and it calmed neutrophil-driven inflammation inside the tumors.
pmc-13471578:
Antenucci and colleagues dripped CGRP, the migraine-signaling peptide, onto the brain coverings of mice to see how it switches on pain and emotion circuits. Their 2026 study tested male and female mice three hours after exposure, pairing behavior tests with recordings from the central amygdala, the brain's threat hub.

Face sensitivity appeared only in females: CGRP produced periorbital mechanical allodynia, pain from light touch, selectively in female mice, while paw sensitivity rose in both sexes but more strongly in females. Both sexes also avoided open arms and bright spaces more after CGRP. Recordings showed right-side amygdala neurons grew more excitable in CGRP mice, with the strongest synaptic changes again in females, matching migraine's female bias.
pmc-13472878:
Neil Carleton leads a twenty seven author team modeling in 2026 how aging, hormones, and chronic inflammation conspire to make breast tissue permissive for estrogen driven tumors in older women. Estrogen receptor positive cancer is the commonest breast cancer type and rises with age, yet the aging tissue logic behind it stayed murky. An aged rat model showed age shifted tumor development and immune features, and patient samples filled in the human side.

Older patients blood carried an estrone heavy estrogen pattern, and their tumors raised an enzyme that converts estrone into the stronger estradiol locally. Blocking that enzyme in organoids grown from older women tissue cut both conversion and growth programs. Their tumors also brimmed with a chemokine tied to suppressive macrophages. Hitting hormone and chemokine paths together blunted the macrophage shift in dishes.
pmc-13472978:
Mariah F. Calubag and colleagues report in 2026 that cutting one amino acid, valine, from the diet helped mice stay healthier for longer. Valine is one of three branched-chain amino acids found in protein foods. Mice fed low valine stayed leaner and handled blood sugar better at many ages. Both male and female mice showed less frailty and fewer cancers with age.

Male mice on the low valine diet also lived notably longer at the median point. Gene checks pointed to liver pathways tied to cell power plants working harder in males.
