Readers learn that a single food part, not protein as a whole, may drive many gains seen with low protein diets. The team sees promise for future care aimed at aging.
pmc-13473378:
Debertshaeuser and colleagues tested in 2026 whether brain imaging can be combined with fixed-bike cycling to study exercise and thinking. Nine young healthy adults cycled for twenty minutes at low, mid, and high intensity in a randomised crossover design. Forehead sensors using near-infrared light tracked prefrontal activity during number memory tasks before and after exercise.

The team checked practicality: dropout, timing, sensor reliability, and how well target loads were hit. The two ways of computing blood-oxygen signals agreed closely, showing good data from the moving setup. Memory task performance and brain responses varied with task load as expected. The authors conclude the joint protocol is feasible. They suggest minor design changes and better fitness testing to cut dropout and improve load targeting in future studies.
pmc-13474478:
Rounak Mukherjee, Tripthi P. Shetty, and Padmaraj J. Hegde compare two ways to fix cheekbone fractures in 2026. Breaks of the cheek and jaw joint area are among the most common mid-face injuries. The standard fix opens the site and holds bones with plates, which adds surgical strain. The newer way lifts the bone from inside with a small balloon catheter, plus glue in place of hardware.

Forty-two patients were split evenly between the two methods. The balloon method took far less time in surgery. Scores for ease, stability, and scan results all favored the balloon group. Pain and side issues after surgery were also lower there. A gentler fix may suit many cheek fractures.
pmc-13474978:
Piccolo and colleagues piloted a rural palliative care program for heart failure patients in Maine in 2026, testing whether the model could work at all before any larger trial. A primary care complex care team, trained in comfort-focused care, met weekly with city-based specialists by video for coaching on their cases. Patients joined from one rural clinic, and the team tracked recruitment, completion, and how the experience felt to everyone involved.

Of 31 patients approached, 13 enrolled, and 12 of them, or 92.3 percent, completed every part of the program offered. All 12 finished a serious illness conversation and an advance directive, and 11 also spoke directly with the specialist physician by telehealth. Care team members attended at least 90 percent of the weekly meetings and reported stronger skills and confidence, and patients said the goal-setting talks felt manageable, not overwhelming.
pmc-13475178:
Yutaro Kaneko and co-authors compare two add-on ablation styles in 2026 for persistent atrial fibrillation. Standard vein isolation alone often fails in this lasting form of the rhythm fault. One group got extra burns guided by scattered signal zones, while a past group got burns guided by low-voltage zones. A total of 107 patients were tracked for two years.

Freedom from rhythm return at two years ran higher with signal-guided care, near seventy-six percent versus fifty-eight percent. The signal group also received more extra burns overall. Longer disease duration and larger left heart chamber size predicted return on their own. Signal mapping may refine who gains from extra ablation.
pmc-13475378:
Kanagavel and colleagues report a 2026 case of a giant neurofibroma, a benign nerve sheath tumor, in the abdomen and pelvis of a 29-year-old man. Such tumors in this location are very uncommon, with only about 60 cases reported. He had six months of growing abdominal swelling, frequent urination, and constipation.

Scans showed a large pelvic mass pressing on his rectum and bladder, which had backed urine up into both kidneys. Surgeons removed the mass completely through an open abdominal operation. Tissue testing confirmed a neurofibroma, and his recovery was smooth, with no return of the tumor at six months. The authors stress careful imaging and tissue diagnosis, since these rare masses can mimic other pelvic diseases.
pmc-13476778:
Tanzina Tanu and co-authors find in 2026 that faults in an RNA cleanup factor fuel cancers by freeing ancient viral RNA. The factor, ZC3H18, is cut short by mutations in about thirty percent of cancers. In zebrafish, the cut form sped melanoma onset and raised viral RNA levels. Human tumors and cell lines with the fault showed the same viral RNA rise.

The cut factor gripped viral RNA and moved it out of the nucleus instead of destroying it. Melanoma growth in fish needed that viral RNA to proceed. Human melanoma cells likewise depended on the freed RNA to grow. An old viral echo becomes a drug target.
pmc-13476878:
Mairim Alexandra Solis and co-authors warn in 2026 about unproven stem cell treatments marketed in Panama. Clinics have sold such treatments for over a decade for many diseases without solid proof of safety or benefit. The authors track online marketing and count new businesses entering the market. Harms reported worldwide span clots, tumors, vision loss, and death.

Panama first drew notice in 2013 when a clinic chain moved there from other countries. Ads used celebrity praise in papers, travel magazines, and social media. Weak enforcement let the market grow, the authors argue. Urgent action is urged to protect patients and steer funds to proven care.
pmc-13479578:
Anqi Huang and colleagues present a 2026 feasibility study of a culturally adapted dialectical behavior therapy coaching program for Chinese parents of adolescents with mental disorders. These parents carry heavy distress, and structured caregiver support is scarce in China. Forty-two parents joined a ten-week program of weekly online group sessions plus home practice.

The mixed-methods design tracked numbers at baseline, program end, and three months, alongside parents' own accounts of the experience. Dialectical behavior therapy teaches emotion regulation and relationship skills, and the adaptation reshaped examples and delivery for Chinese family culture. Feasibility questions came first: would parents enroll, stay, and practice? Preliminary effectiveness signals on distress and family functioning were secondary, guiding whether a full trial is justified.
pmc-13479978:
Jin Zhou and coauthors published a 2026 multi-omics study of gestation length in Large White pigs, a trait that directly affects litter size and piglet survival. The dataset was large: 22,783 reproductive records from 9,057 pigs across five populations. Genome scans and a combined meta-analysis searched for DNA regions tied to how long pregnancies last.

New associated regions appeared on four chromosomes. Statistical fine-mapping narrowed the credible causal variants, and studies linking genes to traits and traits to health outcomes added functional evidence, alongside chemical mark profiling of the genome. Two genes, GNAZ and SLC5A4, emerged as critical regulators in the combined analysis. Breeders gain markers for selecting sows whose gestation length supports larger, hardier litters.
pmc-13480078:
Taiqing Luo and colleagues report a 2026 survey of doctors and their plans to work through internet hospitals in China. These online platforms let doctors treat patients at a distance. The team polled 233 doctors at eight public hospitals in Shanghai in late 2022 and modelled how support at work, felt risk, and expected gains shape plans to join.

Good support at work linked directly to stronger plans to use the platforms. Support also worked through two middle paths, by lowering felt risk and by raising expected gains, and those paths chained together as well. Together the indirect paths made up close to forty-five percent of the total effect. Junior doctors leaned more on workplace support, while senior doctors weighed risk more heavily. Hospitals that want uptake should build support systems, show clear gains, and ease risk worries.
pmc-13480678:
Pham and colleagues surveyed neonatal clinicians in 2026 about sending babies with bronchopulmonary dysplasia home on oxygen, the lung disease that ranks as the commonest complication of preterm birth. The anonymous online survey, offered in four languages, drew 610 responses from 44 countries between December 2022 and August 2023. Three quarters of respondents worked in richer countries, and one quarter in low and lower-middle income settings.

Most clinicians, 84 percent, would discharge these infants on home oxygen, but in poorer countries only 65 percent could do so, against 91 percent in richer ones. Clinicians credited home oxygen with better growth and brain development, and home oxygen monitoring was also commoner in richer settings, at 78 versus 67 percent of respondents. Saturation targets and weaning rules varied widely, and over three quarters called wearable monitors with parent-led control important for fixing the gaps.
pmc-13481078:
Sudakou and colleagues worked out in 2026 new maths for diffuse optics, a method that reads tissue by watching how light spreads through it. Time-based versions record how long light takes to cross tissue. Analysts then turn shifts in that timing into shifts in how much light the tissue soaks up or scatters. Standard formulas assume tiny shifts, so large ones break their accuracy.

Sudakou extended the maths from tiny shifts to large ones, in uptake, scattering, and the gap between light source and sensor. Their formulas cover both deep tissue and surface tissue models, with no added guesses. They include a fixed form of a known light law used in steady-light tools. They also tested how wrong starting values skew the results, and how scattering shifts can fake uptake shifts. The work aims to sharpen light-based tissue readings in medicine.
pmc-13482278:
Behrens and colleagues measure how laboratory embryo production alters the earliest tissues of cattle embryos. Their 2026 paper compares day-15 bovine conceptuses made in vitro with counterparts conceived by artificial insemination, examining the embryonic disc, which forms the calf, and the extra-embryonic membranes. Both DNA methylation, a chemical control layer, and gene activity were sequenced, then integrated with machine learning.

In the embryonic disc, one gene set stood out. It covered body segment formation, mesoderm development, and gastrulation. Those genes were enriched among ones over-methylated and switched down in lab-made embryos. In the membranes, the affected genes clustered around epigenetic regulation itself. Effects persisted even though lab embryos spent a week developing inside the mother after transfer. The authors conclude in vitro procedures leave marks on both main lineages before implantation.
pmc-13482578:
Pezeshki and colleagues test a belief-based teaching program in 2026 for a neglected pairing, mouth care in people with type 2 diabetes at the Fasa Diabetes Center in Iran. Diabetes multiplies gum and tooth disease rates, yet oral self-care rarely features in routine diabetes education. The experimental study randomized 220 patients into two equal groups, one receiving six teaching sessions built on the Health Belief Model and one receiving routine care.

Sessions ran 50 to 55 minutes each, mixing group discussion, questions, demonstrations, and printed material on why mouth care matters for diabetes control. Six months later the taught group scored significantly higher than controls on every measure tracked, knowledge, perceived risk, severity, benefits, barriers, confidence, and prompts to act. Their actual oral and dental health behaviors improved significantly too, and the authors recommend weaving belief-based oral health teaching into standard diabetes center programs.
pmc-13483578:
Jia and team traced a chain of brain inflammation that may explain memory loss after severe body-wide infection. Their 2026 mouse study modeled sepsis-associated brain dysfunction, a condition striking most sepsis patients and often leaving lasting cognitive damage. The team focused on microglia, the brain's immune cells, and one of their proteins, the protein-3, in the hippocampus, the region central to forming memories.

Infection signals drove the protein-3 sharply upward, which switched on further immune machinery inside microglia. The resulting stress selectively harmed parvalbumin interneurons, fast-signaling cells that keep brain rhythms coordinated. With those cells damaged, the memory-area rhythms that support memory fell out of sync. Blocking the protein-3 eased the cascade in the experiments described. Jia names the protein a candidate drug target for protecting sepsis survivors' thinking.
pmc-13484478:
Rasheed and team crossed maize lines to learn which genetic patterns help seedlings survive drought, a growing threat to Pakistan's third-largest crop. Their 2026 study grew seven commercial genotypes and their crosses under full watering and half watering, measuring roots, shoots, and leaves at the seedling stage. Stress chemistry, including damage markers and protective enzyme activity, was assayed in parallel.

Genotypes differed strongly on every trait measured, giving breeders real variation to work with. Some traits, like the root-to-shoot length ratio, were governed mainly by additive gene effects, which respond well to straightforward selection. Root length and leaf area leaned on dominant gene effects under drought instead. One genotype, E-322, combined high heritability for key traits with stable drought performance. Rasheed cautions that environment swayed several traits, so multi-site trials must confirm the winners.
pmc-13486478:
Durgadevi and co-authors paired two artificial intelligence methods to keep voltage steady in power grids crowded with solar and wind farms. Renewable output swings with weather, which makes voltage drift and wastes energy as losses. Their 2026 framework uses ant colony optimization, a search method modeled on ant trails, to plan voltage profiles, while a reinforcement-learning controller adjusts reactive power moment by moment.

The combined controller settled on good settings within about 45 to 50 search rounds across the scenarios tested. Voltage stability improved and system losses fell compared with the baseline strategies in their simulations. The learning controller trained on historical and simulated data, so it reacts without waiting for a fresh optimization run. Durgadevi presents the hybrid as a scalable option for grid operators facing rising shares of variable renewable generation.
pmc-13488178:
Shengze He and colleagues measure delirium after shoulder rotator cuff surgery in United States hospital data in a 2026 retrospective study. Delirium is sudden confusion after an operation, and national figures for this common shoulder procedure were lacking. The team used a large inpatient database covering 7,216 patients treated from 2016 to 2019, comparing those coded with delirium against those without on age, other illnesses, complications, stay length, and cost.

Delirium was coded in about seven to eight percent of inpatients, a share the authors call far from trivial. Affected patients were older, sicker, stayed longer, cost more, and suffered more medical and surgical complications during admission. Older age, substance misuse, anemia, and brain or mental disorders raised risk, while elective admission lowered it.
pmc-13490578:
Kollapudi and Singh simulated a switch device-based sensor that detects targets by how they change the electrical behavior of a tiny cavity near the device's passage junction. Label-free sensors skip the dyes and tags of lab assays, promising bedside speed. Their 2026 design uses a gate overlapping the source channel on an insulated silicon platform, modeled with realistic imperfections like uneven probe placement and targets crowding each other.

Response depended strongly on where captured targets sit, peaking when they lodge right at the passage junction. For gelatin samples the device's current response reached a figure on the order of hundreds of millions relative to baseline in the model run. Charged and neutral targets both registered, through varied mixes of the modeled passage mechanisms. Kollapudi presents the asymmetric gate and cavity placement as the keys to the extreme response claimed.
pmc-13491778:
Manlin Yan and three colleagues work in 2026 with a yellow mutant of the green alga Chlorella that barely makes chlorophyll, a trait that could simplify production of the eye-health pigment lutein. Less green pigment means a purer lutein extract at the end of processing. The team grew the original strain and the mutant under three feeding modes and compared pigments and gene activity.

The mutant's chlorophyll a fell to about a ninth of the original strain's level, and its chlorophyll b nearly vanished. The original strain made lutein fastest when fed both light and carbon, while the mutant did best growing on sugar in the dark. Glucose suited the mutant better than acetic acid. Gene comparisons between the strains traced how the two pigment pathways are regulated together.
pmc-13492078:
Alisa Dewald and four colleagues audit in 2026 how many of America's two hundred largest health systems run programs that tackle homelessness among their patients. The year 2024 set a national record for people without housing, and hospitals absorb much of the fallout. The team mined each system's website for mitigation programs and tested which state and system traits predicted having one.

Just over half, fifty-six percent, advertised a homeless mitigation program. Affordable and permanent supportive housing led the list, followed by outreach teams and shelter-based medicine. Systems in states that had expanded Medicaid had more than double the adjusted odds of running a program. Richer shelter capacity in a state also nudged the odds upward. With federal safety-net spending shrinking, the authors expect these programs to matter more.
pmc-13493478:
Filipe R Valeriano leads a ten-author team comparing in 2026 how three Brazilian blackberry varieties withstand a rust fungus that invades their leaves. Blackberry growing supports family farms in Brazil, and the fungus Kuehneola uredinis colonizes the leaf's middle layer, swelling cells before bursting through the surface to release spores. Microscopy and chemical staining compared healthy and infected tissue across the cultivars.

Guarani answered invasion with vigorous tissue expansion, thickening its leaf blade and upper skin. BRS Xavante suffered the worst structural losses, losing nearly half the thickness of its light-catching cell layer. BRS Tupy held its anatomy steadiest, looking the most tolerant. Infected zones everywhere accumulated defensive phenolics, proteins, and oils, although the weakest cultivar made fewer protective oils. Breeders, the authors say, now know which parent stock to favor.
pmc-13493778:
Zhang and a large team examine how neuroticism, the personality trait of reacting strongly to stress and negative feelings, affects visual attention. In their 2026 experiment, 31 young adults scoring high on neuroticism and 31 scoring low searched displays for targets while the researchers recorded brain waves. Those recordings capture tiny voltage changes that reveal each stage of attention, from spotting a target to holding it in short-term memory.

The high group answered less accurately than the low group, despite their brains working harder at several stages. Signals linked to selecting a target and storing it in visual memory ran larger, suggesting extra effort that still fell short of the task's demands. Another signal, tied to noticing new distracting items, was also bigger, which the authors link to trouble letting go of distractions. They read the pattern as inefficient use of attention resources rather than a simple lack of effort.
pmc-13494078:
Eigbefoh-Addeh and colleagues examine whether folate, a B vitamin needed to build DNA, affects sperm quality in healthy men, an angle far less studied than folate in pregnancy. Their 2026 study recruited 197 men aged 18 to 40 in Spain. It measured folate in blood plasma and red cells plus related vitamins, checked gene variants in the folate pathway, and graded semen by World Health Organization criteria.

Outright deficiency was uncommon, affecting only a small share of the men, but gradations mattered. Those in the lowest third for plasma folate had clearly lower sperm counts than those in the highest third, and red-cell folate showed the same pattern. One gene variant, the AA form of a gene called MTHFD1, was likewise tied to worse semen measures. The authors say even sub-deficiency folate levels may quietly undermine male fertility.
pmc-13495078:
Chen and colleagues measured in 2026 how the brain responds to astringency, the dry puckering feel of tannin-rich drinks. They used near-infrared light sensors on the forehead to track blood flow in the front of the brain. Volunteers tasted proanthocyanidin, the compound behind astringency, in water, in ethanol, and in red wine, at several strengths. Responses were split into the tasting phase and the aftertaste phase.

Perceived intensity rose with concentration, but its size and time course differed by drink base. During tasting, frontal blood-flow responses were limited and inconsistent. During aftertaste, responses became broader and stronger across the prefrontal area. Different channels over regions for reward, planning, and control showed distinct drink-related patterns. The authors argue that the lingering feel involves spread-out judging, not a simple readout of intensity.
pmc-13499478:
Chao and colleagues report a 2026 genetics study of follicle density in yellow-feathered broilers, a trait buyers of chilled chicken judge by eye. The team measured leg and back follicle density in 1,382 birds, then combined a genome-wide scan with gene activity data from skin.

Back skin carried clearly denser follicles than leg skin, and the two measures rose together. Denser follicles in both regions went with lower body and carcass weights and less belly fat, a trade-off breeders must manage. Gene activity comparisons named several candidate genes, and the genome scan highlighted SERPINF1 as a regulator of the trait. Knowing the gene behind a cosmetic trait lets breeding programs select for appearance without blindly sacrificing growth, the balance the chilled market demands.
pmc-13501278:
Lindgren and colleagues tested whether patterns of co-occurring gut bacteria can forecast health, in a 2026 study of Finland's FINRISK cohort followed for twenty years. Single species give signals, so the team used a signature approach that splits each person's gut mix into mixtures of co-varying species groups, at levels of ecosystem detail.

Lindgren found signatures that went on to predict mortality and the onset of diabetes, liver disease, and sepsis. The study recovered an earlier reported Escherichia-driven signature of imbalance. It also found new signatures driven by Prevotella subspecies, a genus usually cast as benign, that were linked to poorer future health. The signatures predict outcomes years ahead rather than merely describing current illness. The authors argue that viewing the gut at several levels at once reveals risk structure that single-species views miss. That opens a route to microbiome-based risk screening.
pmc-13501778:
Valeria A Sansone leads a fourteen-author team reporting a 2026 global patient survey, called ENSA, on how myotonia disrupts daily life in myotonic dystrophy. Myotonia, a stiffness where muscles relax too slowly, affects most people with type 1 disease yet blends confusingly with weakness. The anonymized online survey ran across eight major countries with thirty-two questions. In total 386 people aged 18 to 82 completed it; 62 percent were women, and 74 percent reported a genetically confirmed type 1 diagnosis.

Hand and arm myotonia plus upper-body weakness scored worst in type 1, while lower-body weakness dominated in type 2. Leg myotonia scores rose with age in both types. Some respondents blamed myotonia for symptoms clinicians would not link to it, showing patients need help separating the sensations. Most were untreated: 78 percent of type 1 and 69 percent of type 2 respondents took no antimyotonic drug. Treatment rates peaked in Italy, where satisfaction was also highest.
pmc-13502578:
Chia-Min Hsieh leads a thirteen-author team reporting a 2026 study on printing resins whose stiffness can be programmed before the printer runs. The resins are carbon-dioxide-based block copolymers pairing a glassy, crosslinkable block with a soft, non-crosslinkable one. The team varied the block sequence, ABA, BAB, or statistical, and chose curing solvents that swell one block. Photoreology and small-angle X-ray scattering tracked how those choices steered gelation and the nanoscale phase pattern frozen in during curing.

Identical ingredients produced wildly different solids. By adjusting sequence and solvent, the materials ran from brittle to ductile, with toughness spanning three orders of magnitude, from 0.003 to 9.1 megajoules per cubic metre on the reported scale. The lever is accessibility: swelling decides how many photocrosslinkable vinyl groups meet during curing and in what environment. The authors offer sequence and selective solvation as dials for vat photopolymerization design.
pmc-13503778:
Mason L. Hatwan and three colleagues track how daily movement and stress relate to drinking signs among college students, in a 2026 study. Young adults move through many settings each day, and those settings can raise or lower stress and drinking risk. Phone-based daily reports let the team watch both patterns shift together.

The study followed 185 undergraduates, most of them women with a mean age near 18. Each day they logged places visited and stress felt. Stress tended to carry over from one day to the next, while movement did not. Later checks found stress and movement feeding each other across days. Students with higher drinking scores at the start moved more on average, though their stress was no higher.
pmc-13504978:
Al-Jobur and colleagues measured Yemeni adults' dental arches to check whether the ready-made wires orthodontists bend teeth with actually fit local mouths. Forcing teeth into a wider arch than nature built risks instability and gum damage, yet preformed nickel-titanium archwires are sold in standard shapes drawn from other populations. Their 2026 cross-sectional study digitised pretreatment casts from 222 patients aged 16 to 28 and traced twenty-seven commercial wires against the measured widths at canines and first molars.

Ovoid was the commonest natural arch form, and men's arches ran wider than women's across the measurements. Most preformed wires were too wide at the canine level, overshooting the natural upper arch by a few millimetres on average. The lower arch was overshot by even more, with smaller excesses at the molars. No single product matched the sample on every measure.
pmc-13506578:
Cristina Vecchio and colleagues survey, in a 2026 review, how lasting inflammation pushes fatty liver disease toward a more harmful stage. The mild form, called MASLD, involves fat buildup in the liver tied to body weight and blood sugar problems. The advanced form, called MASH, adds liver cell injury, scarring, and a higher risk of liver cancer.

The review traces roles for insulin resistance, harmful fats, cell stress, and gut imbalance in keeping inflammation active. Immune cells and liver support cells turn that signal into scar tissue over time. Treatment choices remain limited for advanced disease. The authors map open questions that new drugs will need to answer.
pmc-13507078:
Adam G Bainbridge and colleagues characterize, in 2026 work, a DNA repair enzyme from Aspergillus fumigatus, a fungus that causes severe lung infections in people with weak immunity. The enzyme, Af-PARP1, adds ADP-ribose tags at DNA damage sites to call in repair help. Its shape and behavior differ from human and plant versions.

A fungus-only part, the BRCT domain, proved central to spotting damage and starting the tag signal. Tree analysis and lab tests set out how the fungal enzyme turns on and what DNA breaks it prefers. Since the fungal pathway diverges from the human one, it may offer a selective target for new antifungal drugs.
pmc-13507178:
Riccardo Lanari and colleagues run 2026 bench models that couple magma pushing upward with rain-driven surface erosion, to probe volcanic risk under a changing climate. Heavier rain is expected as the world warms, and erosion unloads rock above magma chambers. Their box models injected a magma-like fluid at varied rates while artificial rain fell at varied strengths.

Dome height did not simply fall as rain grew stronger. Only under heavy rain did erosion strip the dome top and pile material at its rim, leaving the lowest dome and the most room below. The team suggests that unloading could raise chamber pressure and push the system closer to eruption. Results are early and call for field checks.
pmc-13508278:
Hilda Pena leads a ten-author team studying a widespread parasite in rescued birds of prey near São Paulo, Brazil, in 2026 work. The parasite, Toxoplasma gondii, can infect people and warm-blooded animals alike. Little was known about it in raptors from this busy metro region. The team sampled 151 hawks, falcons, vultures, and owls from two wildlife rehab centers, spanning 19 species. Blood tests checked for antibodies, and mouse tests tried to grow live parasites from bird tissue. Genetic typing then sorted the recovered strains.

About four in ten birds carried antibodies, showing past infection. Hawks and falcons tested positive far more often than owls. Live parasites were recovered from 27 of the mouse tests, across nine bird species. The strain mix showed the wide genetic variety typical of this parasite in Brazil. Rehab centers, the authors note, offer a useful window into infections moving through urban wildlife.
pmc-13508378:
Marta Pérez-Sancho leads a thirteen-author team reporting an unusual outbreak of salmonella disease in captive Iberian wild goats in Spain, in 2026 work. Salmonella commonly strikes farm animals and people through food, yet wild goats were thought poor hosts. This outbreak brought abortions, newborn deaths, and scattered blood infections in adult goats. Lab work pinned the cause on the Enteritidis type, the serovar most often reported in European food-borne cases.

Seven isolates were sequenced and proved almost identical, differing by at most one DNA letter. All carried the same set of 140 virulence genes. Sponge sampling of surfaces hunted the source across enclosures and nearby animals like pigeons, rats, rabbits, and partridges. Salmonella turned up only in the wild goat enclosures, which pointed away from those outside sources. The report gives wildlife managers a rare full picture of a wild goat outbreak with food safety stakes.
pmc-13509378:
Daniel Cernach Ayres leads a fifteen-author team studying small RNA molecules in blood as possible markers for cystinuria, in work published in 2026. Cystinuria is an inherited condition where cystine builds up and forms repeated kidney stones. The group compared sixteen patients with confirmed cystinuria against eleven healthy people with no stone history. They measured eight candidate molecules chosen for their links to genes already tied to the disease.

Four molecules came out lower in patients than in healthy controls. Higher levels of three of them went with a greater number of past stone operations, and higher levels of one also went with weaker kidney function. The authors suggest these molecules reflect how severe the disease is, rather than acting as a simple yes-or-no test, and they call for larger studies to confirm the pattern.
pmc-13511678:
Tobias Jhala and five co-authors gather the published record on a rare eye emergency in children, in a 2026 systematic review. In this emergency, bleeding after injury raises pressure inside the eye socket and threatens sight. Three databases were searched from their start, with later updates, for case reports and series on traumatic cases in children. Care guidance today leans mostly on adult data.

Cases in children most often involved a blood collection under the bone lining of the socket and often followed minor blunt injury. The condition seems to behave differently in children than in adults, in both cause and course. Fast recognition and prompt pressure release may save vision. The authors propose a practical child-focused approach that weighs age-specific injury patterns, giving emergency teams a firmer base than adult rules alone.
pmc-13512278:
Ramírez-Pereira developed a 2026 grounded theory study of life with chronic kidney disease in Chile, where poorer patients face deep health inequality. People on long-term dialysis must rebuild daily life around an irreversible illness and its demanding treatment. Clinical outcomes are well studied, but that rebuilding process is not.

Through qualitative work with patients, Ramírez-Pereira built a theory explaining how reconstruction unfolds over time. The process is held up by a shifting balance between resignation and survival, and helped along by understanding the disease, social support networks, and nursing care. Chances to rebuild depended on supportive social and health conditions, not only personal effort. The author urges policy to fund health education, person centred nursing, steady care, and access to support resources.
pmc-13514978:
Ahmet Mehmet Somuncu and Ahmet Taner Uysal report a 2026 retrospective study of MicroPulse laser trabeculoplasty in eyes that had never received glaucoma treatment. The laser lowers eye pressure with chopped, gentle pulses. The team reviewed seventy patients, one eye each, tracking pressure and detailed corneal cell measures before treatment and at one, three, and six months.

Pressure fell by roughly a fifth at one and three months, a clear early gain, then drifted back near its starting point by six months. The share of eyes holding at least a twenty percent pressure cut collapsed from about three-fifths early on to under five percent at six months. Corneal cell density, cell size, and corneal thickness stayed steady throughout, with all changes inside the measuring device's repeatability limits.
pmc-13515778:
Ionel-Daniel Nati leads a twelve-author team testing urine-based HPV screening in Romania in a 2026 prospective study. Fewer than twenty percent of Romanian women take up cervical screening, and the invasive swab is a named barrier. The team collected paired samples from 230 women aged twenty-five to seventy at three clinics. Each woman gave a clinician-taken cervico-vaginal sample and a first-void urine sample, tested for fourteen high-risk HPV types, with biopsy as the referee.

The two tests agreed substantially, best of all for HPV16 and HPV18 taken singly. For serious cell changes confirmed by biopsy, urine testing caught about eighty-six percent of cases, close to the swab's ninety-two percent, and a negative urine result was nearly as reassuring. Urine positivity climbed steadily with lesion severity.
pmc-13517478:
Hernandez and colleagues exposed human brain vessel cells to indoxyl sulfate, a toxin that builds up when kidneys fail, to test whether it damages the blood-brain barrier. Their 2026 cell study used two toxin levels matching severe kidney disease and measured barrier leakiness, the sealing protein claudin-5, gene activity. Aging-like changes in the cells forming the barrier.

Hernandez found the toxin raised barrier permeability by about half at one and two days without killing the cells, while claudin-5 staining faded. Because no pathway was blocked experimentally, the authors present the links as associations needing inhibitor studies to prove cause.
pmc-13518878:
Julian Buchrieser and a large team finally grow the common cold coronavirus HKU1 reliably in 2026, using gut-derived Caco2 cells engineered to display extra copies of its receptor, TMPRSS2. Entry worked at both temperatures, while RNA copying and particle stability favored the cooler setting. Antiviral interferon defenses also switched on more slowly at 33 degrees. pmc-13518978:

pmc-13520178:
Bekalu Getachew Gebreegziabher and Soressa Abebe Geneti pool Ethiopian studies in 2026 on fetal macrosomia, babies born unusually large, which complicates delivery for mothers and newborns. Single studies disagreed, and no national pooled figure existed. Their review searched six databases plus Google Scholar and graded quality with standard tools.

From 3,670 single births, the pooled rate came to 10.84 percent, ranging by region from 7.41 percent in Amhara to 13.24 percent in Tigray. Studies varied a lot, and figures fell after 2019 compared with before. Five candidate risk factors, including prior macrosomia and male sex, showed no firm pooled link because the figures were too rough. Robustness checks found no single study swaying the result.
pmc-13522378:
Monica E Brown and colleagues offer a 2026 commentary on how to judge whether laboratory-grown gut tissue truly resembles the human intestine and colon. Such miniature tissues, called organoids, can be grown from primary gut tissue or from stem cells. Their use has spread widely since early reports in 2011, raising questions about accuracy across laboratories.

Examples drawn from single-cell RNA sequencing show how targeted and broad comparisons can reveal both matches and gaps. Readers gain guidance on what validation should look like before organoid findings are trusted as models of human gut biology and disease.
pmc-13522478:
Ziwei Le and colleagues trace a brain circuit that supports learning in male mice in a 2026 neuroscience study. Signals from the mediodorsal thalamus, a relay deep in the brain, reach the orbitofrontal cortex, a region involved in judging value. The mice learned an odor task in which one smell called for a response and another did not.

Turning off the thalamic input impaired new learning, while performance stayed intact once the task was well learned. During learning, neurons in both regions sharpened how they represented cue value and outcomes. The input also acted through inhibitory interneurons in the cortex, and blocking those cells weakened the learning-related changes. The circuit thus helps the cortex update value signals while associations form.
pmc-13522578:
Kusumiyati Kusumiyati and colleagues combine light scanning with machine learning to judge mango quality without cutting the fruit in a 2026 study. Near-infrared spectra were collected from one hundred thirty-six intact mangoes and corrected before modeling. Five regression methods, from a traditional linear approach to boosted trees and a neural network, were tuned to predict total acidity and vitamin C content.

Nonlinear models clearly beat the traditional method, with the neural network reaching the highest accuracy on both measures. Performance scores indicated the predictions were strong enough for practical sorting use. The authors present the combined method as a fast, non-destructive option for quality control, supply chain decisions, and breeding programs that need reliable measures of fruit chemistry.
pmc-13523378:
Huihong Shi and collaborators compare magnesium handling in the two founding sugarcane species in a 2026 study. Magnesium is central to chlorophyll and photosynthesis, yet how the two species regulate it was unknown. The transporter gene family for the mineral was listed in both species, activity was tracked across leaf development and daily cycles, and one carrier gene was tested in bacteria and in rice.

The two species responded differently to mineral supply, and their versions of the transporter gene followed distinct expression patterns. Both versions restored mineral uptake in a deficient bacterial strain, confirming shared transport ability. Boosting the wild species version in rice raised growth under low mineral levels and tolerance of excess. Promoter analysis pointed to different control factors in each species, suggesting distinct strategies for mineral balance.
pmc-13523478:
Nur Efşan Aydın and Sedat Çetiner test, in a 2026 animal experiment, whether melatonin or vitamin E helps bone heal after grafting in weakened bone. Healing in osteoporotic bone is a known difficulty in oral and facial surgery. The team created skull defects under induced osteoporotic conditions and filled most of them with a synthetic graft material.

Thirty-five male Wistar rats were split into five groups. One group received no graft, one received graft alone, and the rest received melatonin, vitamin E, or both given systemically. No healing appeared without a graft, while graft alone produced mild to moderate new bone. Melatonin produced pronounced, high-grade formation. Vitamin E gave no clear gain over graft alone, on its own or combined. The authors present melatonin as the more promising support agent.
pmc-13524878:
Angela Yee-Moon Wang leads an international expert group in a 2026 consensus statement on putting nutritional supplementation into practice for patients on dialysis. Guidelines suggest treating protein-energy wasting with oral or tube-delivered nutrition in this group, yet practical implementation guidance was missing. The panel aimed to bridge evidence and daily care across health systems.

The final document carries twenty consensus statements and thirty-four practice points. Themes include screening and regular review for every patient, respect for patient preference in oral support, attention to kidney-specific formulas, and a defined place for nutrition delivered during dialysis when wasting persists.
pmc-13525878:
Muhammad Umar Farooq and others set out, in a 2026 paper, a protocol for rebuilding complex defects at the side of the skull base. The protocol distills over two decades of work at a busy United Kingdom tertiary center. This region packs fine nerves and vessels between the cranium and face, so tumors there challenge both removal and reconstruction.

Care is built around a team spanning ear surgery, neurosurgery, plastic surgery, anesthesia, radiology, oncology, and nursing. Planning, choices during surgery, care around it, and long-term rehabilitation are shown as one pathway. The authors report high complete removal and repair rates with modest harm rates, and they offer the refined protocol as a reference for centers set up the same way.
pmc-13526478:
Baayoud and colleagues report a 2026 case, with a review of past reports, of a 30-year-old man whose bulging left eye revealed IgG4-related disease. He had nine months of painless eye protrusion and eyelid swelling, and scans showed an orbital growth reaching back into the skull.

The biopsy confirmed IgG4-related disease, an immune condition where certain antibody-carrying cells invade and scar tissue. Steroid treatment then gave a good clinical outcome. The authors stress that scans alone cannot separate this condition from tumors or other orbital disease, so tissue testing is essential before choosing treatment for unexplained eye protrusion.
pmc-13527478:
Wu and colleagues present a 2026 case report linking an outbreak of gouty panniculitis, urate crystals inflaming the fat under the skin, with a rare immune disorder. The patient, a 42-year-old Pacific Islander man, developed the skin eruption as idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease began, . A lymph node biopsy confirmed the diagnosis.

He responded well to siltuximab, a drug that blocks the immune signal interleukin-6, a known driver of this disease. The exact link between the two conditions remains unclear. The case adds a visible skin clue to the early picture of a dangerous, hard-to-spot disease.
pmc-13527978:
Yi Gao and four colleagues investigate a gene called FBXW7 in intervertebral disc degeneration, a common cause of back pain. pmc-13528078:
Suprapto and seven colleagues explore how to lift health service quality in Indonesia in a 2026 qualitative study. Transcripts were coded for themes, with peer checks and member feedback for rigor.

Weak internet, low digital skill, and unlinked systems blocked progress. Policies often stalled at facility level under red tape. Community input channels were rare and thin. pmc-13528278:
Gizem Erdem, Nilüfer Kafescioğlu, and Gökçenay Başer put a chatbot therapist on trial in a 2026 study. A model tuned for family therapy methods held a session with a volunteer client. pmc-13529578: Peter and colleagues published a correction in 2026 in the European Stroke Journal to their article on calibrated non-inferiority margins. That method sets fair comparison thresholds in stroke trials when patient populations shift. The correction fixes panel B of Figure 3, whose graph did not match the data in Table 1. It supplies the corrected figure caption describing how prognostic factors were distributed across the historical meta-analysis and the new trial datasets.
pmc-13529778:
Shilin Yin and five colleagues tie a body clock gene to cholesterol making in mouth cancer in a 2026 study. The gene, PER2, runs daily rhythms. It was scarce in oral squamous cancers. pmc-13534378:
Hadi Kooshiar and colleagues review in 2026 how well a balance confidence scale works for adults aged 50 and older living in the community. Five databases were searched through July 2025 under a standard quality framework.

Twenty-two studies covered three scale versions in 11 languages. Consistency and repeat scores were strong, and most validity checks passed. Gaps remained in error measures, cross-cultural checks, and response to change over time, so some versions still need local testing before firm use.
pmc-13534878:
Makena P McLean and colleagues test in 2026 radio frequency tags for tracking human remains during disaster victim identification. All but two tag types stayed readable through decomposition and burial. Tags tended to shift position, so bone attachment is advised for keeping them in place. Handwriting survived best when done dry and shielded from fluids, and two tag types stood out as most useful for field teams.
pmc-13536678:
Maria-Jose Fernandez-Cotarelo and colleagues chart Clostridioides difficile infection in Spanish hospitals from 2016 through 2022 in a 2026 report. Overall, about one in nine patients died in hospital, with the highest share in 2020. pmc-13536778:
Hao Wang and co-authors review how daily body clocks shape tumor immunity in a 2026 synthesis. Proposed responses include timing treatments to the clock and pairing clock-targeted steps with immunotherapy. The authors present clock-aware care as a route to sharper, stronger cancer treatment.
pmc-13536878:
Garoma Desa and colleagues check vaccine protection against peste des petits ruminants in sheep and goats in southern Ethiopia in a 2026 monitoring study. Older animals converted more often than younger ones, and animals without a movement history converted more often than movers. Species, sex, district, and sampling timing showed no clear gaps. The authors judge the campaign effective and recommend tracking animal movement to limit entry of unvaccinated stock.
pmc-13538378:
Zoran Kovacevic and Christoph Stadtfeld study how people recall positive ties inside a student community in a 2026 analysis of repeated surveys with 820 participants. Patterns held steady across people and network types, while shifting within each recall run and as the community matured. The authors present social memory as a structured search shaped by layered social cues.
pmc-13539878:

Specimens are stored in a Brazilian reference collection for future checking.
pmc-13539978:

pmc-13540878:

pmc-13541578:

pmc-13543378:

pmc-13543478:

pmc-13543578:

pmc-13545078:

pmc-13548478:

pmc-13548578:

pmc-13549978:

pmc-13550278:

pmc-13551378:

They examined 350 leave-on and 300 rinse-off products. About a quarter of sunscreens and a fifth of day creams contained at least one alkyl glucoside, while only one of fifty lip salves did. Across leave-on products the share was 16.9 percent in the reported count, giving clinicians local exposure figures.
pmc-13551778:

pmc-13551978:

Just over half the teens fell in the higher addiction group. Addiction severity rose with depression, anxiety, and bullying in simple links. In adjusted models, bullying stayed tied to addiction in both the depression and anxiety models. Depression also held on its own. Anxiety lost its link once bullying entered the model. A check using girls only addressed the skewed sex mix.
pmc-13554278:

Timing, the authors stress, decides success.
pmc-13554778:

Rates were higher for re-narrowed stents than for new disease, at 16.3 percent versus 10.5 percent respectively. pmc-13555878:

Rats with induced joint disease then received the compound, a steroid, or salt water.

Tissue tests showed a whole inflammatory chain turned down, from signal proteins to helper cell drivers. Parts of the cell's alarm assembly were also suppressed. Joint damage markers, though, did not move, so the authors call for more work.
pmc-13558578:
Barış Reşitoğlu and nine colleagues worked in 2026 on squeezing the most medicinal chemistry from a wild mint of eastern Turkey. Mentha longifolia subspecies typhoides is rich in two triterpene acids valued by drug and supplement makers. The team collected seventeen samples from fourteen localities, macerated them in seven solvents of differing strength, and profiled the extracts with two kinds of mass spectrometry.

Alcohol extraction won on overall yield and carried the target acids well, alongside a strong load of rosmarinic acid and other protective plant compounds. The richest chemistry concentrated in leaves and flowers rather than roots or stems. Fine-tuning settled on mild warmth and neutral conditions for the extraction. pmc-13558878:

pmc-13560178:

Participants gave eighty-five factors covering the person, the setting, and what was done.

Reactions warmed when recipients had anticipated the news or when the disclosure mentioned a same-sex relationship. Machine learning caught tangled links among factors with fair hit rates. pmc-13560578:

This system records biometric border crossings. The App4EES project tested the app in real operations. The site was Stockholm Arlanda Airport. Users had a positive experience. The design was intuitive. Travellers finished pre-registration easily. This supports wider rollout of such pre-registration tools.
pmc-13562078:

Online forms fed both scale-level and symptom-level network models.

Shared decision making linked strongly to decisional conflict, while incontinence strain tied in a middling way to workout habits and weakly to mood. Inside the depression network, thoughts of self-harm and low energy were the most central symptoms. Hard-to-control worry anchored the anxiety side. pmc-13562678:

Their 2026 algorithm, ED-CHSS, scores each candidate on leftover energy, communication cost, and a trust index fed by past behaviour. Lightweight encryption then guards traffic inside each cluster.

Election odds also adapt to local node density and link steadiness. The authors pitch the design for mission-critical sensing where battery life and honest relays both matter.
pmc-13563778:

Their 2026 study followed 10,860 adults at Fresenius clinics who began the drug between 2016 and 2022, comparing the three months before starting with a year after. Most took the lowest dose once daily, and dose changes were rare.

Use of the lowest-potassium dialysis fluid fell away as the drug took over. Hospital visits dipped for all causes and more for potassium crises. With no comparison group, the authors read the hospital trend cautiously, while calling the potassium control solid.
pmc-13563878:
Khushboo Yadav and three colleagues publish the complete genome of a bacterium that lives inside a medicinal plant and makes compounds able to kill priority drug-resistant germs. Its chemistry hinted at rich biosynthetic machinery. Their 2026 data report sequences that machinery end to end, so the genes behind the effects can be found and mined.

Mining software flagged 39 biosynthetic gene clusters, spanning non-ribosomal peptide makers, polyketide assembly lines, terpenes, and melanin pathways. Those clusters line up with the compound families earlier chemical profiling had detected. The authors present the sequence as a working map for turning a plant-dwelling microbe's hidden chemistry into candidate medicines.
pmc-13570978:
Keren Gueta and Carmit Klar-Chalamish study, in a 2026 online qualitative survey, how the October 7 war affected Israeli survivors of earlier sexual violence. In these lives, collective war trauma lands on top of personal trauma. One hundred twenty-six survivors described their mental and physical state, what made things worse, and how they coped.

Many described reliving the earlier trauma, with worsened post-traumatic symptoms and disruption to sleep, eating, and relationships. Feeling pushed to the bottom of social priorities deepened the harm, while some participants named protective resources and offered advice for health services during wartime. The exploratory account warns responders that war planning must include people carrying earlier sexual trauma.
pmc-13571378:
Chhayroud Heng and colleagues describe, in a 2026 multicenter Asian case series, five patients whose fast heart rhythms ran through nodoventricular accessory pathways. These are rare leftover connections between the heart's relay node and its lower chamber. Careful stimulation tests proved the ventricle took part in each circuit while the atrium did not.

Two patients also had Ebstein anomaly, a malformed tricuspid valve, supporting a developmental link the authors explain through displaced valve and node anatomy. Ablation targets differed widely by patient, succeeding at several distinct sites guided by tiny pathway signals. The series warns electrophysiologists to map the exact signal rather than burn a standard region.
pmc-13572178:
Mengxin Hu and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether tiny RNAs from two medicinal herbs can fight duck viral hepatitis across the species barrier. Such cross-kingdom effects are proposed for plant molecules in herbal decoctions. Sequencing found fourteen abundant candidate RNAs, which were synthesized and screened in duck embryo liver cells for protection against the hepatitis virus.

Both stayed stable under heat, cut virus replication, cell death, and oxidative damage in dishes, and improved survival when fed to infected ducklings, with calmer liver enzymes and less liver damage. One mainly curbed cell death while the other mainly curbed inflammation. The pair gives herbal medicine a concrete molecular story to test further.
pmc-13572378:
Bavani Gunasegaran, with three colleagues, reports a 2026 study that hunts for virus proteins inside glioblastoma, a fast and deadly brain tumour. Whether viruses play a role in this cancer has long been unclear. Tests in past work gave mixed results, in part due to the limits of each tool.

The team ran a protein-wide scan on tumour and control tissue from a public data set of 192 samples. A second group of 81 samples served as a check. Virus proteins from many species turned up, and human herpesviruses 1, 2, and 8 showed up more often in tumours than in controls. Host proteins tied to gene control, RNA handling, and energy use in cells also shifted. Links between virus and host proteins hint at paths for later work.
pmc-13572478:
Adrianna Wielgopolan, with two colleagues, reports a 2026 investigation of how mixed-feeling words affect a memory task. Most words feel clearly good or bad, yet some feel both at once. The team asked whether that mix, and mixes on two other scales, change how people hold letters in mind and where their eyes rest.

Two experiments used the N-back task, where people flag when a letter matches one seen steps back. Words mixed on good-bad tone or on how the feeling arises helped accuracy, while mixes on arousal did not. Eye tracking showed more and longer fixations for all mixed word groups than for clear words. The results suggest mixed feelings reach beyond tone alone and shape both thought and gaze. The work adds origin as a scale that matters.
pmc-13573378:
Sijia Huang, with six colleagues, presents a 2026 wound patch that treats infection and shows its own drug release by colour. Infected wounds heal slowly, with lasting swelling and weak new vessel growth, and carers cannot see how much drug a dressing has left. The patch answers with microneedles made of a crystal gel.

Near-infrared light heats copper sulfide particles in the needles, which kills germs and frees a second drug load on demand. That load pairs tannic acid with berberine for germ killing and damage control. The crystal structure shifts colour as drug leaves, so staff can read release by eye. Lab tests killed over 95 percent of two common bacteria and mopped up reactive damage near fully. In infected rats, the lit patch closed wounds to 94 percent by day ten.
pmc-13573478:
Yuko Tsurumi, with six colleagues, reports a 2026 case where an ultrasound probe inside a neck artery caught a problem the X-ray missed. Stenting a narrowed carotid artery can leave plaque or clot poking through the stent, a source of stroke during the procedure. Dye-based angiography is the standard final check, yet it can overlook such pokes.

The patient was a 92-year-old Japanese man with two tight spots in his right carotid artery. After stenting under balloon protection, the dye check looked clean. The ultrasound probe, though, showed a marked poke inside the far stent. A second overlapping stent, placed at once under renewed blockage, flattened the poke on a repeat probe check. The man recovered well and went home on day four. The authors back probe checks to guide rescue.
pmc-13574278:
Mackenzie Fernandez, with five colleagues, presents a 2026 lab protocol that clears mouse rib bone for imaging while keeping fluorescent tags bright. Clearing turns tissue transparent so whole organs can be viewed without slicing. Bone and cartilage resist most recipes, and harsh ones dim the glow that genetic tags provide.

The method adapts a water-based clearing family, Scale CUBIC, for adult rib bone and needs no decalcification step. Transparency arrives in about 48 hours. In transgenic mice bred to glow in set cells, both the glow and the tissue's natural shape survived the bath. Growth plate and repair zones in the rib stayed readable. The authors offer the recipe as a dependable route for hard tissue imaging in mouse models.
pmc-13576578:
Evy Á Lakjuni Guttesen, Hugin Reistrup, Anders Gram-Hanssen, Jacob Rosenberg and Jason Joe Baker published this 2026 nationwide Danish study on how badly reoperation statistics understate hernia recurrence. After ventral hernia repair, studies often count only patients who return for another operation as recurrences. The authors instead linked national registers with an electronic survey of patients who had primary ventral or incisional hernia repair between 2014 and 2024, counting self-reported recurrences too.

The study included 20,703 patients with a median follow-up of 5.5 years and an 80 percent survey response rate. After primary ventral repair, total recurrence was 15.5 percent, yet only 3.3 percent had been reoperated, a roughly fivefold underestimate. After incisional repair, recurrence reached 27.2 percent against 7.0 percent reoperations, about a fourfold gap. The authors conclude that reoperation alone badly biases studies of repair success, and that patient-reported recurrence deserves a place in outcome measurement.
pmc-13579878:
Belinda Garth and colleagues set out a national plan to move women into healthcare leadership in Australia, in a 2026 protocol paper. Women form over seventy percent of the health workforce yet hold a small share of top posts, a gap that drags on care quality. Past fixes mostly coached single women, leaving the systems that block them untouched. This plan targets rules, culture, and structures across hospitals, colleges, and agencies at once.

The mixed methods design pairs records and policy reviews with interviews and surveys, all built with the people who must live with the changes. Set frameworks guide rollout and judge reach, uptake, and staying power. Findings will feed a shared toolkit, refined in learning cycles. No results are claimed yet; the paper's value is the blueprint and its built in checks.
pmc-13580678:

Their 2026 laboratory study used red cells from healthy volunteers and tested for eryptosis, the programmed death of red blood cells that can contribute to anemia during chemotherapy.

Alajeyan found that solasodine triggered modest red cell rupture alongside clear death signals, including surface changes that flag cells for removal, cell swelling, and spiky cell shapes. Supplying energy fuels such as ATP reversed much of the damage, as did removing calcium from the fluid around the cells. Several targeted blockers also protected the cells, and the death process needed three signaling proteins working together. The results warn that solasodine's cell-killing power is not cancer-specific and suggest protective add-ons for future drug development.
pmc-13584478:
Zhijie Pan and colleagues weigh the cost of waiting for hip fracture surgery in older patients in this 2026 study. The breaks at issue sit between the neck and shaft of the thigh bone and are usually fixed with screws and plates. Working from a United States hospital database covering 2002 to 2014, the team sorted more than 228,000 patients by wait time. The wait groups were within a day, one to two days, or three to seven days.

Waits brought longer stays, higher bills, and more complications after surgery. A short delay of a day or two showed no clear link with death in hospital once other factors were counted. A longer delay, though, raised the death rate clearly. The authors urge hospitals to ready these patients fast and aim for early surgery where it is safe.
pmc-13584578:
Zhiyong Zhang, Ming Ye, and Lin Zhang pool trial results on music therapy for young people's mental health in this 2026 review. Music therapy uses guided musical activity with a trained therapist, and earlier single studies hinted it might ease low mood and worry. The team searched seven sources for randomized trials in children and teens aged 6 to 18, with programs lasting at least four weeks.

Nine trials with 690 young people fit the rules. Music therapy cut depression scores by a clear margin against comparison groups and lifted both self-esteem and quality of life. Worry eased too, though only two trials measured it. Longer and more frequent sessions, and younger children, seemed to gain most, but the authors treat those patterns as early hints because the trial count is small.
pmc-13587278:
Xueqiang Wei and colleagues report a near-fatal bleed forty days after lung cancer surgery in this 2026 case paper. A 53-year-old man had his right upper lung lobe removed, and the cut airway stump sat close to the main lung artery, as it often does after this operation. He arrived coughing up large amounts of blood without warning.

A first attempt to plug the bleeding vessel through a catheter failed. Emergency surgery found a tiny hole in the lung artery wall and a small channel at the airway stump, worn through, the team believes, by steady rubbing between the two. Surgeons patched the artery with heart-sac tissue and wrapped both repairs in a muscle flap taken from between the ribs. The man recovered smoothly and was well three months later. The authors warn that stump-to-artery friction deserves a place on the danger list.
pmc-13591278:

The team irradiated mice, rebuilt their blood systems with marked donor marrow, and tracked whose plasma cells remained weeks later. A second setup used mice whose plasma cells carry time stamps.

Counts bounced back within four weeks, yet a solid share of plasma cells still came from the irradiated host at eight weeks. Many were newly made by host B cells that had survived. When donor B cells were scarce, host cells made even more. Webster and the team read this as proof of a hardy, long lived pool plus rivalry for space.
pmc-13591878:
Ningqi Zhu and six colleagues hunt, in 2026, the genes switched on by a mutant driver of liver cancer. The driver, CTNNB1, locks a growth pathway in the on position in roughly a third of these cancers. The team built mouse liver tumors with the mutant gene, read their gene activity, and merged the results with human tumor data from two large banks. pmc-13592478:

Registry data from Spanish centers covered 166 patients who had started the drug at least a year before records closed. Most patients stayed on the drug, rescue medicine use fell, and carers reported gains in thinking for many. pmc-13593678:

pmc-13594978:

They urged personalised recovery care, including high-protein diets and careful handling of the patient's other medicines. The group also backed a whole-person view covering nutrition, mental health, and patient expectations.
pmc-13595678:

The horizon is three decades. The authors conclude that preventing recurrences with these drugs pays back a large share of its price to society at large.
pmc-13602678:

pmc-13612378:

pmc-13612878:

That loss stood for 3.1 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalents, 9,250 euros in buying costs, plus 93 kilos of protein and 29 kilos of fibre thrown away. The hot kitchen, trolley returns, and crew meals produced the largest share, while animal foods drove most of the climate cost.
pmc-13614178:

The starting copper complex could capture carbon dioxide but broke down under electric conditions.

That change steadied the fragile copper form and let electrons flow back and forth cleanly. Adding a ring-shaped piece improved the design further. pmc-13618378:

Their patient, a seventy-three-year-old man with diabetes, developed progressive weakness in all four limbs with neck and back pain, spastic paralysis, and loss of position and vibration sense.

Cord decompression was planned, but the patient died before the operation could happen. pmc-13619078:

pmc-13619678:

The authors judge the fungus a contributor to decline rather than a lone killer, and they recommend extra watering in drought plus steady health checks.
pmc-13623378:

pmc-13626978:

Both retrievals succeeded without surgery. A prepared second catheter, the authors suggest, can turn a looming fracture into a controlled exit, and interventionists should rehearse the move before they need it.
pmc-13628978:

The authors blame the low variety on recent splitting plus clonal persistence.
pmc-13629278:

The aids mirrored the barriers. Mentors and training helped. So did unit-level backing and bold leadership. The authors build a framework across levels. They recommend paid release time. They also urge easy access to librarian and statistics help, plus funding routes. Research-active nursing, they argue, underpins safer, better care.
pmc-13631278:

Bulk measures hide how uneven that conversation is.

Added signal raised the volume without evening things out. Cells responded to their own peptide by preference. They shared less with neighbours producing none. The authors suggest this patchiness, amplified by self-signalling, may itself be a survival strategy.
pmc-13632078:

pmc-13632678:
